The key idea is to introduce an auxiliary vector field, termed the \emph{vorticity-diffusion potential}, which recasts the viscous Laplacian diffusion term as a Lie-bracket advection term. On solutions of the defining equation for this potential, the viscous vorticity equation takes the form of a pure Lie-transport equation along a modified divergence-free velocity field, while the defining constraint itself is encoded as the curl-free compatibility condition for an auxiliary scalar potential. We further show that the reduction of this three-dimensional system to two spatial dimensions yields a Lax representation for the two-dimensional Navier--Stokes vorticity equation, which we generalize to a family parametrized by an arbitrary smooth function of one variable.

title: Critical Growth for Stochastic Adaptive Stabilization with an Unknown Input Gain
authors: Zhaobo Liu
abstract: This paper studies adaptive stabilization of a class of scalar discrete-time nonlinear systems with unknown drift coefficients and an unknown nonzero input gain. Under iid Gaussian noise, we establish a necessary and sufficient polynomial criterion for global stabilizability, characterizing the admissible combinations of growth exponents. When the criterion holds, we construct a feedback combining finite calibration with adaptive control. The time average of the squared output converges almost surely to the noise variance, attaining the smallest possible value. If the criterion fails, then for every Borel causal feedback there exist fixed parameter values and an initial state for which the output magnitude diverges with positive probability.

title: Honeypots for AI Agent Insider Threats
authors: Jan Wehner, Jam Kraprayoon
abstract: AI agents deployed inside organizations can pose an insider threat if they make mistakes, are compromised by an attacker, or pursue misaligned objectives. We propose honeypots as an AI control method to improve the security of internal agent deployments. Rather than only using honeypots for pre-deployment evaluations, defenders should plant decoy opportunities for harmful actions throughout the production environment to detect misbehavior, incriminate malicious agents, and deter attacks. Such honeypots can elicit misbehavior under real deployment conditions, identify malicious agents even if chain-of-thought monitorability degrades, provide reliable warnings about agent misbehavior to security teams, and scale cheaply to many agent instances. The presence of honeypots also introduces uncertainty about which opportunities are real, thus deterring malicious agents from attacking and reducing the rate of misbehavior. We discuss the limitations of honeypots and give reasons to expect them to remain effective as agent capabilities increase. Finally, we outline key research questions to measure and improve the effectiveness of honeypots: testing the robustness of honeypots, comparing their detection effectiveness with other monitoring methods, understanding their incrimination and deterrence effects, and building supporting infrastructure.

title: Dynamic clustering of active chemotactic Janus particles
authors: Joël Mabillard, Frédéric van Wijland, Jean-Baptiste Fournier
abstract: Modeling self-propulsion as an emergent diffusiophoretic effect, we come back to the dynamic clustering experiment of active Janus colloids. Working in the original three-dimensional geometry, and using the chemical solute concentration as a control parameter, we find that the dynamic clustering region occupies a robust fraction of the phase diagram. This behavior is rationalized using a linear stability analysis that efficiently captures the instability of the gas phase to dynamic clusters. We also find that dynamic clustering results from the combined effects of a Keller-Segel collapse and of a motility-induced phase separation, either being arrested by the orientational coupling to the chemical field in agreement with previous work.

title: Direct Sample-Average Learning for Queueing Control: Gradient-Free Top-$K$ Coarse-to-Fine Optimization
authors: Mehrdad Nozohour Yazdi, Yiqiang Q. Zhao
abstract: We study steady-state queueing control when decisions must be learned from a single persistent operating trajectory: only the implemented action produces data, and the queue is not reset when the action changes. Fixed-event-count cycles yield a direct ratio-of-totals sample-average approximation (SAA) of each action's steady-state cost rate. A Top-K coarse-to-fine search ranks these estimates, retains several promising refinement paths, and concentrates later operation on finer candidate sets, without requiring gradients, convexity, or differentiability. We decompose direct-SAA error into accumulated conditional transient bias and martingale fluctuation. For regenerative queues, a bias-function representation reduces transient effects within contiguous action blocks to boundary terms. Finite-sample stagewise bounds then link estimation accuracy to master-grid identification through guardian retention, and the required queueing and sampling conditions are verified for a persistent-workload M/M/1 implementation. At a common active set, Top-K has a weakly larger guardian margin than Top-1, and an exact-objective example shows Top-1 can discard the optimal refinement branch. Numerical experiments delineate scope rather than universal dominance: Top-K improves terminal identification in the reported LiQUAR and mixed staffing comparisons, while LiQUAR can have lower cumulative learning cost, and GOLiQ is markedly stronger on a smooth benchmark with reliable queueing sensitivities. Direct ranking is therefore best viewed as a complementary method when model-specific gradients are unavailable, inconvenient, or poorly matched to the decision space.

title: Resolving the Thermal Labyrinth inside 3D-IC Stacks
authors: Xufei Guo, Yiyun He, Zirou Chen, Zifeng Huang, Runsheng Wang, Zhe Cheng
abstract: The heat pathways in 3D-ICs have long been a labyrinth lacking experimental investigations into spatial distribution of thermal properties, severely limiting study of internal thermal management inside chips. For the first time, we established a methodology for 3D thermal characterizations of advanced 3D-ICs, implemented through a systematic workflow that enables layer-resolved thermal property extraction and the construction of a location-specific thermal database. We demonstrated its application to an advanced sample featuring 2.2-μm-diameter TSVs and ~2-μm-pitch face-to-face hybrid bonding (HB). Time-domain and steady-state thermoreflectance were used to extract the thermal conductivities (TCs) of Al traces, TSV, BEOL interconnects and HB pads, indicating HB structure enables efficient thermal transport with 9 W/m-K TC. Further, we mapped and visualized the TC distribution of TSV structures and RDL Cu wires with small step sizes down to 0.2 μm. Utilizing these results, we proposed an experiment-based thermal model to reveal that co-evolution of interconnect and substrate TCs is essential for thermal design and fabrication towards effective cooling optimization.

title: Rigidity of algebraic sets with small distortion
authors: Alexandre Fernandes, Edson Sampaio
abstract: We prove that for positive integers $k$, $n$, and $d>1$, there is a maximal $c(k,n,d)>1$ such that if $X \subset \mathbb{C}^n$ is a connected $k$-dimensional complex algebraic set with degree at most $d$ and $dist(X) < c(k,n,d)$, then $X$ must be a complex affine linear subspace, where $dist(X)$ denotes the distortion of $X$ and is given by the supremum of the ratios $d_{inner}(p, q)/d_{outer}(p, q)$ for all $p,q\in X$ with $p\not= q$. We also prove that $c(1,n,d)=\sqrt{2}$ for any positive integers $k$ and $n$. This result provides a sharp rigidity phenomenon for curves in the $c$-LNE category, showing that near-isometric behavior of the inner and outer metrics forces the curve to be as simple as possible.

title: CAOS-SLAM: Class-Agnostic Object-Aware Real-Time vSLAM for Dynamic Environments
authors: Gaia Borghi, João Carlos Virgolino Soares, Angelo Bratta, Shahab Heshmati-Alamdari, Claudio Semini
abstract: Robust visual Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (vSLAM) in dynamic environments faces challenges due to the presence of moving objects that may introduce erroneous observations, corrupt the map reconstruction and overall degrade localization accuracy. Existing vSLAM approaches often rely on predefined semantic classes or costly pixel-wise classification, limiting their robustness or applicability in real-world scenarios. This paper presents CAOS-SLAM, a dynamic vSLAM framework that extends ORB-SLAM3 with a hybrid perception pipeline to detect, track, and filter both semantically known and previously unseen moving objects in real-time. On-demand panoptic segmentation is performed for object discovery, with candidate unknown objects instantiated through depth-based clustering of unclassified regions. Between panoptic updates, persistent object tracks are updated using lightweight detection when available or temporal mask propagation based on world-frame Kalman prediction, depth consistency, and appearance similarity. The estimated object motion is then used to reject dynamic features from the SLAM pipeline. Experimental results on multiple dynamic RGB-D datasets and real-world experiments demonstrate improved localization accuracy over state-of-the-art dynamic vSLAM approaches, achieving up to 59% lower localization error in scenes characterized by unknown dynamic objects and up to 88% lower error in heavily occluded scenes, while achieving a median processing rate of 30 FPS on a laptop. Furthermore, the tracking module provides estimates of object trajectories and velocities, supporting potential future applications in perception, navigation, and motion-planning tasks in dynamic environments. Code and dataset will be released upon acceptance.

title: From TCP/IP to MCP: Security and Governance Lessons from Internet Protocols for Agentic AI
authors: Ben Bucknall, Andrew Byrley, Lewis Hammond
abstract: The past two years have seen considerable interest in protocols for managing how AI agents interact with human users, external tools, and each other. In many ways, these protocols, including the Model Context Protocol (MCP) and Agent2Agent (A2A), mirror the suite of protocols that underlie the modern internet. Motivated by this parallel, this paper draws lessons from the development, history, and governance of internet protocols with the aim of informing the responsible development of AI agent protocols. Based on our analysis, we make two conclusions. First, if AI agent protocols do not sufficiently prioritise security in the early stages of development, they risk accumulating a security deficit that becomes increasingly costly to address over time due to practical and economic challenges. Second, current governance structures for AI agent protocols centralise decision-making power in a small number of individuals and companies, raising important questions regarding legitimacy, especially if they become critical digital infrastructure. We conclude with a discussion and implications for policymakers and developers of AI agent protocols.

title: On the denominators of signed harmonic sums
authors: Quan-Hui Yang
abstract: Let $\eps=(\eps_i)_{i\ge1}$ be a sequence with $\eps_i\in\{-1,1\}$, and let $v_n(\eps)$ be the positive denominator of $\sum_{i=1}^n\eps_i/i$ in lowest terms. We prove that $|\{1\le n\le x:v_n(\eps)\ne v_{n+1}(\eps)\}|=o(x)$ uniformly in $\eps$. In particular, the set of positive integers $n$ with $v_n(\eps)=v_{n+1}(\eps)$ has asymptotic density one for every sequence of signs. This answers a problem of Wu and Chen, \emph{J. Number Theory} \textbf{200} (2019), 397--406.

title: Global Time-Aware Conditioning (GTC): A Mechanism for Time-Aware Pediatric Sleep Representation Learning
authors: Saurav Raj Pandey, Harlin Lee
abstract: Sleep physiology evolves throughout the night, with changes in sleep cycles, respiratory stability, and cardiovascular dynamics. However, self-supervised learning (SSL) methods for sleep typically process short, fixed-duration windows without explicitly modeling where each window occurs within the full sleep session. We introduce Global Time-Aware Conditioning (GTC), a mechanism that complements local positional encodings by conditioning latent representations on the global time-of-sleep of each input window. We integrate GTC into three representative SSL frameworks and evaluate them on five clinically relevant tasks with extreme class imbalance across two independent pediatric cohorts. GTC generally improves F1 and AUPRC across architectures and tasks, with gains persisting under cross-cohort transfer, highlighting the value of global temporal context for sleep representation learning.

title: Statistical decision theory in thermodynamics
authors: Yoshihiko Hasegawa
abstract: We introduce statistical decision theory in stochastic thermodynamic systems. Statistical decision theory integrates several statistical tasks, such as estimation, hypothesis testing, and classification. In this study, we consider statistical decision theory in stochastic thermodynamics, which unifies sensing, classification, and uncertainty relations. In particular, we focus on the minimax risk, the smallest achievable expected loss under the worst-case parameter choice, even with an optimal estimator. We derive lower bounds on the minimax risk using Le Cam's two-point method. The derived relationships can be used across a broader range of thermodynamic scenarios. To illustrate these relations, we study classification and distribution estimation problems in a Markov process. We demonstrate that the minimax risk provides lower bounds given by the dynamical activity in these problems. Furthermore, by examining particular dynamics, we establish that the resulting bounds simplify to uncertainty relations involving dynamical activity or entropy production.

title: Bootstrap percolation on the hypercube
authors: Fengxing Zhu
abstract: In this paper we obtain the critical probability $p_c(Q_{n},r)$ for bootstrap percolation with the infection threshold $r=f(n)n^a$ on the $n$-dimensional hypercube $Q_{n}$, where $0<a<1$ and $f(n)=n^{o(1)}$. More precisely, we obtain the exact first-order and second-order terms of $p_c(Q_{n},r)$ by extending the main theorem of Balogh, Bollob{á}s, and Morris (2009).

title: Conducting Reliable Keyword Estimation with Unreliable ASR in Police Audio Data
authors: Robert Cole Molloy, Rhiannon N. Miller, Stephen Morgan, Anjalie Field
abstract: Extracting insights from large audio data sets using human transcription is expensive and time-consuming. Off-the-shelf Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) systems offer an easy-to-use scalable alternative, but systematic transcription errors, especially in domain-specific settings, can bias downstream analyses and lead to unreliable conclusions. We investigate whether imperfect ASR transcripts can still be used to obtain statistically valid keyword frequency estimates by combining model outputs with a small set of human-labeled examples, following Prediction Powered Inference and Design-based Supervised Learning frameworks. We evaluate this approach on police radio communications from Baltimore and Chicago, a domain in which keyword distributions could provide valuable insights into police activity, but off-the-shelf ASR systems exhibit systematic errors on operationally important terminology. Using bootstrap-based confidence interval coverage as our evaluation metric, we find that our approach substantially increases the number of domain-specific keywords that can be analyzed with statistically valid confidence intervals, from 43.0% using ASR alone and 27.2% using only a small set of human-labeled transcriptions to 56.2% in the Baltimore dataset, with similar improvements observed in Chicago data. Our results demonstrate that post-hoc error correction can improve statistical validity of downstream analyses even for poor-quality transcriptions, offering an avenue for better leveraging off-the-shelf ASR models for large-scale speech analysis.

title: The two-step spectral locus of the octonionic structure operator
authors: Sergey Grigorian
abstract: We continue the study of the octonionic spectrum of the octonionic structure operator $h$ on $W=\mathbb O\otimes_{\mathbb R}V$, where $V$ is the seven-dimensional representation of $G_2$. The real spectrum and the octonionic one-step spectrum, given by the equation $h(w)=wλ$ for real or octonion $λ$, have been determined in earlier work. In this paper, we study the two-step equation $h(w)=(wλ_1)λ_2$. Due to non-associativity, this does not in general reduce to the one-step problem. An adapted quaternionic frame represents successive right multiplication by an operator with four real coefficients. The $SU(2)$ subgroup fixing the frame splits $W$ into invariant sectors of dimensions $16$, $12$ and $28$. We factor the determinant of the resulting 4-parameter operator pencil and characterize the pairs for which a nonzero solution exists. The singular locus of this pencil in $\mathbb R^4$ is the union of an explicit algebraic set and a round $3$-sphere. The $12$-dimensional sector carries the one-step problem at the reversed product $λ_2λ_1$. The $28$-dimensional sector contributes no additional real singular points; the fixed sector produces solutions even when neither product lies in the one-step right spectrum.

title: CQTwin: A Digital-Twin Toolkit for Operational Analytics of HPC Schedulers
authors: Kanglin Xu, Yash Kurkure, Yihe Zhang, Michael E. Papka, Zhiling Lan
abstract: HPC facilities collect years of job scheduler records, yet much of this operational data remains underused because accessible tools for turning it into actionable insight are scarce. We present CQTwin, an open-source digital-twin toolkit for operational analytics of HPC scheduling data. CQTwin addresses this gap through two complementary modes: offline trace replay and online event-driven simulation. Built on the Python-based CQSim discrete-event simulator, CQTwin combines a fidelity-validated, high-performance C++ engine with an interactive browser-based dashboard and a Snapshot Lab, enabling facility staff, operators, and researchers to characterize workloads, compare scheduling policies, and explore what-if scenarios. As an offline twin, CQTwin replays archived workload traces under alternative policies to show how the same workload would have unfolded under different scheduling decisions. As an online twin, it consumes job events as they arrive and projects how alternative policies would process the currently queued jobs, providing guidance for real-time decision-making. The dashboard supports the complete analysis workflow, including workload characterization, experiment configuration and monitoring, and multidimensional comparison of simulation results, allowing users to determine visually which policies best suit a workload and what trade-offs they entail. We validate CQTwin using production traces from the Argonne Leadership Computing Facility spanning 2016-2023.

title: TapID: Rapid touch interaction in virtual reality using wearable sensing
authors: Manuel Meier, Paul Streli, Andreas Fender, Christian Holz
abstract: Current Virtual Reality systems typically use cameras to capture user input from controllers or free-hand mid-air interaction. In this paper, we argue that this is a key impediment to productivity scenarios in VR, which require continued interaction over prolonged periods of time---a requirement that controller or free-hand input in mid-air does not satisfy. To address this challenge, we bring rapid touch interaction on surfaces to Virtual Reality---the input modality that users have grown used to on phones and tablets for continued use. We present TapID, a wrist-based inertial sensing system that complements headset-tracked hand poses to trigger input in VR. TapID embeds a pair of inertial sensors in a flexible strap, one at either side of the wrist; from the combination of registered signals, TapID reliably detects surface touch events and, more importantly, identifies the finger used for touch. We evaluated TapID in a series of userstudies on event-detection accuracy (F1 = 0.997) and hand-agnostic finger-identification accuracy (within-user: F1 = 0.93; across users: F1 = 0.91 after 10 refinement taps and F1 = 0.87 without refinement) in a seated table scenario. We conclude with a series of applications that complement hand tracking with touch input and that are uniquely enabled by TapID, including UI control, rapid keyboard typing and piano playing, as well as surface gestures.

title: Synthetic Control: An Exact Geometric Formulation
authors: Alberto Abadie, Yucheng Shang
abstract: The synthetic control method matches a treated unit to a convex combination of donor units, with the relative importance of each predictor determined by a weight matrix $V$. In standard practice, $V$ is selected through a bi-level optimization problem that is nonconvex and lacks convergence guarantees. This article derives an exact geometric solution for synthetic control estimators. For any positive definite $V$, a synthetic control is given by the projection of the treated unit's predictors onto the convex hull of the donor predictors under a $V$-weighted norm. As $V$ varies over its candidate class, these projections trace out the set of attainable synthetic controls. We characterize this set. When the predictor vector of the treated unit lies outside the convex hull of the donor predictors, the attainable set under general positive definite $V$ is the union of the facets of the donor hull that are visible from the treated unit. For diagonal $V$, a sign-compatibility test identifies the attainable set. When the treated unit lies inside the hull, exact matches exist. We select the one that minimizes the average of the pairwise matching discrepancies between the treated unit and each of the donors contributing to the synthetic control. These characterizations replace bi-level optimization with a fast enumeration method that is guaranteed to deliver the global optimum over the attainable set. Moreover, the Karush-Kuhn-Tucker conditions for the selection of donor weights characterize the set of positive definite predictor weight matrices that rationalize any given set of donor weights. Applications to the California tobacco control program and to the economic effects of German reunification illustrate the advantages of the proposed procedure over existing practice.

title: Powers and Functional Calculus for $m$-Selfadjoint and Skew $m$-Selfadjoint Operators
authors: M. Faghih-Ahmadi, T. Bermúdez, K. Hedayatian, H. Zaway
abstract: We study powers and functional calculi of higher-order selfadjoint and skew higher-order selfadjoint operators on complex Hilbert spaces. First, we compare the behavior of their powers with the corresponding theory for $m$-isometries. We prove that if $T$ is invertible and two powers $T^r$ and $T^s$ are, respectively, $m$- and $\ell$-selfadjoint, then $T^{\gcd(r,s)}$ is $\min\{m,\ell\}$-selfadjoint. In particular, invertibility yields the expected converse for consecutive powers. We also show that two consecutive skew $m$-selfadjoint powers must be non-invertible; in fact, nilpotent. For polynomials, we obtain coefficient characterizations under a cardinality assumption on the spectrum. Finally, for holomorphic functions we give spectral characterizations according to whether the spectrum is finite, or the domain of analyticity is a region, and we derive consequences for Möbius transformations and $m$-isometries. Several examples illustrate why the spectral hypotheses cannot be omitted.

title: Bayesian Analysis of Inclusion Transaction Fee Mechanisms with Multiple Concurrent Proposers
authors: Jason Milionis, Kushal Babel
abstract: The goal of this paper is to distill insight around the trade-offs present on Bayesian equilibria of transaction fee mechanism (TFM) design under $n$ multiple concurrent proposers (MCP). We conceptualize a technical toolkit that unlocks the analysis of hard-to-characterize equilibria of finite Bayesian MCP TFM games by examining sequences of joint user--proposer mixed equilibria as the number of users increases and keeping the relative congestion $ρ$ that they cause fixed in the sequence limit. We first consider the popular mechanisms of "pay-once" (which charges transactions its bid only once regardless of the duplicate copies that end up being included by proposers) and "pay-per-inclusion" (PPI in short, which charges a transaction for each copy that appears). We prove that PPI is efficient in the limit of equilibria sequences, and incentivizes users to route to only one proposer. We characterize $m$ users' asymptotic behavior in PPI even in finite markets varying with $O(\sqrt{m})$, where we show users in a $Θ(n\sqrt{ρ(1-ρ)/m})$ window near an efficient cutoff exhibit fixed inclusion probability akin to a normal distribution's CDF. We additionally show that on a value-dependent basis, pay-once exhibits a higher degree of duplication and lower probability of inclusion for higher-value transactions than PPI. Pay-once's inefficiency persists even in the large market limit and even in regimes with ample blockspace where all transactions fit across all blocks. We study interpolations between these two mechanisms proving that some higher coefficients (towards PPI) reduce duplication and increase inclusion probability. We then use our tools to show that exclusive proposer payments yield inefficient equilibria (in fact, with maximal possible duplication), even if users still pay multiple times when included more than once and their payment is burnt when non-exclusive.

title: Reward Objectives for Robust (PO)MDPs: A Law-Preserving Equivalence with (Partially Observable) Games
authors: Durgam Latha, Dion Reji, Dorde Zikelic, Shankaranarayanan Krishna
abstract: Robust partially observable Markov decision processes model agents that act under partial observability while adversarial environment resolves uncertainty in the transition probabilities. Reward objectives such as discounted-sum, long-run average and cumulative reward under finite and infinite horizons allow quantifying the utility of an agent. We consider the problem of solving RPOMDPs under all four reward objectives, where the goal is to decide whether the value of a risk measure with respect to a reward objective exceeds a given threshold. We consider different risk measures, such as (1)~expected value, (2)~mean-variance (MV), (3)~conditional value-at-risk (CVaR), and (4)~entropic risk (ERisk). Our results can be summarized as follows. First, we formalize the class of law-invariant risk measures, that subsume all four risk measures above. Second, we propose a unified framework for solving RPOMDPs with discounted-sum, long-run average and cumulative reward objectives under any law-invariant risk measure, by reducing the problem to solving partially observable stochastic games (POSGs). Our unified framework applies to (s,a)-rectangular RPOMDPs with polytopic uncertainty sets, which we show to be {\em equivalent} to POSGs, for each of the four reward objectives and any law-invariant risk measure. We prove equivalence by designing logspace reductions between the RPOMDP and POSG models, that map strategies to strategies and preserve the distribution of the reward objective, up to a constant rescaling factor. Third, as a corollary, we derive new computational complexity results for R(PO)MDPs and POSGs. In particular, we show that solving (s,a)-rectangular RMDPs is as hard as solving simple stochastic games.

title: From Data to Deployment: A Scoping Review of Empirical Tools, Techniques, and Operational Readiness in Data-Driven 5G/6G Network Optimization
authors: Muhammad Kabeer, Rosdiadee Nordin, Sian Lun Lau
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly applied to 5G/6G network optimization, yet differences in empirical evidence, evaluation methods, and computational requirements complicate comparisons of reported performance. This scop ing review synthesizes 72 peer-reviewed journal studies pub lished between 2022 and 2026, selected through a PRISMA ScR-informed process from 893 records. The review examines empirical tools, AI/ML techniques, optimization domains, and operational readiness. Evidence classification identifies 37 studies (51.4%) using real-world or physical-testbed evidence only, 25 (34.7%) combining measured and simulated evidence, and 10 (13.9%) relying exclusively on synthetic or simulated data. Offline analysis was the most common evaluation setting, accounting for 45 studies (62.5%). Three principal findings emerge. First, empirical measurements improve contextual relevance, while simulation and digital twins support scalable experimentation but introduce validation challenges. Second, algorithmic effectiveness depends on the optimization objective, data characteristics, and computational constraints rather than model complexity alone. Third, predictive accuracy is more consistently evaluated than the network-level effects of optimization decisions. The review there fore introduces the six-module Evidence Fidelity and Operational Reporting (EFOR) checklist to improve evaluation consistency, reporting transparency, and operational relevance.

title: PRISMS/U13151. A Glimpse into the Earliest Phases of Galaxy Formation through an Ultra-Faint System $\approx$ 500 Myr after the Big Bang
authors: Pierluigi Rinaldi, Javier Álvarez-Márquez, Alejandro Crespo Gómez, Luis Colina, Stefano Carniani, Sarah Kendrew, Edoardo Iani, Angela Adamo, Abdurro'uf, Marianna Annunziatella, Stacey Alberts, Leindert A. Boogaard, Karina I. Caputi, Marco Castellano, Michele Catone, Rui Marques-Chaves, Ryan Cooper, Seiji Fujimoto, Mahmoud Hamed, Yuichi Harikane, Santosh Harish, Takuya Hashimoto, Jakob M. Helton, Tiger Y. -Y. Hsiao, Vasily Kokorev, Álvaro Labiano, Jens Melinder, Ikki Mitsuhashi, Göran Östlin, Lorenzo Napolitano, Borja Pérez-Díaz, Pablo G. Pérez-González, Carlota Prieto Jiménez, Giulia Rodighiero, Paola Santini, Ana Varo-O'Ferrall, Jorge A. Zavala, Yongda Zhu
abstract: Detailed UV-to-optical studies of galaxies at z >= 10 have largely focused on bright systems (MUV <= -20 mag), leaving intrinsically faint galaxies virtually unexplored to date. Combining NIRCam, NIRSpec, and MIRI imaging and spectroscopy, we investigate UNCOVER-ABELL2744-13151 (U13151), an ultra-faint galaxy at z = 9.7995 (MUV = -17.44 mag), magnified by Abell 2744 ($μ$ = 12.8). U13151 is very blue ($β$ ~ -2.64), ultra-low mass (log10(M*/Msun) ~ 6.68), young (~ 5.5 Myr), metal-poor (Z ~ 3-6% Zsun), and compact (Re ~ 122 pc). It exhibits negligible dust attenuation, extreme ionization conditions, and intense star formation (sSFR(Ha) ~ 94 Gyr-1, or equivalently M*/SFR(Ha) ~ 10.6 Myr). Despite similarities with much brighter galaxies, its low C/O, approximately solar Ne/O, and undetected nitrogen emission suggest enrichment dominated by core-collapse supernovae, in stark contrast with similar nitrogen-enhanced systems. U13151 might be undergoing its first major episode of star formation, assembling most (if not all) of its M* through five unresolved clumps. Its high ionizing photon production efficiency (log10($ξ_{\rm ion}$/ (Hz erg-1)) ~ 25.64) suggests, through a simple toy model, suggests, through a simple toy model, that similarly short-lived episodes could contribute significantly to the ionizing photon budget of low-mass galaxies during Cosmic Reionization. We explore different evolutionary scenarios, from U13151-like galaxies potentially representing the progenitors of Blue Monsters at higher redshifts to the possibility that such systems could be the early building blocks of present-day Milky Way-like galaxies. Our results highlight the fundamental role of MIRI in studying galaxies in the early Universe and the urgent need to investigate the faintest, lowest-mass systems to shed light on the fundamental physics driving the earliest phases of galaxy formation.

title: Beyond Finite-Sum Optimization: A Primal-Dual Method for Decentralized Finite-Max Optimization
authors: Zhouxing Luo, Lei Wang, Xin Liu
abstract: Many decentralized systems are judged by their worst-performing agents rather than their average performance. We study finite-max optimization over a connected undirected network, where each agent knows only its own smooth, possibly nonconvex objective. Quadratic regularization yields a smooth finite-sum representation with a scalar dual variable and locally computable clipped weights. We develop an alternating primal-dual gradient tracking (APDGT) method, using neighbor communication without any global or centralized projections. Under smoothness and level-boundedness assumptions, a localized Lyapunov analysis with vanishing regularization establishes bounded primal iterates and Clarke stationarity of every accumulation point of their network average. The averaged sequence contains an $\varepsilon$-stationary point, measured by near-active gradients, within $O (\varepsilon^{-3})$ iterations. Synthetic tests and decentralized logistic regression on Fashion-MNIST illustrate convergence behavior and potential improvements in worst-agent performance.

title: On Exact Dihedral Angle Sum Ranges for Orthocentric and Isogonic Tetrahedra
authors: Sergey Korotov
abstract: For a nondegenerate Euclidean tetrahedron T, let Σ(T) denote the sum of its six interior dihedral angles. We establish the exact range [6 arccos(1/3), 3π) for the orthocentric and isogonic classes. The orthocentric part gives a short alternative proof of the sharp lower bound; the main new result is the corresponding isogonic theorem. Starting from classical insphere-contact geometry, we derive a reciprocal half-angle identity and a sharp defect inequality controlled by the scale-invariant dispersion of the reciprocal tangent-length parameters. This quantitative refinement shows that any nonzero dispersion forces a positive dihedral-angle-sum gap, and that near equality forces the normalized reciprocal parameters to be close to equality. Finally, the common kite subfamily realizes every value in the interval and proves sharpness of both endpoints.

title: Invariance of logarithmic plurigenera and adjoint volumes in Kähler families
authors: Kefeng Liu, Xueyuan Wan
abstract: We consider smooth proper families of compact complex manifolds over a disk whose total space is Kähler, together with a boundary divisor with relative simple normal crossings. We prove that, if the boundary is a rational divisor with coefficients in $[0,1)$, every logarithmic pluricanonical form on a fiber extends to a neighborhood of that fiber, and hence that the logarithmic plurigenera are constant. No positivity of the log canonical class is assumed. We prove further that, for real boundary coefficients in $[0,1]$, a log-adjoint class twisted by a smooth semipositive form has the same volume on every fiber, and that it is pseudoeffective either on every fiber or on none. When the log-adjoint class is nef on every fiber, we give a second proof of the extension theorem, which does not use the minimal model program.

title: First-Order Primal-Dual Repairs for Scalable Branch and Bound
authors: Francesco Pivi, Jiachang Liu, Andrea Lodi
abstract: Mixed-integer programs have found applications in many real-world problems but remain difficult to solve at scale. To improve scalability, there has been increasing interest in incorporating first-order methods as subroutines for solving node relaxations, with success primarily on problems involving specific types of constraints. However, when more general constraints are considered, first-order methods cannot be directly applied because, at finite iterations, they typically produce infeasible primal and dual solutions, preventing their direct integration into branch-and-bound. To overcome this limitation, we introduce repair procedures that extract valid primal and dual bounds from infeasible first-order iterates. These bounds enable node pruning, incumbent updates, and early stopping at any iteration. Empirically, our approach achieves one to two orders of magnitude speedups when solving real-world instances (with another order of magnitude speedup when running on GPUs) and certifies optimality on instances that are difficult for commercial solvers.

title: Atomic-level study of dose-dependent lattice thermal conductivity degradation in irradiated tungsten
authors: Mary K Chessey, José Julio Gutiérrez Moreno, Sajjan Singh Mehta, Paolo Settembri, Arda Erbasan, Dominik Freinberger, Marina García Romero, Mervi J Mantsinen
abstract: Plasma-facing components (PFCs) in future fusion reactors must withstand extreme environments, making tungsten (W) a prime candidate material due to its high thermal conductivity, high melting temperature, low sputtering yield, low tritium absorption. However, neutron irradiation introduces complex nanostructural defects that severely degrade these critical properties. In this work, we use Non-Equilibrium Molecular Dynamics (NEMD) simulations coupled with the Creation Relaxation Algorithm (CRA) to investigate the lattice thermal conductivity (kappa) of W across a wide range of irradiation doses. Systems treated with different doses up to 1.8 canonical displacements per atom (cdpa) were simulated to generate and study diverse defect structures, including vacancies and self-interstitial atom (SIA) clusters. By correlating spatially-resolved temperature gradients with local defect concentrations, we show that even small changes in defect type and distribution significantly affect thermal transport. We employ Machine Learning (ML) models to develop a quantitative relationship between the defect features and the resulting thermal conductivity degradation. The ML analysis identifies vacancy density as the dominant structural factor controlling thermal transport. We found a significant, nonlinear suppression of kappa with increasing defect density. Predictive multi-defect mapping built upon our ML model resolved a step-like degradation transition at a critical vacancy threshold of 0.05 at.%, beyond which phonon scattering completely saturated and capped the maximum relative lattice thermal conductivity degradation at approximately 30 at.%. This integrated simulation and ML approach provides a powerful, predictive framework for quantifying the complex relationship between structure and thermal conductivity in irradiated fusion materials.

title: On Learning Expand-and-Sparsify Representations
authors: Alireza Asghari, Parikshit Ram, Kaushik Sinha
abstract: Expand-and-sparsify ($\texttt{EaS}$) representations lift an input to a much higher dimension through a linear map and keep only the $k$ largest coordinates. Existing theory builds that map at random and needs the expanded dimension to grow exponentially in the input dimension, which puts the construction out of practical reach. We ask what is gained by learning the map by gradient descent instead, and how that gain depends on how wide the expansion is. We sweep $73$ OpenML classification tasks and $48$ regression tasks under a protocol that holds the datasets, expanded dimensions, sparsity levels and splits fixed across every method, and we summarise each comparison by a median over datasets and a Wilcoxon signed rank test. We report four findings. First, learning the expansion helps most when the expansion is narrowest, and its advantage over a random map decays to nothing by the widest expansions we run, so a learned $\texttt{EaS}$ layer can be made small. Second, with the map learned, a top-$k$ representation that keeps at most a tenth of its coordinates is indistinguishable from a dense $\texttt{ReLU}$ layer of the same expanded dimension at every expansion factor we test, while GELU and SiLU are not. Third, when the representation is forced to be binary the sparse code is the better of the two, and the reason is that binarization costs it nothing while it costs the dense layer accuracy. Fourth, how sparse the representation can be is governed by how wide it is: the sparsity level that is free rises as the expansion grows, so there is no fixed limit on how sparse it can be. The regression tasks reproduce the first finding and qualify the second and third.

title: VeriCUA: Learning Proactive Verification for Reliable GUI Agent Rewards
authors: Zhizhou Wang, Yaxi Lu, Zhong Zhang, Zikun Hu, Xin Cong, Yankai Lin, Fangming Liu
abstract: Reinforcement learning for computer-use agents increasingly relies on proactive reward agents that interact with the post-execution GUI environment to verify what recorded screenshots cannot reveal. The reliability of such verification hinges on two coupled decisions: what to check and when to stop. Existing methods leave these decisions to prompted foundation models. However, neither scaling up the model nor providing few-shot examples reliably improves verification: prompted Judges ranging from 4B to GPT-5.4 all plateau at 68%-70% macro-average agreement. This is because the value of a check depends on the environment rather than the task alone, and becomes apparent only through execution. Learning from execution is itself constrained, as the Actor's terminal state cannot be faithfully replicated during training, allowing only one verification attempt per state. We introduce VeriCUA, a proactive reward agent that learns its verification strategy from these single attempts. A trainable Judge decides what to check and when to stop, while a frozen Probe executes the checks in the live environment. Online reinforcement learning optimizes the Judge for both verdict correctness and efficient Probe use, with returns normalized across terminal states. Trained only on OSWorld and evaluated without further training on MobileWorld and WebArena-Verified, VeriCUA achieves the highest reward agreement across all three benchmarks and lies on the agreement-cost Pareto frontier among proactive verifiers. It surpasses few-shot GPT-5.4 by 5.36 points with 47.6%-59.8% fewer Probe tokens, and even a 1B VeriCUA exceeds every prompted Judge. As the reward for Actor RL, it raises task success by 3.21 points overall and 5.40 points on held-out multi-application tasks. These results identify the verification strategy, not verifier scale, as the key to reliable GUI rewards.

title: The Four-Qubit Hyperbolic Quadric Has Contextuality Degree 315
authors: Zhengyu Li, Amandeep Gupta, Vijay Ganesh
abstract: The contextuality degree of a set of Pauli contexts is the least number of contexts that every noncontextual $\pm1$ assignment violates. For the four-qubit hyperbolic quadric $\mathcal{Q}^{+}(7,2)$, with $135$ points and $1575$ lines as contexts, Muller et al. conjectured from heuristic searches that the degree is $315$ and that the violated contexts of every optimal assignment form a dual polar space $DW(5,2)$. We prove both conjectures. The lower bound has a short proof by hand: every doily ($GQ(2,2)$) of the quadric contains ten Peres-Mermin grids covering each of its lines four times, so every assignment violates at least three of its fifteen lines, and averaging over the doilies gives $1575/5=315$. The equality case is local: an assignment is optimal exactly when it violates one ruling of one grid in every doily. Using this as a SAT encoding, we show that there are exactly $240$ optimal violated sets, one orbit of $\mathrm{O}^+(8,2)$, each isomorphic to $DW(5,2)$. The same argument gives the first lower bounds $\lceil L/5\rceil$ for all quadrics with $L$ lines in $N\ge4$ qubits. The degree theorem is kernel-checked in Lean 4, and the completeness of the enumeration is certified by a DRAT proof checked by the verified checker cake_lpr.

title: Limits of Besov Norms on Quantum Euclidean Spaces
authors: Qingquan Deng, Guixiang Hong, Ping Li, Yanzhen Long
abstract: We extend the Bourgain--Brézis--Mironescu (BBM) and Maz'ya--Shaposhnikova (MS) limit formulae to higher-order Besov norms on quantum Euclidean spaces $\R^d_θ$, a fundamental class of noncompact noncommutative manifolds obtained by deformation quantization of $\R^d$. A central ingredient is a Banach realization of the homogeneous Sobolev endpoint that forms a compatible couple with \(L_p(\R_θ^d)\), together with the equivalence \[ K\bigl(\x,\varepsilon^k; L_p(\R_θ^d),\dot W_{p,0}^k(\R_θ^d)\bigr) \approx ω_p^k(\x,\varepsilon). \] This framework yields a unified proof of both endpoint formulae through the endpoint continuity of real interpolation scales. The principal new ingredient at the MS endpoint is the sharp large-translation asymptotic \[ \lim_{|h|\to\infty}\|T_h\x-\x\|_p = 2^{1/p}\|\x\|_p, \qquad \x\in L_p(\R_θ^d),\quad 1\leq p<\infty, \] whose proof combines oscillatory decay of the non-pure terms in the tracial expansion with weighted spectral-measure arguments adapted to the semifinite trace.

title: Remembering Has a Price: Learning Memory Worth under Resource Constraints
authors: Guannan Lai, Zi-Yang Bai, Jun-Peng Jiang, Han-Jia Ye
abstract: Lifelong agents continually accumulate and reuse experience to improve after deployment, yet in practice they often operate under tight generation, interaction, and memory budgets. Under such stringent joint constraints, we find that existing lifelong-memory methods can become ineffective, with several sophisticated approaches offering little advantage over simple retrieval or even no-memory agents. This reveals a more fundamental problem: resource scarcity makes each memory decision more consequential. When only a small amount of past experience can be retained or reused and opportunities for reasoning and recovery are limited, retrieving a relevant but ineffective memory can consume scarce context and hinder downstream execution. The key challenge is therefore not simply to retrieve relevant experience, but to determine which experiences are actually worth retaining and reusing. To address this challenge, we propose TokenWorth, a lightweight online memory framework that learns query-dependent memory worth from sparse execution feedback and applies it consistently to memory retrieval and bounded memory management. Across three LifelongAgentBench environments and both local and API-based deployments, TokenWorth achieves the highest task success rate while using the fewest output tokens among the evaluated methods. These results suggest that effective lifelong adaptation under resource constraints depends not on remembering more, but on learning what is worth remembering. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/AIGNLAI/TokenWorth.

title: A Human-in-the-Loop Comparison of Proportional Control and Adaptive Gravity Compensation in Elbow EMG-Driven Exoskeletons
authors: Francesco Pascucci, Eldison Dimo, Davide Costanzi, Mario Sedilesu, Andrea Calanca
abstract: Electromyography (EMG)-driven control enables wearable robots to assist users based on their neuromuscular activity. Upper-limb exoskeletons typically rely on proportional myoelectric control (PMC), which amplifies user effort but may compromise stability at high assistance levels. EMG-driven adaptive gravity compensation (AGC) offers a promising alternative, counterbalancing gravitational torques while continuously adapting to neuromuscular activity. However, these approaches have not been systematically compared in a human-in-the-loop setting. This study evaluates five control algorithms: two PMC strategies at different assistance levels, a purely integral AGC (AGC-PI), a kinematics- and acceleration-aware model-based (MB) AGC (AGC-AW), and a novel MB AGC approach based on Recursive Least Squares (AGC-RLS) for online payload estimation. Fourteen healthy participants performed target-reaching tasks using an active elbow exoskeleton under 0 kg and 2 kg loading conditions. Performance metrics included muscular activity, movement accuracy, task efficiency, and subjective workload. PMC exhibited a trade-off between physical effort and task performance: low assistance levels required greater physical effort under load, whereas high gains impaired task execution. AGC-PI reduced agonist activity but induced antagonist activation. In contrast, both model-based AGC approaches effectively compensated for external payloads, reducing physical and cognitive demands while improving movement accuracy and completion time.

title: Simultaneous Sharp-Interface Limits for a Diffuse-Interface Landau--de Gennes Droplet Model
authors: Sisi Guan, Wei Wang, Lei Zhang
abstract: Nematic droplet models based on diffuse interfaces involve competing microscopic transition layers whose interaction is lost if the small parameters are sent to zero successively. We study this interaction for the diffuse-interface Landau--de Gennes model of Shi et al., with phase-field thickness $\varepsilon$ and exterior $Q$-tensor relaxation length $κ_\varepsilon$, and show that their relative scale selects the effective sharp-interface theory. Within a regular-interface class, we establish the corresponding sharp-interface limit for every limiting ratio $r=\lim_{\varepsilon\to0}κ/\varepsilon\in[0,+\infty]$. Three qualitatively different regimes emerge. When $r=+\infty$, the two transition layers separate asymptotically and the interfacial costs decouple, recovering the previously obtained iterated limit. When $r\in(0,+\infty)$, the layers overlap and produce a genuinely coupled, $r$-dependent anisotropic surface density. When $r=0$, finite energy forces the interior trace of $Q$ to vanish on the limiting interface. The comparable-scale regime requires a genuinely coupled interfacial analysis. Thus the exterior relaxation length is not merely a regularization parameter: together with the phase-field thickness, it determines the macroscopic surface energy and anchoring law of the sharp-interface limit.

title: Physiology-Aware Graph Attention for Early Ventricular Reentry Prediction
authors: Ma{ë}lis Morier, Jairo Rodr{í}guez Padilla, Patrick Gallinari, Maxime Sermesant
abstract: Sudden cardiac death mostly originates from post-infarct ventricular tachycardia. This reentry is sustained by propagation around scar tissue, but its risk remains difficult to predict from infarct imaging alone. While in silico induction studies can reveal these mechanisms, exploring many substrates and pacing locations remains computationally expensive. We propose a graph attention classifier for early prediction of sustained ventricular reentry from simulated cardiac electrophysiology. Each simulation is represented as a graph with early nodal voltage samples and edge attributes encoding geometry, stimulation frequency, tissue labels, amplitude, and diastolic interval. These descriptors are computed only from the first two paced activations, before sustained reentry is observed. On a balanced independent test set of 1000 simulations, the classifier achieves 94.6% accuracy, 95.4% sensitivity, 93.8% specificity, 94.6% F1-score, 0.987 ROC-AUC, and 0.985 PR-AUC. Ablation experiments show that diastolic interval is the most critical descriptor. Qualitative attention inspection suggests that different heads focus on border-zone, stimulation location, and early propagation path. These results support graph attention as a fast early-prediction approach for large-scale in silico ventricular reentry studies.

title: Triebel - Lizorkin spaces of dominating mixed smoothness are algebras with respect to pointwise multiplication
authors: Van Kien Nguyen
abstract: We continue our investigations on pointwise multipliers for spaces of dominating mixed smoothness. In this paper we prove that under a certain conditions Triebel - Lizorkin spaces of dominating mixed smoothness form algebras with respect to pointwise multiplication.

title: Where Does Rhetorical Distortion Live? A Multi-Platform, Multi-Language Measurement of Influencer Content
authors: Xucheng Yu, Jiangping Chen, Haohan Wang
abstract: Much of the manipulation in online influencer content is not false but disproportionate: an accurate fact is framed as historic, urgent, or catastrophic. Fact-checking and clickbait detection are not designed to capture such framing, and little is known about where it originates: with the creator, the topic, the platform, or the audience that replies. We operationalize rhetorical distortion through five literature-grounded dimensions (Significance Inflation, Anxiety Manufacturing, Novelty Claims, Loaded Language, and Temporal Distortion) and measure it with a three-tier pipeline in which bilingual lexical rules propose candidates, negative filters cancel known false-positive contexts, and an LLM verifies or relabels the candidates. Applying the pipeline to 13,060 posts from 330 accounts on six platforms (RSS/newsletters, YouTube, Bluesky, Reddit, Weibo, and X/Twitter), we find that platform is far more strongly associated with account-level distortion than content category (Kruskal-Wallis $\varepsilon^2=0.33$; two-way ANOVA $η_p^2=0.49$ for platform vs. $0.09$ for category). X/Twitter scores highest (DI 7.74 vs. 0.78 for RSS). Classifying tweets and their replies separately shows where this comes from: the reply layer readers see under a post (its top-5 replies) carries 3.5x the distortion of the tweet it answers (7.65 vs. 2.17, $p<10^{-6}$, 36 of 43 accounts), driven by Loaded Language. At equal text length the gap shrinks to 1.5x but remains significant, and creator tweets alone are statistically indistinguishable from YouTube and Bluesky. Two independent human annotators confirm the reply gap, and the platform ordering and the reply gap replicate with GPT-4o as a second classifier. On threaded platforms, measured distortion thus lives largely in the audience layer, which motivates measurement that separates creator and reply text.

title: Decomposing the Action of Macdonald Operators for Classical Types
authors: Hieu Trung Vu
abstract: We study Macdonald operators associated to classical root systems of types $B_N$, $C_N$, and $D_N$. We provide explicit formulas for decomposing the cumulative action of these operators as the sum of the actions of lower-rank operators and auxiliary operators. We also discuss the same idea in the elliptic case, also known as Ruijsenaars operators, and show that under the trigonometric limit, the identity reduces to type-$A_N$ decomposition.

title: Higher-order Parity Constraints for Quantum Approximate Optimization
authors: Anita Weidinger, Glen Bigan Mbeng, Roeland ter Hoeven, Wolfgang Lechner
abstract: The Parity Architecture was originally introduced in the context of quantum optimization algorithms to overcome hardware connectivity constraints. Here, we show that its benefits extend beyond this role by identifying specific parity transformations that enhance the success probability of the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) for optimization problems defined on hardware-native and sparse graphs. Numerical simulations suggest that this enhancement originates from the higher-order operators introduced by the Parity representation, which accelerate the propagation of correlations across the physical device. We investigate this mechanism for the Signed Max-Cut problem on 3-regular graph instances and demonstrate its practical relevance on IBM Heron quantum processors. QAOA parameters are first classically optimized on small training instances containing up to 14 vertices and subsequently transferred to larger instances executed on quantum hardware. We consider Signed Max-Cut instances of up to 40 vertices and find that, together with an error mitigation technique, the parity-based QAOA identifies the optimal solutions for all the considered 40-vertex instances, whereas the conventional QAOA fails under the same conditions.

title: Entropic metastability for drifted reflected Brownian motion: quasi-stationary distributions, regularity, and the exit position distribution
authors: Louis Carillo, Lo{ï}s Delande, Boris Nectoux
abstract: Motivated by entropic metastability and the narrow escape problem, we investigate quasi-stationary distributions for reflected, drifted elliptic diffusions under mixed absorbing-reflecting boundary conditions on a bounded domain. We address two problems, which are solved completely independently of each other. First, using purely probabilistic tools, we prove the existence and uniqueness of a quasi-stationary distribution under minimal regularity assumptions on the coefficients (the case of an unbounded domain is also analyzed). Second, using spectral theory and the theory of strongly continuous semigroups on L p spaces, we study the analytical properties of the quasistationary distribution. We relate it to the principal eigenfunction of the adjoint of the associated (non-symmetric) infinitesimal generator with mixed absorbing-reflecting boundary conditions, and we establish its regularity up to the interface between the two boundary parts. We also fully characterize the law of the exit point when the process is initially distributed according to its quasistationary distribution. In particular, we work on domains in which the absorbing (Dirichlet) and reflecting (Neumann) parts of the boundary meet tangentially, without forming any non-trivial angle, a configuration that raises genuine regularity difficulties for the solutions of the associated mixed boundary value problem.

title: The Milky Way's Early Disk Was Built in Bursts. I. Evidence from Low-angular-momentum, High-$α$ Stars Scattered Out of the Protodisk by Merger Events
authors: Tiancheng Sun, Maosheng Xiang, Shaolan Bi, Jifeng Liu, Meng Zhang, Yaqian Wu
abstract: Stars born in the high-$α$ disk can later acquire low angular momentum through dynamical scattering during early merger events. Their age--metallicity distribution thus provides a fossil record of the history of both star formation and dynamical perturbations in the early Milky Way disk. Here we identify a sample of 2,078 such stars from more than two million Gaia DR3 subgiants with robust determinations of ages, kinematics, and abundances. From this sample we reconstruct their intrinsic age--metallicity distribution with a forward modeling approach. Our results confirm that these scattered stars are older and more metal-poor than the bulk of the high-$α$ disk on average. In particular, the joint age--metallicity distribution reveals a robust two-component feature: a broad, dominant component with a peak age of $\sim$11.5~Gyr and ${\rm [Fe/H]}\simeq-0.59$, and an older and more metal-poor component with a peak age of $\sim$12.5~Gyr and ${\rm [Fe/H]}\simeq-0.86$. The presence of this two-component structure suggests that the high-$α$ disk experienced episodic phases of star formation and chemical enrichment. The age distribution of the younger Splash component, compared with that of the high-$α$ disk, provides evidence for a substantial dynamical perturbation at a lookback time of 10.8--11.5~Gyr, possibly associated with an early passage of Gaia--Sausage--Enceladus (GSE). The older Splash component, with a peak age of $\sim$12.5~Gyr, may preserve signatures of an earlier interaction, possibly associated with the proposed Low-energy--Kraken--Heracles (LKH) event.

title: Self-Oscillating Photonic Frequency Comb for Sub-THz Local Oscillator Generation in Earth Observation Systems
authors: Dimitrios Kastritsis, Ioannis Stratakis, Stavros Iezekiel
abstract: Earth observation missions rely on microwave and sub-terahertz radiometry for retrieving atmospheric parameters such as temperature, humidity, and cloud properties, with the 183- and 229-GHz spectral regions being particularly relevant. Local-oscillator (LO) generation at these frequencies requires low phase noise and high frequency stability while meeting stringent size, weight, and power (SWaP) constraints. Conventional architectures employ dielectric resonator oscillators followed by cascaded frequency-multiplication stages, requiring dedicated generation chains for different frequency bands and increasing hardware complexity. Furthermore, frequency multiplication degrades the phase noise of the generated signal. This work proposes and numerically investigates a reconfigurable self-oscillating microwave photonic architecture for LO generation in Earth observation receivers. Cascaded Mach-Zehnder and phase modulation within an optoelectronic feedback loop generate an optical frequency comb with enhanced higher-order components. A combination of optical filters is used to select the required comb line. First, a conventional bandpass filter with a bandwidth of approximately 10 GHz isolates the spectral region containing the desired component, after which a narrowband dual cavity Bragg grating ring resonator (BGRR) with a bandwidth of approximately 3 MHz provides the final line selection. The selected comb line is then combined with an optical reference derived from the same laser and photodetected to generate the desired millimeter-wave or sub-terahertz signal through optical heterodyning. Numerical simulations are presented for 183- and 229-GHz generation, demonstrating the ability of the same underlying architecture to address multiple LO frequencies by tuning the OEO electrical filter to the appropriate oscillation frequency and selecting the corresponding comb order.

title: An Empirical Study of Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning for Mixture-of-Experts LLMs
authors: Minglei Li, Peng Ye, Haonan He, Jingqi Ye, Qingyu Yang, Tao Chen
abstract: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods are critical for adapting large models under resource-constrained settings. However, as mixture-of-experts (MoE) architectures, which offer efficient inference at massive parameter scales, gain increasing prevalence in the community, a critical gap arising from the lack of systematic recipes for applying PEFT to MoE models. To narrow this gap, we conduct a large-scale systematic study that investigates a set of essential design recipes, including which modules should be adapted, which granularity should be used to adapt MoE modules, which PEFT method to use, and to what extent should the load-balancing objective be used, across three MoE backbones on downstream tasks and general knowledge tasks. Our experiments yield several key insights. First, adapting MoE experts alone achieves the highest downstream performance with competitive general capability retention under a comparable parameter budget. Second, native expert-weight updates offer a better downstream--retention trade-off than adapters that bypass experts or entire MoE modules. Third, LoRA and DoRA together define the strongest operating region for high downstream accuracy among the evaluated PEFT methods. Fourth, no nonzero load-balancing coefficient Pareto-dominates the zero baseline. We finally evaluate a weight-level redesign of MoE$^2$-LoRA on Qwen3. Moving its module-level bypass pool into native expert weights improves all four upstream endpoints by 2.4 to 17.9 points with 17% fewer trainable parameters and a 3.2-point average downstream cost.

title: Constructive Arithmetic Regularity for Abelian Groups
authors: Swarnalipa Datta, Arijit Ghosh, Chandrima Kayal, Manmatha Roy
abstract: The arithmetic regularity lemma of Green is a fundamental tool in additive combinatorics, providing a decomposition of arbitrary subsets of finite Abelian groups into pseudorandom pieces with respect to Fourier analysis. Over the years, it has found numerous applications in combinatorics, property testing, and theoretical computer science. However, Green's proof is existential, and many algorithmic applications require an efficient procedure for constructing the underlying regular decomposition. De, Nadimpalli, and Servedio (SODA 2022) developed a query-efficient constructive regularity framework over $\mathbb{F}_2^n$ and explicitly raised the problem of extending their dimension-independent sumset-estimation algorithm to other finite Abelian groups. In this work, we resolve this question for finite Abelian groups of constant torsion. We develop the first constructive version of Green's {\em Arithmetic Regularity Lemma} in this general setting. Given oracle access to a subset of the group, our algorithm computes an implicit description of a regular decomposition together with an oracle representation of a structured subset satisfying the guarantees of Green's lemma. The algorithm runs in time and query complexity polynomial in the regularity parameters and the tower bound, while remaining independent of the size of the ambient group. As applications, we obtain efficient algorithms for removing linear configurations and approximately counting linear images, including weighted sumsets and suitable matrix systems of Cauchy--Schwarz complexity one, over finite Abelian groups of constant torsion. Our results provide a unified algorithmic framework extending dimension-independent constructive arithmetic regularity and its applications beyond $\mathbb{F}_2^n$.

title: A Sarkisov Involution from a Rational Cubic Curve on a Quartic Double Solid
authors: Joseph Cutrone, Nicholas Marshburn
abstract: Building on an earlier classification of smooth weak Fano threefolds of Picard number two with small anticanonical morphism, we prove that Case~28 of the table of E1-E1 links from that classification is geometrically realizable. We construct the link by blowing up a smooth rational cubic curve on a degree-two del Pezzo threefold $V_2$, realized as a quartic double solid. A lattice calculation on an anticanonical K3 surface shows that the anticanonical morphism of the blow-up is small, and the covering involution of the anticanonical double cover realizes the flop. The resulting Sarkisov link is a birational involution with the numerical invariants of E1-E1 Case~28.

title: ReInsVLN: Revisiting Historical Evidence for Training-Free Vision-and-Language Navigation
authors: Siwei Cheng, Hao Wu, Zitong Qi, Xinming Zhang, Haoyu Xi, Peiran Yin, Haozhe Hu, Xudong Wang, Xiaoyu Shen, Wei Zhang
abstract: Vision-and-language navigation (VLN) relies on retaining and using relevant observations. Yet growing histories introduce redundancy, and retained information may remain underused. We introduce ReInsBench, a diagnostic benchmark that examines history utilization through controlled continuation trials. Its results show that history-review reinstruction can recover navigation failures using the existing task context. Motivated by this finding, we propose ReInsVLN, a training-free framework supporting memory construction and utilization in frozen navigators. Coverage- and Instruction-Aware Compression constructs compact visual context through temporal redundancy reduction, coverage-aware protection, and instruction-guided token selection. Forgetting-Inspired History Reminders guide navigators to revisit retained observations according to a predefined schedule, without additional model calls. On R2R Val-Unseen, ReInsVLN improves success rates by 8.48 and 3.37 percentage points over the native StreamVLN and InternVLA-N1, reaching 64.27% and 64.44%, respectively. Visual compression largely preserves navigation performance while reducing prefill latency and KV cache memory by up to 21.77% and 32.25%, respectively, on matched observation workloads. Real-world trials on humanoid and quadruped robots further support the applicability of ReInsVLN to sequential instruction following and ordinal navigation.

title: Pangolin: Efficient DAG-based BFT State-Machine Replication with TEE-Accelerated Commitment
authors: Paul Franke-Bergmann, Maya Kuhlmann, Alexander Heß, Marc Leinweber, Rüdiger Kapitza, Hannes Hartenstein, Franz J. Hauck, Christian Berger
abstract: Currently many Byzantine fault-tolerant (BFT) protocols use directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) to let replicas propose blocks of requests in parallel for improved throughput. Yet, the existing DAG-based designs mainly consider the atomic-broadcast layer: They typically do not describe an efficient client interaction layer, their garbage collection is either unspecified or relies on trusted external storage, and the lowest-latency designs rely on timing assumptions that may be violated in geo-distributed deployments. In this paper, we propose the Pangolin protocol: It introduces a novel low-latency DAG-based atomic broadcast layer and completes it into an efficient state-machine replication (SMR) framework. To preserve system throughput, clients issue requests to a single replica and verify replies efficiently via compact execution proofs. Furthermore, Pangolin introduces a new garbage-collection scheme for DAGs which bounds memory usage even under full asynchrony. Pangolin leverages trusted execution environments to tolerate f Byzantine faults with only n >= 2f + 1 replicas and accelerates vertex commitments significantly: Broadcasting certified vertices requires only a single communication step, and commit rules are refined to commit both frequently and early without revealing the coin-elected anchor. This way, Pangolin overtakes the fastest partially synchronous DAG protocols while being live under asynchrony: In our evaluation, Pangolin achieves an average 1.27x (up to 1.52x) latency speedup over Mysticeti.

title: Capillary forces between two identical spherical particles
authors: Stefano Onofri, Thejas Hulikal Chakrapani, Stefan Luding, Elke Scholten, Ahmed Jarray, Wouter K. den Otter
abstract: The properties of colloidal suspensions and granular matter change drastically upon adding a small amount of liquid capable of forming capillary bridges between the solid particles. The attractive forces exerted by these liquid bridges induce the formation of particle aggregates and networks, which radically changes the macroscopic mechanical and rheological behaviour. Predicting these forces across bridge sizes, particle separations and wettability is therefore central to particle-scale modelling of capillary suspensions and wet granular matter. While the Young-Laplace equation governing the properties of the liquid bridges is well known, it lacks a convenient analytical solution. Current simulations therefore employ approximate analytic expressions, typically developed for contact angles below ~40° and bridge volumes below ~2.5% of the solid particle's volume. We compare several frequently used expressions from the literature with numerical solutions of the theoretical capillary forces. An overall good agreement is observed in the aforementioned parameter ranges, while the approximate expressions start to deviate outside their intended domains. We propose accurate and computationally efficient expressions for the capillary force that model this behaviour, for contact angles from 5° to 80° and bridge volumes from $10^{-6}$ to 0.15. We also explore mesoscopic 'fluid-scale' simulations of bridges by Multi-body Dissipative Particle Dynamics (MDPD), to ascertain whether this coarse-grained fluid model faithfully captures the continuum capillary forces. Remarkably, a good agreement is observed even for liquid bridges described by a mere few dozen fluid particles. Together, these results offer two approaches, at different resolution scales, for simulating bridges over a wide range of bridge volumes and contact angles.

title: Cutoff beyond non-negative curvature
authors: Max Fathi, Arnaud Guillin, Cyril Labbé, Justin Salez
abstract: We study how a relaxed gradient estimate is enough to prove cutoff for several new families of Markov processes, within the varentropy framework of [Sal25]. In particular, we show how certain regularization estimates from hypocoercivity theory allow one to prove cutoff for kinetic dynamics. Moreover, we prove cutoff for some families of diffusions with non-convex potentials and for mean-field dynamics, as well as for biased random walks on the symmetric group, giving a simple proof of a far-reaching extension of a result of [NY24].

title: Shifted quantum affine symmetric pairs: finite presentations and graded coideal structures
authors: Jian-Rong Li, Tomasz Przezdziecki
abstract: Shifted quantum affine symmetric pair algebras were recently introduced as a trigonometric analogue of shifted twisted Yangians, whose truncations are expected to quantize fixed point loci in generalized affine Grassmannian slices. They are defined via a loop presentation with infinitely many generators and relations. In this paper, we consider anti-dominantly shifted quantum affine symmetric pair algebras of simply-laced split type. Our main result is a construction of a finite presentation à la Levendorskii. We apply it in type $\mathsf{A}$ to construct an embedding of a shifted quantum symmetric pair algebra into the corresponding shifted quantum affine algebra, yielding a graded coideal structure.

title: Reasoning-Aware Multicalibrated Reliability Predictors for Language Models
authors: Ekaterina Fedorova, Alessandro Morosini, Chara Podimata
abstract: As people increasingly rely on large language models (LLMs) for information, model providers need to communicate meaningful estimates of whether individual responses are correct or, more generally, reliable. In the context of hallucinations, existing work uses multicalibration to make such reliability predictions meaningful across application-relevant groups, such as prompt topics. Topic groups alone, however, can conceal systematic errors: within the same topic and confidence level, responses with different chain-of-thought (CoT) properties may exhibit opposing errors that cancel on average. In this work, we introduce reasoning-aware multicalibration, a framework that supplements application-relevant topic groups with groups derived from observable properties of CoT traces. We highlight that, theoretically, groupings based on CoT are "internally important", i.e., groupings for which the multicalibration guarantee is not societally crucial as it is for high-risk topics, but whose inclusion in the multicalibration procedure could easily and significantly improve predictive accuracy of the final reliability predictor. Empirically, we apply our framework to hallucination prediction and unsafe-response detection across a variety of benchmarks, and find that adding CoT groups to topic-based calibration reduces Brier score in both tasks. Interestingly, we find that multicalibrating with respect to CoT groups alone (without any topic information) already improves calibration across topics, suggesting that the predictor's errors depend on how the model reasoned, rather than what it was asked about in the prompt.

title: Sustainable and Envy-free Multi-Period Allocation
authors: Robert Bredereck, Eva Deltl, Till Fluschnik
abstract: Allocating renewable resources fairly requires accounting for how present decisions affect future availability. We introduce Sustainable and Envy-Free Multi-Period Allocation, in which agents are assigned over multiple periods to renewable resources whose quantities evolve over time according to renewal functions. An allocation must respect viability and capacity constraints while being envy-free over the whole time horizon. We study the computational and parameterized complexity of finding such allocations, with a focus on the three dimensions of the problem: the numbers of agents, resources, and periods. We show that finding such an allocation is NP-hard already for unary encoding and any single one of them being fixed to a constant. Whether two small dimensions suffice for tractability depends on the pair, the class of renewal functions, and the numerical encoding. For few resources and periods, binary-encoded instances remain hard in general, whereas unary encoding yields XP-time algorithms. For few resources and agents, binary-encoded instances also remain hard in general but become XP-time solvable when all renewal functions are translations. Few agents and periods yield fixed-parameter tractability, but no polynomial kernel under standard complexity assumptions.

title: Two-qubit cryo-CMOS control of a spin register in diamond
authors: H. B. van Ommen, N. E. Fakkel, M. van Riggelen, J. Yun, L. A. Enthoven, M. A. B. ElBadry, F. Sebastiano, M. Babaie, T. H. Taminiau
abstract: Utility-scale quantum technologies will not only require a well-performing quantum platform, but also classical control hardware that is scalable, efficient, and meets the design requirements set by the quantum system of interest. One approach is the application of silicon CMOS technology, a highly scalable and mature technology, to design application-specific integrated circuits (ASIC) that are optimized for the quantum system. In this work, we present two-qubit control of electron and nuclear spins in NV centres in diamond, using a cryogenic CMOS qubit controller integrated with a diamond quantum device in a cryostat. Using Gate Set Tomography (GST) we characterize the performance of the single-qubit gates on both electron- and carbon nuclear spins, and analyze the limiting noise processes. We use dynamical decoupling to engineer a two-qubit gate, and estimate $F_\text{2q,avg} = 95(2)\%$ for the electron-nuclear two-qubit gate fidelity. Our demonstration of cryo-CMOS-driven two-qubit gates is a key step towards highly-integrated quantum devices based on colour centres.

title: A Bayesian Distance-Weighted Ising Model for Task-Related Regional Analysis of Neuroimaging Data
authors: Heesang Lee, Jongrak Park, Seoyoung Choi, Bokgyeong Kang, Nial Friel, Sanghoon Han, Jaewoo Park
abstract: Neuroimaging analysis commonly involves classifying cognitive conditions, identifying task-relevant brain regions, and examining functional connectivity. These objectives are typically addressed separately, without a model-based framework. In contrast, we propose a Bayesian distance-weighted Ising model that integrates classification, regional importance, and connectivity analysis. The model captures dependence among task labels based on connectivities between functional signals, while region-of-interest (ROI)-specific interaction parameters account for spatial heterogeneity and quantify regional contributions to task discrimination. However, inference is challenging because the signals may be observed on unequal time grids and the likelihood function contains an intractable normalising constant. To address this, we use a basis expansion and an auxiliary variable Markov chain Monte Carlo algorithm. We apply the method to functional near-infrared spectroscopy data from younger and older adults, comparing resting-state and task-related activity. The model achieves high classification accuracy and reveals age-dependent patterns of regional importance and connectivity. Among younger adults, the left orbitofrontal cortex contributes more strongly to task discrimination than the dorsolateral prefrontal and frontopolar cortices, whereas regional differences are less evident among older adults. Older adults also exhibit greater bilateral connectivity between corresponding ROIs, consistent with reduced hemispheric lateralisation.

title: Bounds on the Service Rates of Linear Codes and their Connections to Combinatorial Designs
authors: Monika Yadav, Priyanka Choudhary, Maheshanand Bhaintwal
abstract: The service rate region of a distributed storage system describes the set of concurrent demand vectors that can be served without overloading any individual server, and is a fundamental measure of how effectively redundancy is used. In this paper, we investigate aggregate service rates in distributed data storage systems based on linear codes over arbitrary finite fields.
