We propose a multi-step pipeline based on grammatical annotation models, fine-tuned large language models, and a teacher-student setup to produce the alignments. We evaluate the lexica against reference dictionaries and manually corrected gold alignments. We release the lexica and the fine-tuned span annotation model, together with a web interface for looking up headwords and their attested senses.

title: A fast Laguerre--Fourier spectral method for the polyatomic Boltzmann collision operator with continuous internal energ
authors: Pei Zhang, Yanli Wang, Zhenning Cai
abstract: The polyatomic Boltzmann equation extends the classical kinetic description to gases whose molecules possess internal energy in addition to their translational motion. The distribution function then has one more variable than in the monatomic case, and the collision operator becomes an eight-fold integral whose evaluation dominates the cost of solving the equation. In this work, we propose a fast Laguerre--Fourier spectral method for the polyatomic Boltzmann equation with continuous internal energy, which evaluates the collision operator in $O(K^2MN^4\log N + K^3MN^4)$ online operations after a solution-independent precomputation, where $N$ is the number of Fourier modes in each velocity direction, $K$ is the number of Laguerre modes and $M$ is the number of quadrature points on the sphere. Specifically, the distribution function is expanded in generalized Laguerre functions in the internal energy and in Fourier modes in velocity. A sequence of changes of variables then separates the internal-energy integrals from the velocity convolutions, so that the former no longer involve the distribution function and are computed once and stored. Numerical experiments are presented for both the spatially homogeneous and the spatially inhomogeneous Boltzmann equation. They confirm the spectral accuracy of the proposed method and its agreement with the direct simulation Monte Carlo method.

title: LEAPS: Long-context Evaluation of Adaptive Pattern Learning and State Tracking
authors: Howard Yen, Nitya Mani, Alex Renda, Christopher S. Hardin
abstract: Long-context language models (LCLMs) power agents that act over long trajectories, from improving a codebase to running research experiments to forecasters that condition on lengthy histories. These applications draw on three distinct long-context capabilities: recall, where the answer is a fact present in the context; state tracking, where the outcome can be computed by performing a series of transformations to a specified state; and pattern learning, where the goal is to make a prediction by sampling from a distribution inferred from many observations. Existing benchmarks primarily focus on the first capability. In this work, we introduce LEAPS (Long-context Evaluation of Adaptive Pattern learning and State tracking), a collection of 12 novel datasets, spanning agentic workflows, behavioral modeling, and forecasting of market and world events. By construction, LEAPS is resistant to data contamination, extends to millions of input tokens, and uses reliable metrics. We evaluate 30 API and open models from 8K to 512K input tokens. LEAPS distinguishes models that perform near perfectly on recall tasks, finding that such models' state tracking and pattern learning abilities can vary significantly and degrade much more dramatically with increasing input lengths--even for pattern learning, where more observations should make learning a theoretically easier task. Moreover, thinking models often underperform their base counterparts, exhausting their generation budget or oversimplifying the task. We hope LEAPS can guide the development of the next generation of LCLMs.

title: An Analysis of Semantic and Spatio-Temporal Co-evolution for Edge Classification on Dynamic Text-Attributed Graphs
authors: Tyler Bonnet, Marek Rei
abstract: Dynamic edge classification on text-attributed Web graphs, such as review networks, community forums, and news-derived knowledge graphs, requires high quality, adaptive semantic representations in the context of network evolution. Existing dynamic graph architectures typically initialize text feature vectors with pretrained language models and hold them static during training to preserve their semantic structure, forgoing the potential benefits of allowing them to co-evolve with network topology. In this work, we investigate the effects of enabling such co-evolution with a unified text-graph alignment framework that integrates a lightweight Transformer adapter to update token-level text representations via spatio-temporal gradients from a contrastive pretraining objective. To prevent detrimental semantic distortion, a language model maintenance objective anchors the evolving text embeddings to their original semantic structure. Evaluations on the Dynamic Text-Attributed Graph Benchmark demonstrate that this anchored text-graph co-evolution consistently improves upon the edge classification performance of frozen-text baselines across diverse Web-related domains. Representational analyses reveal that the framework reduces anisotropy, improving the linear separability of text embeddings, and effectively encodes structural and temporal information into the semantic space. A computational efficiency analysis confirms that this beneficial semantic and spatio-temporal co-evolution is achieved without incurring the prohibitive computational overhead typical of end-to-end joint training.

title: SWE-Residual: Evaluating Starting-State Robustness of Coding Agents
authors: Jinze Li, Weijie Liu, Jinfeng Xu, Shuo Yang, Xin Yang, Yang Zhang, Yijin Wang, Zifei Shan, Edith C. H. Ngai
abstract: Software engineering (SWE) benchmarks are the primary way to measure the capabilities of coding agents: an agent is placed in a code repository or machine environment, given a request, and judged by hidden tests. These benchmarks almost always start the agent from a clean state that contains no earlier work on the task. In practice, however, agents often continue work that a developer or another agent has already done and reported as complete, with no indication of what remains incorrect or missing. We introduce SWE-Residual, a benchmark for Starting-State Robustness: the ability to maintain performance on a task when the starting state already contains earlier work on that task. SWE-Residual contains 198 Residual States drawn from 111 tasks in DeepSWE and Terminal-Bench, where the earlier work modifies a code repository or a whole machine environment. Each Residual State is the state a predecessor agent left behind after submitting its work as complete, although the hidden tests still fail. The evaluated agent receives only the original request and this state, without the predecessor's trajectory or any sign that the attempt failed; because the request and hidden tests are unchanged, the starting state is the only difference from the source benchmark. Across five frontier agents, success drops by 20.6--53.5 percentage points on DeepSWE and 20.6--34.9 points on Terminal-Bench relative to a Clean Start, and agent rankings on DeepSWE reverse. Failed continuations show a pattern we call acceptance bias: agents treat the inherited work as the definition of what remains to be done instead of checking it against the request. On DeepSWE, in 58.9--88.2% of failed runs, they submit with exactly the same tests failing, although they pass most of these tests from a Clean Start. SWE-Residual thus exposes a capability gap that clean-start evaluation does not capture.

title: A double-logarithmic lifespan bound for axisymmetric Euler equations with a small initial swirl
authors: Zijin Li, Xu Xiao, Linbin Yang
abstract: We study the three-dimensional axisymmetric incompressible Euler equations in $\mathbb{R}^3$ with a small initial swirl. Fix $s>7/2$, and let $\boldsymbol{v}_0\in H^s(\mathbb{R}^3)$ be axisymmetric and divergence-free. If $\varepsilon=\|{\nabla\times(v_{0,θ}\boldsymbol{e}_θ)}\|_{L^\infty}$ is sufficiently small, then the lifespan $T_*$ of the corresponding $H^s$ solution satisfies $$ T_{*}\geq\frac{C_s}{1+\|{\boldsymbol{v}_0}\|_{H^s}} \left[ \log\log (\varepsilon^{-1}) \right]^{3/7}\,. $$ Moreover, if $\boldsymbol{v}_0$ only belongs to $H^3$, we improve the fourfold iterated-logarithmic lifespan bound by Li and Zhou (Z. Angew. Math. Phys. 75:219 2024) to a threefold iterated-logarithmic bound.

title: Two-step nilpotent Lie algebras obtained by quivers and geometric structures
authors: Fumika Mizoguchi
abstract: In the study of geometric structures on nilmanifolds, two-step nilpotent Lie algebras obtained by graphs play an important role. Recently, additional examples of nilpotent Lie algebras have been constructed from finite quivers without cycles. These latter examples can have arbitrarily high degrees of nilpotency, and admit Riemannian Ricci soliton metrics. In this paper, we study nilpotent Lie algebras obtained by finite quivers without cycles that are two-step nilpotent, and we prove that they can also be obtained by graphs. Using this relationship, we demonstrate that every two-step nilpotent Lie algebra obtained by a finite quiver without cycles admits a pseudo-Riemannian Ricci-flat metric. Additionally, we also classify these nilpotent Lie algebras that admit symplectic structures.

title: Learn the Interface, Not the Implementation: Output Representation Dominates Training Regime in LLM-Based RTL Generation
authors: Siddharth Patel, Vikram Singh, Siddharth Savyasachi Malu, Rohit Singh
abstract: Large-language-model register-transfer-level (RTL) generation has concentrated on how to train the model: fine-tuning, continued pre-training, and reinforcement learning from a verifier. We argue this is the second-order question. On a bounded, formally specifiable task of generating single-error-correcting, double-error-detecting (SECDED) ECC memory wrappers, we hold the task, data, and correctness oracle fixed and vary two axes independently: the training regime (seven settings) and the output representation (four levels, from fully expanded flat Verilog to an eight-field configuration expanded by a deterministic generator). Because a reference generator exists, correctness is decided by formal equivalence over a design space of approximately ten million points, rather than sampled from a hand-written testbench. Two results follow. First, representation dominates: every representation close to raw RTL reaches a pass rate of at most 0.17, while the configuration reaches 0.83 with no training at all. Once the model emits the configuration, every training regime achieves a pass rate between 0.89 and 1.00. Second, raw RTL hits a hard output-length limit: a 512-bit design requires 44,237 tokens of flat Verilog compared with just 69 tokens for the configuration. Consequently, raw generation becomes infeasible above 32-bit data words rather than merely inaccurate. A model trained from scratch with fewer than 50 million parameters, combined with the verified generator, achieves 0.89 formal equivalence, compared with 1.00 for a 32-billion-parameter fine-tuned model, while using approximately 1600 times less inference energy per correct design. Inference energy also dominates amortized training energy. The lesson is to learn the interface, not the implementation.

title: DeltaTrace: Efficient Signed Attribution for Reasoning Language Models
authors: Chen Liang, Daoping Wu, Donghua Yang, Zhiyu Liang, Ying Zhang, Shuguang Xiong, Hongzhi Wang
abstract: We study how words in the context support or oppose a language model's response and present DeltaTrace, a novel attribution framework that explains the effect of input tokens on a fixed model response. DeltaTrace measures how the response's log-probability changes when the context tokens being explained are masked. To distribute this difference among source tokens, it constructs operator-specific local rules for finite changes and composes them backward through the computational graph using effective secant slopes. Each token is assigned a signed attribution as the inner product of its embedding displacement and the corresponding backward-propagated slope. Local conservation makes these contributions sum to the measured score difference and preserves their meaning when aggregated over sentences or passages. DeltaTrace supports both attention and linear-attention models, with auxiliary memory growing linearly with sequence length at fixed model dimensions and chunk size. On the evaluated attention model, DeltaTrace achieves the lowest deletion-faithfulness scores (RISE and MAS) on most retrieval and reasoning tasks and the highest needle-in-a-haystack Recall, exceeding FlashTrace by 5.67-24.33 percentage points. On the evaluated hybrid attention and linear-attention model, DeltaTrace lowers RISE on 9 tasks and MAS on 12 relative to FlashTrace.

title: Constant mixed Chern curvature on complete type-A flag manifolds
authors: Yuqin Guo, Donmei Zhan
abstract: We prove that the complete flag manifold SU(m)/T m-1, with m >= 3 and its standard complex structure, admits no invariant Hermitian metric with constant mixed Chern curvature when the coefficient of the holomorphic sectional curvature is nonzero. This extends the preceding nonexistence result for a particular Wallach metric on SU(3)/T2 to all invariant Hermitian metrics and to complete type-A flags of arbitrary dimension. Curvature evaluations on holomorphic root spheres contradict a necessary trace identity, covering both Kahler and non-Kahler invariant metrics and excluding both zero and nonzero curvature constants.

title: Effects of Nonmagnetic Impurities on Nonequilibrium Phase Transitions in Microwave-Driven Superconductors
authors: Taira Kawamura
abstract: We investigate the nonequilibrium steady states of a microwave-driven BCS superconductor in the presence of nonmagnetic impurity scattering and energy relaxation. Using the Floquet-Nambu-Keldysh Green's function method together with the self-consistent Born approximation, we self-consistently determine the superconducting order parameter in the microwave-driven steady state. We find that the nonequilibrium phase diagram depends strongly on the impurity-scattering strength. When impurity scattering is absent or weak, the steady-state order parameter is single-valued at each temperature and drive frequency. At intermediate scattering strengths, we find bistability between microwave-enhanced and microwave-suppressed superconducting states. As the impurity-scattering strength increases further, we instead find bistability between the superconducting and normal states. This evolution reflects competition between two effects of microwave driving: Eliashberg-type enhancement through the redistribution of thermally excited quasiparticles and suppression through pair-breaking-induced quasiparticle generation. In contrast to the robustness of equilibrium $s$-wave superconductivity against nonmagnetic impurity scattering, our results demonstrate that nonmagnetic impurity scattering plays a central role in determining the character of nonequilibrium superconducting phase transitions under microwave driving.

title: Are Self-Evolving Agents Continual Learners?
authors: Xiaoyin Chen, Yizheng Huang, Yinglun Xu, Ziyun Zhao, Emmett McQuinn, Julie Liu, Hope Yao
abstract: Large language model agents are often deployed in environments where new knowledge, tools, and workflows keep arriving. Such an agent is therefore expected to adapt continually, learning new tasks as they arrive without forgetting earlier ones. This resembles the continual learning problem, but at a pace that conventional gradient updates cannot sustain. Nonparametric self-evolving agents are a natural alternative: they adapt by rewriting their own harness, such as prompts, memory, and skills, from task feedback while the model weights stay frozen. We study whether such agents are effective continual learners across four drifting task streams that shift in topic, workflow, or domain (built from BIRD, BFCL, and ScienceWorld). Evaluating three representative methods spanning experience retrieval and self-modification (ReasoningBank, GEPA, and Meta-Harness), we find that although self-evolution improves aggregate performance on most streams, higher plasticity consistently comes at the cost of stability. Specifically, self-modifying methods apply global edits to a shared prompt or workspace, interfering with unseen tasks and overwriting earlier knowledge as the stream shifts. Conversely, similarity-based memory retrieval localizes updates across distant domains, but still retrieves foreign memories on unseen tasks and suffers from retrieval collision when similar queries require conflicting workflows. These findings show that current self-evolving agents remain incomplete continual learners.

title: Statistical Learning Theory for Direct Preference Optimization
authors: Joel Wills, Yuanfan Li, Yiming Ying, Ding-Xuan Zhou
abstract: Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) learns from pairwise preferences through a logistic objective whose score-difference parameterization follows the Bradley--Terry model. We study how failure of this modeling assumption limits DPO, distinguishing structural misspecification from limited model capacity and finite-sample estimation. Our main contribution is a characterization of structural approximation error through the triangle-curl of the preference log-odds, which vanishes exactly when preferences admit a Bradley--Terry representation. We upper bound the achievable excess logistic risk by a score-class approximation term and a triangle-curl term, and establish a lower bound proportional to triangle-curl under additional boundedness assumptions. For ReLU score models, including clipped models, we derive explicit approximation rates showing that increasing capacity can eliminate the score-approximation term while leaving the structural obstruction unchanged. We further establish finite-sample bounds for clipped empirical risk minimizers that separate network approximation, structural misspecification, and estimation error. We place these results within a surrogate-risk framework by identifying contextual preference accuracy (CPA) as a natural measure of agreement between preference judgments and changes in pairwise probability ratios relative to the reference policy. Standard logistic consistency and calibration results connect DPO's objective to this policy property and transfer our excess-risk upper bounds to CPA, without treating CPA as a complete measure of generated-response quality.

title: ACE-Trader: Adversarial Co-Evolution for Generator-Critic Trading Systems
authors: Chang Zhou, Jiarun Zhou, Xingtong Yu, Hong Cheng, Hui Zhang, Xinming Zhang
abstract: Generator--critic trading systems pair an LLM-based trader that makes trading decisions with a red team agent that evaluates these decisions and provides feedback for revision. However, improving individual trading decisions does not ensure that both agents learn from experience and improve together over time. This raises an important question: how can the trader and red-Team select useful experience and learn from each other's evolving behavior? On one hand, experience that benefits decisions under one market condition may become ineffective or harmful under another. On the other hand, trading outcomes reflect both agents' actions, making it difficult to derive appropriate experience for each role. In this work, we propose ACE-Trader, an adversarial co-evolution trading framework. Specifically, we first develop separate context-dependent memory selectors that learn to identify useful experience for the current trading decision. Both selectors receive shared feedback from net-return differences between complete memory-assisted and memory-free trading pipelines, with online updates emphasizing recent outcomes. We further design a co-evolution mechanism that links role-specific memories through shared trading records. We use these records to evaluate the Red-Team's risk assessments and the effects of the Trader's revisions against realized market outcomes, then derive experience for their respective memories. By linking this experience to the corresponding records, we enable the Trader to improve its proposals based on prior critiques and the Red-Team to adjust its review focus as the Trader's behavior changes. Experiments on U.S. stock trading show that ACE-Trader outperforms all 22 active baselines in cumulative return and achieves the highest Sharpe ratio and lowest maximum drawdown across both active methods and passive benchmarks.

title: Measurement Validity and Representation Dynamics of Confidence Signals in Large Language Models
authors: Debojeet Ghosh, Shreyansh Kumar, Ayushman Garg
abstract: Whether a language model "knows what it knows" matters for trustworthy deployment and for deciding when it should abstain. Prior work usually measures this through one channel: verbalized confidence, a linear probe on hidden states, or agreement among sampled answers (semantic entropy), and often treats these as interchangeable. We compare all three in a pre-registered audit of five Qwen2.5 models (0.5B-7B, including a base/instruct pair at 7B) on factual retrieval (PopQA, SimpleQA) and multi-step reasoning (GSM8K, MATH). First, probes trained on prefill states to predict whether sampled answers will disagree become informative earlier for retrieval (about 7% of layer depth on average) than for reasoning (about 28%). The pre-registered five-layer test supported this only marginally; a finer 21-layer follow-up, designed after those results, supports it more clearly. In most retrieval cells, however, a prompt-only TF-IDF classifier matches the probe, so the early signal may reflect surface features of the question. Second, verbalized confidence is unstable: slightly different prompt templates yield scores that barely correlate. Third, Expected Calibration Error is misleading: verbal confidence looks well calibrated because it clusters near the base rate while discriminating poorly, whereas sampling agreement has worse ECE but about twice the resolution. Of five pre-registered hypotheses, two were falsified, one was partly supported, one was not supported, and one could not be tested because the base model's verbal confidence was degenerate.

title: Exact minimum Birkhoff decompositions of doubly stochastic matrices with finite precision
authors: András Czégel
abstract: The minimum Birkhoff decomposition problem asks for a representation of a doubly stochastic matrix as a convex combination of as few permutation matrices as possible. This NP-hard problem arises in the scheduling of switches in data centers and satellite systems, in random assignments in economics and in the statistics of rankings. We consider doubly stochastic matrices whose entries are given with a fixed number of decimal digits and look for exact decompositions whose weights have the same precision. We propose a parallel method with three parts. For matrices built from few permutation matrices, the first part reads the weights from the frequencies of the entries and places them on the matrix positions by a rule that, given the correct weights, never fixes a position wrongly. The second part computes lower bounds from pairs of rows or columns, which remain valid for real weights, and from certificates of a satisfiability solver. For matrices built from many permutation matrices, the third part runs a beam search over steps that each make at least one entry zero. On 375 test instances with up to 100 rows, the method proves optimality for 208 instances, and 197 of these proofs also hold for real weights. Of the 190 instances built from few permutation matrices, 187 are solved to proven optimality, 180 of them within one second. Compared with the best exact decompositions known before, the new decompositions are shorter for 278 instances and never longer.

title: Piercing spanned lines and hyperplanes
authors: Ben Lund
abstract: Motzkin, Grünbaum, and Erdős and Purdy asked how many noncollinear blue points can coexist with $t$ red points in the real plane if every blue-spanned line contains a red point. We prove that there are at most $2.35t-3$ blue points, even over the complex numbers. For the complex higher-dimensional problem of Campbell, Kroeker, and Lund, we prove $b_k(t)\le1.40k^2t$. Colorings of cyclic Dowling geometries give a matching lower bound in order of magnitude for all $k\ge2$ and $t\ge3$. The planar proof uses frame normalization and a second-moment estimate; the higher-dimensional proof combines the degree bound of Kroeker and Lund with principal truncation.

title: When Retrieval Partially Conflicts with Skills: Understanding Procedural Hallucination in Language Models
authors: Guanqun Jiang, Pengfei Cao, Kang Liu, Jun Zhao
abstract: Language models increasingly use skills that provide reusable instructions and procedures for task execution. After a relevant skill has been selected, the model may need to apply its governing procedure together with retrieved task context. When the retrieved context is useful but contains cues that violate the skill, the model must retain compatible information while rejecting the conflicting cues. We study failures in which the model adopts such cues and produces a retrieval-supported but skill-invalid answer, which we call procedural hallucination. We introduce SourceClash, a matched benchmark with 1,271 bundles and 6,355 prompts across ten procedural domains. Each bundle fixes the task, skill specification, and answer space while varying the relation between the skill and retrieval. Across nine models, valid-answer rates average 25.7% under conflicting retrieval, compared with 78.2% and 72.8% under two supportive retrieval settings. Mechanistic analysis of open-weight models shows that the answer-preference difference typically reaches its maximum shortly after generation begins. Residual replacement moves the model toward valid answers, while attention decomposition attributes most of the repair to value vectors. Intervention at the identified value pathway also improves final answer validity. These results characterize how partly conflicting retrieval changes skill-guided generation.

title: Classification of all non-split central extensions of naturally graded 2-filiform non-Lie Leibniz algebras
authors: Kobiljon Abdurasulov, Jobir Adashev
abstract: This paper deals with the naturally graded 2-filiform non-Lie Leibniz algebras over the field of complex numbers. There are two finite series of such algebras, defined in every dimension starting from five, and two further algebras which occur only in dimension five. For each of these algebras we classify, up to isomorphism, all of its non-split central extensions, of every possible dimension. The one-dimensional central extensions are already known from an earlier work, so the main part of the paper is devoted to the extensions of dimension two and higher. As usual, the classification is reduced to the description of the orbits of the automorphism group of the algebra on the subspaces of its second cohomology space with trivial coefficients. For each algebra and each dimension we give the complete list of these orbits together with the multiplication tables of the corresponding algebras, and we point out the extensions whose annihilator coincides with the added central ideal. Among the algebras obtained there are 2-filiform Leibniz algebras which are not naturally graded; this class of algebras has not been systematically studied so far.

title: Modal Sense Disambiguation in Language Models: The Role of Context, Training Domain, and Input Frequency
authors: Ezgi Başar, Yevgen Matusevych, Annemarie van Dooren, Arianna Bisazza
abstract: Modals such as may and must can take on different senses depending on discourse context, alternating between root interpretations (e.g., permission, obligation) and epistemic interpretations (e.g., knowledge, belief). While modals are known to be notoriously difficult for children to acquire, limited research exists on whether language models (LMs) can reliably distinguish between different modal senses. We evaluate seven LMs that vary in architecture, size, and training data type using vector-based similarity and surprisal measures across four datasets. Specifically, we investigate whether LMs can leverage contextual information to disambiguate modal senses and whether their performance reflects the distribution of modal senses in their training data. We show that larger LMs trained on diverse text successfully leverage additional contextual information when available. In the absence of context, they tend to favor the dominant sense based on corpus statistics. Smaller developmentally plausible LMs, including those trained on child-directed language (CDL), fail to show consistent sensitivity to modal sense distinctions and do not benefit from context to the same degree.

title: 2-Local Derivations on Conformal Galilei Lie Algebras and Their Central Extensions
authors: Bekzod Sultonboyev, Bakhtiyor Yusupov
abstract: We classify 2-local derivations on the finite-dimensional conformal Galilei Lie algebras in three natural settings: the algebra without central extension, the mass central extension, and the exotic central extension. No additivity or linearity is assumed in the definition of a 2-local derivation. We prove that in every case each 2-local derivation is an ordinary derivation. For the unextended algebra, the proof combines characteristic-quotient normalization with separating vectors, invariant bilinear forms, rank-two mixed zero anchors, and a semisimple-perturbation argument for the standard module. For the mass central extension with $2\ell\ge3$, the residual map is first reduced to the center and then eliminated by a symplectic-anchor construction on the Heisenberg radical; a dimension argument in the centralizer of a regular semisimple element simultaneously handles singular reductive actions and the additional central shear that occurs in spatial dimension two. The endpoint $\ell=\tfrac12$ is the Schrödinger algebra; a self-contained symplectic-anchor proof includes all spatial dimensions, with explicit treatment of dimensions one and two. For the exotic extension, after center normalization we use conjugate middle-weight positions and an affine middle anchor to eliminate every central translate, including the one-sided middle-weight configurations. Consequently the set of 2-local derivations coincides with the derivation algebra for all admissible parameters, and hence every 2-local derivation in these families is automatically linear.

title: Amortized Neural Filtering for Calibrated Posteriors in Statistical Arbitrage
authors: Minkey Chang
abstract: Statistical arbitrage trades on an estimate of the state of a residual spread, and conventional practice discards the uncertainty of that estimate. We keep the uncertainty and use it in the trading decision. A Neural Filter Estimator (NFE) is trained on simulated paths of a mean-reverting process whose innovation law is selected by testing candidates against real residuals; once trained, it returns the posterior over the latent state of every spread in a cross-section in one forward pass. Three results follow. On simulated paths with known truth, every practical estimator, ours included, falls in one narrow band of accuracy well below an estimator given full information, so the posterior gains no accuracy over a point estimate; its contribution is a correct account of its own uncertainty. On Korean equities, net of costs, the conventional point estimate forecasts about a thousand basis points per holding period more than it realizes, and the amortized methods cut that gap by a factor of roughly two to eight. Sizing positions from the posterior on the same learned factors as the end-to-end Attention Factor Model matches the Sharpe ratio of those factors under the base rule within the period's noise, at no more risk.

title: Learning Complementary Agent Groups via Task Hypergraphs for Next-POI Recommendation with Missing Modalities
authors: Jinze Wang, Yuze Liu, Liang Yuan, Gaoyuan Du, Xiaohang Xu, Yong Xiang, Jiong Jin
abstract: Next point-of-interest (POI) recommendation uses visit histories and POI content, but text and images are often missing. Large language model agents have been applied to recommender systems for preference modeling and evidence acquisition. The challenge is to select agents that can jointly analyze the available evidence for each request. We propose \textsc{CATH} (\emph{Complementary Agents via Task Hypergraphs}), which learns to select agent groups for tasks such as comparing candidates or analyzing a POI with missing content. Agents with distinct processing roles are the task hypergraph nodes; each hyperedge connects the selected group and records its analysis goal and target POIs. The policy selects members conditioned on the request, task, and agents already selected. During execution, members share candidate-linked results that guide their subsequent operations. Completed tasks update candidate states and agent memories within the request. A shared ranking head converts candidate states into corrections to a fixed base ranking. Supervised ranking trains the executor, followed by policy optimization that accounts for computation cost. Experiments under natural missingness on Gowalla-CA, Foursquare-NYC, and Foursquare-TKY show 8.4--9.1\% relative NDCG@20 gains over HyperAgent4POI, the strongest prior baseline evaluated. Additional analyses compare group-selection and execution designs, test ranking under additional masking, and characterize quality--cost tradeoffs.

title: SAR: Learning Global Item-Space Matching and Geometry-Aware Placement Ranking for Buffered Online 3D Bin Packing
authors: Xinpeng Lei, Jin Zhang, Yizhe Yang, Yihong Duan, Fucheng Wan
abstract: Online 3D bin packing with a bounded buffer requires irreversible item-selection and placement decisions under limited knowledge of future arrivals. Feasibility alone is insufficient, as feasible actions can produce different residual-space structures and subsequent packing opportunities. A central architectural question is how to allocate spatial reasoning between item selection and placement evaluation. We propose Spatial Affordance Retrieval (SAR), a novel learning-based framework that coordinates global item-space matching with geometry-aware placement ranking. A voxel-token spatial encoder represents 3D container occupancy, enabling a picker to match buffered items to the residual space without requiring item-specific placement proposals as inputs. After item selection, a loader ranks feasible rotation-position candidates using candidate geometry, local geometric features (LGF), and inter-candidate comparison, without directly accessing global spatial tokens. The feasible candidate set connects the two stages, which are jointly optimized under a shared long-horizon packing return. On the Random, JD, and SF datasets, the best SAR variants improve utilization over the strongest evaluated online baselines by 0.96-4.20 percentage points under the no-buffer setting (K=1). With a buffer (K=5), the best utilization rates across SAR variants reach 93.55%, 91.04%, and 90.41%, respectively. Ablations support the complementary roles of global item-space matching and geometry-aware placement evaluation, counterfactual analysis suggests that learned item selection favors greater future packing potential, and experiments demonstrate compatibility with multiple candidate generators.

title: Finite BSC-Decomposition of Binary-Input Symmetric-Output Channels and Applications to Channel Simulation
authors: Jianguo Zhao, Cheuk Ting Li
abstract: We propose a finite BSC-decomposition method for representing an arbitrary binary-input symmetric-output channel (BISOC) as a mixture of binary symmetric channels (BSCs) with at most $\ell+1$ distinct crossover probabilities. We show that the weighted average capacity of the component BSCs exceeds the capacity of the original BISOC by at most $(π^2\log e)/(48\ell^2)+O(\ell^{-5/2})$ bits, and the leading term is asymptotically optimal in the worst case. Based on the finite BSC-decomposition, we design a channel simulation scheme for arbitrary BISOCs. Combined with efficient channel simulation algorithms for BSCs, our scheme achieves a communication rate with $O((\log n / n)^{2/3})$ redundancy over the capacity for simulating $n$ copies of a BISOC.

title: Towards Architectural-Level Safety Control: Relocating Hazardous Knowledge into Removable Experts in Mixture-of-Experts Models
authors: Cheng Jin, Zhongtian Ma, Xiao Wang, Han Qi, Xiaoyu Wen, Xiang Wang, Youbang Sun, Xia Hu, Bowen Zhou, Chaochao Lu, Qiaosheng Zhang
abstract: Large language models acquire broad knowledge from web-scale corpora during pretraining, including knowledge that could be hazardous if misused. Removing such knowledge from the model itself without degrading general capability is desirable but difficult, as it is deeply entangled with general capability within the same parameters. Existing safety alignment and unlearning methods typically adjust these shared parameters, tending to suppress the expression of hazardous knowledge rather than remove it. As a result, the knowledge remains in the model and is readily recoverable by subsequent fine-tuning. To address this limitation, we propose REX (Relocating into Removable EXperts), a knowledge relocation method that separates hazardous knowledge from general capability at the architectural level. Exploiting the modular structure of Mixture-of-Experts models, REX expands the model with a set of new, physically removable experts designated to hold hazardous knowledge. Through expert expansion, selective gradient masking and routing differentiation, it relocates hazardous knowledge out of the original experts and concentrates it in the new ones. Excising these new experts yields a model suitable for public release. This removal holds consistently across Intern-S2, Qwen3.5-35B-A3B and Gemma-4-26B-A4B; on Qwen3.5-35B-A3B, for instance, excision lowers WMDP-Bio accuracy by 48.4 points while MMLU changes by less than 3 points. The excised model matches the strongest of nine unlearning baselines in removing hazardous knowledge, and it is the only one that preserves this removal under subsequent fine-tuning. After 250M tokens of standard fine-tuning on Qwen3.5, the best baseline rebounds on WMDP-Bio from 44.1% to 78.3%, whereas REX rises only from 32.4% to 42.8%.

title: CoMem: Learning to Anticipate Failures from Retrieved Experience
authors: Yun Shen, Ming Shen, Tianjun Yao
abstract: Reflection lets LLM agents improve from their own attempts, but the memory it builds is local to a single task, so an agent reflecting on its own tends to revisit the same explanation for failure. Cross-task reflective memory addresses this in two forms: retrieved memory keeps past experience explicit and looks up related cases, which is specific but bounded by the bank, and parametric memory internalizes experience into parameters, which generalizes but is grounded in nothing beyond the task description. When both are used, existing agents combine them additively, feeding their outputs to the solver side by side, so retrieved experience never changes what the learned memory produces. We introduce CoMem (Compounding Memory), which makes retrieved experience an input to the learned memory itself, at training and at inference. The agent builds a bank of its own successful and failed reflections, learns from retrieved cases to write failure hypotheses, candidate explanations of how an attempt is likely to go wrong, and at test time reasons from newly retrieved cases to guide each attempt. Varying the retrieved cases gives the memory different perspectives, yielding reflective diversity that is not merely sampled but also grounded in retrieved experience. Across two backbones and five benchmarks in math, code, and multi-hop QA, CoMem achieves strong overall performance. Additional evaluations show that it generalizes to out-of-distribution tasks and enables smaller models to provide effective guidance to stronger solvers.

title: Lusztig's asymptotic algebra and a cell factorisation for the second lowest two-sided cell in type $\tilde{B}_n$
authors: James Parkinson
abstract: We determine Lusztig's asymptotic algebra for the second lowest two-sided cell~$Δ_1$ in the equal parameter extended affine Weyl group $\tilde{\mathsf{B}}_n$ for all $n\geq 2$, realising it as a full matrix algebra over the representation ring of $\mathsf{Sp}_{2n-2}(\CC)\times C_2$ with $C_2$ the group of order~$2$. Our result is an explicit isomorphism of based rings, determining the image of each basis element $\mathsf{t}_w$ of the asymptotic algebra. As a consequence we verify that Lusztig's original conjecture from 1989 on the structure of the asymptotic algebra holds for this cell. A key ingredient in our proof is a refinement of Shi's description of~$Δ_1$, giving an explicit parametrisation of the elements of this cell (a \textit{cell factorisation}). This cell factorisation simultaneously describes all intersections of left and right cells, with uniqueness and length-additivity of expressions. Applications include a classification of the involutions in $Δ_1$, and a calculation of the length generating functions for $Δ_1$ and the right cells in~$Δ_1$.

title: Remember Less, Adapt Longer: Bounded-State In-Context Reinforcement Learning with Recurrent Summary Memory
authors: Jiawen Wang, Cheng Xue, Peng Zhang, Jochen Renz
abstract: In-context reinforcement learning (ICRL) enables agents to adapt to new tasks without parameter updates, relying on memory to retain what they learn from experience. For agents operating continually, existing approaches using memory trade off bounded cost against access to past experience. Approaches using growing memories, such as full-history attention and accumulating summaries, incur storage and per-decision costs that increase with task length. Fixed-size memories bound storage but restrict access: sliding windows discard older steps, while recurrent networks compress even recent interactions into a hidden state. We introduce Recurrent Summary Memory (RSM), a Transformer policy that attends exactly to a short working buffer of recent interactions and carries a fixed-capacity summary of earlier experience. When the buffer fills, RSM rewrites the summary from its previous contents and the buffer, then clears the buffer, so deployment memory and per-decision cost stay $O(1)$ in task length. On long-running partially observable tasks, frozen RSM policies sustain their adapted performance for eight times the training horizon with about 1% of full-history memory, ending ahead of every evaluated baseline while growing memories deteriorate. When the task configuration changes mid-run, RSM re-adapts better than growing and recurrent memories. Clearing the summary or blocking the policy's access to it removes its benefit, while swapping in another task's summary steers behaviour towards that task. Together, these results show that our fixed-capacity summary can sustain in-context adaptation far beyond the training horizon.

title: Fundamental Limits of Information-Theoretic Secure Aggregation with User Dropouts in Federated Learning
authors: Jinbao Zhu, Kai Wan, Giuseppe Caire
abstract: Secure aggregation enables a server to compute the sum of users' gradients or model updates without revealing individual values. With user dropouts, correlated random keys protect local gradients while allowing recovery of the desired gradient sum. We consider three phases: key distribution, masked-gradient upload, and mask elimination. Users establish correlated keys, upload masked gradients, and provide additional messages to eliminate residual aggregate masks. Existing information-theoretic schemes typically design mask-elimination communication for a prescribed dropout threshold and evaluate its cost under worst-case dropouts across the masked-gradient upload and mask-elimination phases. Such designs cannot adjust communication to actual dropout scenarios. Moreover, the randomness and communication costs of establishing correlated keys remain largely unexplored. To address these limitations, we formulate an adaptive secure aggregation framework under the T-colluding security constraint and construct a single scheme that supports all feasible dropout scenarios by adapting its communication to the actual number of dropouts. We establish converse bounds on four resources: key randomness, key-distribution communication, masked-gradient communication, and mask-elimination communication. The latter two bounds are characterized for each realized dropout set in the masked-gradient upload phase. The proposed scheme achieves the optimal masked-gradient communication rate for every feasible dropout scenario and the optimal mask-elimination communication rate in almost all feasible regimes. Its key rate and key-distribution communication rate are each optimal or within a factor of two of their respective information-theoretic optima. These results characterize the fundamental randomness and communication costs of secure aggregation with user dropouts.

title: Functional Cross-layer Experts Routing for One-step Diffusion Distillation
authors: Zile Huang, Ser-nam Lim
abstract: One-step distillation compresses diffusion trajectories into a single forward evaluation, yet how internal capacity should be structured within that remaining pass remains largely unexplored. In this setting, identical parameters must simultaneously preserve general generative priors and resolve prompt-specific details without iterative refinement. We formalize this challenge as functional allocation. Our analysis reveals that decoupling representations is beneficial only when expert interference outweighs shared transfer, favoring an always-active shared backbone augmented with conditionally routed residuals over standard isolated MoE architectures. We propose DeMoE, which pairs a persistent shared expert with conditionally routed expert slices across image FFNs, trained under a one-step distribution-matching objective with executed-route supervision. On one-step FLUX.2-4B generation, DeMoE achieves a GenEval score of 0.8220 while activating only 80.5% of the image-FFN width, substantially outperforming dense one-step baselines, matching the 50-step teacher overall, and surpassing it on complex composition and counting. Across COCO-10K, DeMoE establishes state-of-the-art fidelity and diversity among single-step models, demonstrating that structured internal computation reallocation provides a superior compression paradigm for diffusion models. Code is available at https://github.com/toffeecat/demoe-ttt-router.

title: Periodic orbits and gravitational-wave emission from extreme-mass-ratio inspirals around rotating charged black holes in nonlinear electrodynamics
authors: Xi Luo, Meirong Tang, Zhaoyi Xu
abstract: Within general-relativistic descriptions, the no-hair theorem dictates that black-hole geometries possess just three intrinsic physical quantities: mass, angular momentum, and electric charge. Black holes in nonlinear electrodynamics (NED) are equivalent to those composed of anisotropic matter and can develop "hair" structures near the event horizon, serving as ideal testbeds for modified theories of gravity. Working within Einsteinian gravitational theory, we adopt a coupling construction between gravity and NED matter, focusing explicitly on the Einstein-Euler-Heisenberg (EEH) variant with the power-index parameter fixed at s = 2. In this framework, a rotating, charged NED black hole extends the Kerr-Newman geometry with extra correction terms. Treating spin a and NED charge q as primary control variables, we examine test-particle dynamics inside extreme-mass-ratio inspiral (EMRI) configurations. We derive equatorial timelike geodesics and the effective potential. Through numerical evaluation of marginally-bound orbits (MBO) and innermost stable circular orbits (ISCO), we explore how these parameters reshape the energy-angular-momentum (E-L) phase-space. Using the (z, w, v) integer-valued orbit taxonomy, we compute the two gravitational-wave polarization modes h+ and hx via the adiabatic approximation and quadrupole radiation prescription. Larger values for a and q drive inward contraction for bound trajectories while displacing the E-L phase-space toward smaller angular-momentum values. Periodic-orbit zoom-whirl signatures grow increasingly prominent, while larger parameter values shorten the waveform periods and enhance signal amplitudes. Our results provide theoretical support for space-borne gravitational-wave observatories including LISA and TianQin, enabling prospects for discriminating NED black-hole spacetimes and performing observational checks on the no-hair theorem.

title: Don't Rewrite the SID Map: Topology Preservation for Generative Retrieval in Dynamic E-Commerce Search
authors: Jianbo Zhu, Xing Fang, Xiaopeng Chu, Mingmin Jin, Jing Wang, Bokang Wang, Jiaqi Ye, Xiang Zhang
abstract: Generative retrieval assigns each item a discrete semantic identifier (SID) and retrieves items by autoregressively generating SID sequences. In dynamic environments such as e-commerce, new items arrive continuously, requiring periodic updates to the SID-to-Item mapping and model to maintain retrieval timeliness. Each update, however, can invalidate search paths already learned by the retriever, and the quantitative relationship between mapping change and retrieval quality has not been systematically characterized. We study this problem with extensive controlled experiments over 67 days of large-scale e-commerce search logs and obtain three core findings. (1) SID semantic drift causes severe retrieval degradation that may be masked by large beam sizes: mapping updates reduce HitRate by 41.78-62.05% at beam size 1 but only 8.33-10.85% at beam size 1000, as redundant candidate generation conceals the true severity of drift. (2) The fraction of changed SIDs is strictly monotonically related to retrieval quality: as the remapped fraction increases from 0% to 72.75%, HitRate decreases monotonically, dropping up to 42.66% at beam size 1. Full remapping remains substantially worse than the preservation policy under warm-start training, indicating that short-budget continued training alone cannot repair topology disruption. (3) The SID topology-preserving principle makes even the simplest warm-start strategy highly effective: fixing old-item SIDs, inserting new-items, and warm-starting from the previous model improves old-item HitRate by 10% and new-item HitRate by 109%, validated across two non-overlapping update cycles. These findings distill into a concise deployment principle: insert new-items, freeze old-items; warm-start when possible, otherwise freeze; never change SIDs the model has already learned. A three-week online A/B test on TmallAPP shows UCTCVR +0.29% and GMV +1.16%.

title: Millicharged particles and the degree-3 Prouhet-Tarry-Escott problem
authors: Ben Gripaios
abstract: We use geometry to solve a problem in arithmetic relevant for physics. Namely, for any $m$ we find all integer solutions to the equations $\sum_{i=1}^m x_i^k = \sum_{i=1}^m y_i^k$, where $k \in \{1,2,3\}$; this seems to be new for $m \geq 5$. In physics, these are the anomaly cancellation conditions for models with $m$ fermions which can be naturally light and carry small electric charges (a.k.a. millicharged or minicharged particles). The small charges arise by kinetic mixing of the Standard Model $U(1)$ gauge symmetry with an unbroken non-chiral (a.k.a. vector-like) $U(1)$ and the masses are suppressed by a spontaneously-broken chiral $U(1)$.

title: Twitching fiberboids in the collective : A table-top, one-dimensional, active particle gas
authors: Alex Arnhold, Falko Ziebert, Igor M. Kulić
abstract: Fiberboids are filaments that self-propel by rolling along a surface due to a flux normal to that surface. In the last few years, fibers using several materials and driving mechanisms have been developed that are able to roll persistently. Here we show using thermally driven nylon fibers on a slightly curved glass surface, that fiberboids also come in another state, that we call ``twitching'': the fiber rolls for a short time and then switches direction, implementing on large scales a diffusion-like motion. We rationalize the occurrence of this effect and experimentally quantify this new dynamic state. We then analyze ensembles of twitching fiberboids and by confining the fibers inside a circular arena to allow them to roll on a single axis only, we implement a simple, table-top realization of a one-dimensional non-equilibrium active gas. We study experimentally active cluster formation, their non-equilibrium dynamics and we rationalize the observations by a simple lattice model. This model takes into account a Viscek-like alignment of the velocity directions of the individual particles within clusters to yield good qualitative agreement with the experiments. Overall our work opens the path to study collectives of self-rolling fibers as an interesting new class of active matter.

title: Counting Irreducible Components of the Semistable Global Nilpotent Cone
authors: Nicolas Seroux
abstract: We discuss various methods for parametrizing and counting irreducible components of the global nilpotent cone of semistable $G$-Higgs bundles on a smooth complex curve. By restricting our study to the case of generically regular components following previous work of Faergeman and Raskin, we obtain explicit counts of semistable generically regular irreducible components for $G = \mathrm{SL}_n$, and give the first examples of such counts outside type A. These numbers are obtained by counting points in some natural polytopes associated to $G$, but our method requires a finer analysis in cases where the center of the group $G$ is disconnected.

title: CUA-Lite: An Open Platform for Computer Use Agents
authors: Zhanhui Zhou, Weichen Zhang, Haoran Liu, Lingjie Chen, Tianneng Shi, Kevin Lin, Zhengyuan Yang, Lijuan Wang, Dawn Song
abstract: Open resources for computer use agents (CUAs) -- environments, datasets, and models -- remain scattered: without a standard, these resources cannot be integrated and scaled; additionally, evaluation, RL, and SFT cannot share one infrastructure. We present CUA-Lite, an open platform for developing CUAs, built around three standardized abstractions: (1) Unified environment interface, under which we integrate 12 benchmarks across desktop, browser, and mobile, plus lightweight VM-free sandboxes that replicate OSWorld's desktop at much lower cost, providing over 30,000 verifiable tasks. (2) Unified supervised data format, into which we convert the major public CUA datasets, from GUI grounding and understanding to full rollouts, and record our fresh rollouts from frontier CUAs on these verifiable environments. (3) Model harnesses shared across evaluation, RL, and SFT, one per model and implemented for 14 model families. Each harness runs its model in these computer environments, producing the rollouts that evaluation and RL consume, or renders stored supervised data into the model's own training format for SFT. We release reference scores across the integrated benchmarks, and show that RL and SFT through the same harness improve open-weight models. We release our dataset, code, and models, and the platform is open to contributions.

title: FinSafeGuard: A Quality-Driven Synthetic Dataset for Financial AI Safety
authors: Joseph Thomas Thacil, Reetu Raj Harsh, Krati Saxena, Bhaskarjit Sarmah, Stefano Pasquali
abstract: Generating high-quality synthetic datasets at scale remains a fundamental challenge for training specialized AI systems in data-scarce domains. We present a comprehensive methodology that produces 14.3 million quality-filtered synthetic training examples from a structured taxonomy of 632,000 scenario specifications. Our four-stage pipeline ad- dresses critical challenges in synthetic data quality, diversity, and realism through: (1) systematic pre-generation research establishing optimal generation parameters via diminishing returns analysis, (2) conditional auto evolution mechanisms that remediate low-diversity batches during generation, (3) a two-layer semantic deduplication architecture combining lexical and embedding-based methods, and (4) LLM-as-Judge quality evaluation filtering samples based on behavioral correctness and tuple fidelity. Empirical analysis across three domains (Banking, Insurance, Financial Services) demonstrates domain-specific deduplication patterns ranging from 9.9% to 40.6%, with output generation modes exhibiting highest redundancy. Our batch size optimization reveals mode-specific diversity saturation thresholds, enabling principled allocation strategies. The complete pipeline reduces 26.4M raw samples to 14.3M high-confidence examples through merge (20.9% reduction), semantic deduplication (18.7% reduction), and quality-based filtering (15.9% reduction), providing a reproducible framework for domain-specific synthetic data generation with rigorous quality control.

title: A Non-linearizable Action of $S_3$ on Free Metabelian Lie and Associative Algebras
authors: Altyngul Naurazbekova, Ualbai Umirbaev
abstract: Let $M$ be the free metabelian Lie algebra of rank $4$ over the field of complex numbers $\mathbb{C}$. We construct a non-linearizable action of the symmetric group $S_3$, the smallest nonabelian group, on $M$ by automorphisms. We also construct a non-linearizable action of $S_3$ on free metabelian associative algebras of rank $4$.

title: HyQ-LC: Improving Light-Curve Classification with Hybrid Quantum--Classical Learning
authors: Xinghang Yu, Bin Yang
abstract: Light curves reveal stellar variability and support studies of stellar evolution and cosmic distances. Reliable classification is therefore important for large time-domain surveys. We present HyQ-LC for ten-class stellar light-curve classification using 359 handcrafted features and 633,034 training objects. The main model combines a window multilayer perceptron (MLP) backbone with a nine-qubit readout using amplitude encoding and angle re-uploading. Both this hybrid and its pure-MLP control have 44,238 parameters. On a shared 20,000-object test set, the hybrid has macro-averaged F1 (Macro-F1) point gains of 0.8276 and 1.2393 percentage points over the pure MLP on two fine-tuning seeds. A separate fixed-fusion configuration achieves slightly higher Macro-F1 but lower accuracy than approximately budget-matched LightGBM. Its positive class-level differences are concentrated in CEP, RRC, and ROT, while the full-budget LightGBM reference scores higher on both metrics. All circuits are simulated classically. The comparisons retain existing validation-selected checkpoints and use the same test objects, with features, predictions, and recomputation code publicly available. The results identify point-estimate improvements over the tested controls while leaving the specific contribution of the quantum branch unresolved.

title: On Reduced Rank Regression
authors: Th{é}o Rudkiewicz, Manon Verbockhaven
abstract: We propose a decoupled solution to the Reduced Rank Regression (RRR) problem, i.e. a pair of matrices (A*, B*) whose product A*B* minimizes the least squares error under a rank constraint. Using our formalism, we rewrite two other solutions from the literature and compare them with ours. In particular, we prove that all these formulations are equivalent. We then analyze their time complexity, and compare their running time and numerical precision on synthetic data, from which we derive practical recommendations. An open-source implementation of the algorithms and experiments is available here: https://gitlab.inria.fr/trudkiew/reduced\_rank\_regression.

title: Fractal forcing of turbulence by settling particles
authors: Simone Tandurella, Alessandro Chiarini, Marco Edoardo Rosti
abstract: The settling of particles in a fluid medium can trigger complex collective dynamics, dramatically affecting the distribution of energy across flow scales. In this work we present the first fully-resolved observations of the turbulence induced by large particle structures, also known as cluster-induced-turbulence (CIT), obtained through particle-resolved direct numerical simulations at high volume fractions and density ratios in large domains. We find that particles arrange in macroscopic fractal structures, exciting turbulent fluctuations at scales much larger than the individual constituents. By virtue of their fractal nature, these clusters force the continuous-phase in a multiscale, self-similar way. We further show that these cluster-driven, vertically decorrelated fluctuations at large scales coexist with, but are fundamentally distinct from, the established particle-driven high-wavenumber scaling. Beyond unveiling a different form of clustering in particle-settling, these results highlight a naturally arising, self-assembling path to fractal-generated turbulence.

title: The Geometry of the "Gauge Argument"
authors: James Owen Weatherall, Benjamin H. Feintzeig
abstract: We show how the "gauge argument", widely criticized by philosophers as ad hoc and unconvincing, may be reconstructed rigorously, and, we believe, convincingly, as an argument concerning the geometry of vector bundles. In this form, the gauge argument has two parts, the first of which is strongly analogous to the Weyl-Stein argument for Galilean spacetime as the appropriate setting for Newtonian gravitation; and the second of which invokes a classic result in the Yang-Mills theory literature, due to Utiyama [1956, "Invariant Theoretical Interpretation of Interaction", Phys. Rev. 101, 1597].

title: AVTime: Reinforcing Dense Audio-Visual Captions with Bidirectional Alignment
authors: Mingyang Wu, Kaituo Feng, Bohao Li, Kaixiong Gong, Zihao Yin, Xiangyu Yue
abstract: Dense temporal audio-visual captioning is important for multimodal video understanding and generation. However, prior work is constrained by three main limitations: (1) the lack of a dataset combining high temporal resolution, longer videos, and bidirectional alignment between time and events; (2) the reliance of most existing RL methods on checklists; and (3) the lack of a benchmark that bidirectionally evaluates event semantic correctness and temporal accuracy. To address these challenges, we propose: (1) AVTime-50K, a high-quality 50K-scale dataset with temporally precise, semantically accurate captions and longer videos; (2) AVTime, a state-of-the-art model optimized with a novel Bidirectional Temporal-Semantic Alignment (BiTSA) reward that imposes explicit bidirectional constraints between time and events; and (3) AVTime-Bench, a specialized benchmark that introduces a novel bidirectional evaluation of temporal accuracy and semantic correctness. Our code, models, and datasets are available at https://huggingface.co/collections/Apryle/avtime.

title: A Dual-Uplink Dual-Satellite Architecture for Entanglement Distribution
authors: Charilaos C. Angelidis, Ioannis K. Marmorkos
abstract: Satellite-based quantum links are a promising enabler of long-distance entanglement distribution, overcoming the exponential losses of optical fibers. In uplink architectures, entangled photons are generated at ground stations and transmitted to orbiting satellites, reducing space-segment complexity but introducing significant atmospheric and geometric losses. Single-satellite dual-uplink configurations are additionally limited by the requirement of simultaneous visibility between both ground stations and the satellite. In this work, we investigate a dual-uplink dual-satellite network architecture and compare its performance with the single-satellite scheme under identical physical assumptions. The proposed topology introduces an inter-satellite link (ISL) that decouples the ground-station separation from the atmospheric uplink geometry. A realistic channel model is employed, incorporating geometric attenuation, atmospheric turbulence, background noise, and Bell-state measurement efficiency. The overall success probability and practical fidelity are evaluated as functions of satellite altitude and ground-station separation. Our results show that while the single-satellite configuration is suitable for regional-scale networks, it becomes infeasible for large separations due to geometric constraints. The proposed dual-satellite architecture mitigates this limitation and significantly extends the achievable communication distance, representing a key step toward scalable quantum internet infrastructures.

title: Towards instance-dependent regret optimality in Episodic MDPs with Posterior Sampling
authors: Victor Boone, Cyrille Kone, Waris Radji, Odalric-Ambrym Maillard, Dorian Baudry
abstract: We study regret minimization in finite-horizon episodic Markov Decision Processes (MDPs). While minimax-optimal algorithms are known, tractable approaches to instance-dependent optimality are still lacking. Motivated by this gap, we introduce $π_0$-PSRL, a variant of PSRL that uses posterior samples to decide when exploration is needed, while following a fixed reference policy $π_0$ during exploration episodes. This decouples the test for exploration, triggered when the sampled and empirical MDPs have different optimal policies, from the choice of the policy used to gather information. The resulting design addresses a limitation of standard PSRL, where the sampled optimal policy may not be the optimal choice for exploration. We prove instance-dependent regret bounds for $π_0$-PSRL, identifying the logarithmic exploration cost induced by $π_0$ and taking a step toward matching asymptotic lower bounds for episodic RL. Our proof techniques showcase a novel proof structure to derive problem-dependent regret bounds in episodic MDPs, and concentration results for Dirichlet random variables, that may be of independent interest.

title: On the Adaptive Covering Complexity of Strings: Unifying Relative and Self-Referential Compression
authors: Pierre-Fran{\c c}ois Marteau
abstract: We introduce and study the adaptive covering complexity C adapt S (s), defined as the minimum number of contiguous factor blocks required to partition a string s when each block is either a factor of a fixed external dictionary S or a factor of the target's already decoded prefix. This hybrid admissibility model formalizes the structural interaction between static dictionary matching and dynamic nonoverlapping self-referencing. Our main theoretical result is the exact logarithmic law which is tight and proves that dynamic self-reference can reduce phrase count by at most an exponential factor over static dictionary covering alone. We establish structural equivalences showing that the measure bridges word-segmented Relative Lempel-Ziv and non-overlapping LZ77, and we prove exact preset-history LZ77 sandwich bounds. Furthermore, we establish the optimality of the longest-match greedy parse via an exchange lemma and present an optimal implementation based on dual suffix automata running in O(M + n) time and space for a constant alphabet. These analytical results are complemented by counting bounds, stationary-ergodic asymptotic invariance, a dictionaryselection NP-hardness result, and a concise empirical illustration.

title: Phase engineering of odd parity state in a quantum dot Josephson junction
authors: Shohei Kobayashi, Tyler Lindemann, Sergei Gronin, Geoffrey Gardner, Peter Stano, Daniel Loss, Michael Manfra, Seigo Tarucha, Sadashige Matsuo
abstract: Controlling fermion parity in quantum-dot Josephson junctions (QDJJs) enables access to novel superconducting physics. While parity transitions are usually tuned electrically, we study phase-induced transitions in a strongly coupled QDJJ using the superconducting phase difference across the dot terminals, denoted by $φ$. We find that this phase allows control over the ground state parity, with parity transitions observed as the Andreev bound states (ABSs) energies crossing zero. These crossings occur near $φ= π$, and their behavior is in good correspondence to a simple model considering a single-level quantum dot proximitized by a superconductor. These results place phase-controlled QDJJ arrays as a promising platform for exploring exotic phenomena such as Majorana zero modes.

title: Mediation and moderation in distance-based regression with triangular fuzzy data: simulation evidence and an application to academic performance
authors: Fabrizio Maturo, Annamaria Porreca
abstract: We study mediation and moderation in the distance-based regression model for triangular fuzzy responses, in which the center and transformed spreads of the response are linear in the components of fuzzy and crisp covariates. With a common design, componentwise least squares minimizes the unconstrained quadratic extension of the Yang--Ko distance on the transformed scale, for any choice of its shape parameters. Direct, indirect and total effects are defined separately for the center and the spreads of the response as plug-in contrasts on the fitted equations; when the mediator spreads are transformed and carry part of the indirect association, the product-of-coefficients rule no longer holds for the center. Moderation is modeled through triangular interaction regressors and tested with a Freedman--Lane permutation test. In simulations calibrated on real data, percentile bootstrap intervals for the indirect effects had coverage between 0.905 and 0.975, the empirical size of the indirect-effect tests did not exceed 0.085, and ignoring the paths through the mediator spreads biased the indirect effect on the center by 16 to 20\% at every sample size. The fuzzy model predicted better than a centers-only model only from $n=250$. In data on 91 university students collected in 2014, the indirect contrast through a course indicator accounted for about half of the model-based association between prior knowledge and the center of academic performance, the interactions of prior knowledge with sex and with motivation remained after a Holm adjustment, and the spreads of the covariates did not improve leave-one-out prediction.

title: PnP-CF: A Consensus Flow-Matching Solver for General Inverse Problems
authors: Dibyanshu Kumar, Magda Gregorova
abstract: Plug-and-Play (PnP) methods using continuous-time deep generative models as learned data distribution priors enable synthesizing high-quality solutions of model-based inverse problems. The quality of the solutions depends critically on the interplay and consensus between the inverse problem solver and the generative model sampler. We revisit a recently introduced flow-based PnP framework, which we refer to as PnP-CF (Consensus Flow), and extend its application to nonlinear inverse problems, including those with learned neural-network forward operators. PnP-CF combines a flow-matching denoiser with (i) ADMM-like dual variable updates and (ii) a time-adaptive pullback onto the intermediate flow probability path that combines a stochastic and a deterministic component. We discuss how these two features stabilize the algorithm and promote consensus, and demonstrate on a set of experiments that PnP-CF not only solves standard linear inverse problems with quality at least comparable to state-of-the-art baselines, but also extends gracefully to nonlinear inverse problems, including forward operators realized by pretrained neural networks, for which existing methods produce unsatisfactory results or fail completely.

title: Procedural Memory for Language Agents: A Neurosymbolic Perspective on Explicit Goal Structure
authors: Jonathan Leung, Zhiqi Shen, Deheng Ye
abstract: Large language models remain unreliable on long-horizon tasks requiring procedural reasoning. We argue that a key cause is the absence of explicit procedural memory: accessible, modifiable knowledge of how tasks are accomplished, distinct from semantic and episodic memory. Goal-Oriented Graphs offer such a representation, encoding goals and prerequisite dependencies as inspectable symbolic structure. We examine their construction, the challenges they pose, and principles for integrating them with neural reasoning.

title: Auditor-Assisted Summary-Channel Verification for Hosted LLM Identity Substitution
authors: Ziyi Zhang, Ziyao Wang, Guoheng Sun, Ang Li, Jian Li
abstract: Hosted LLM services increasingly expose model identity as a product claim, but external users and auditors often cannot inspect which model configuration served a request. We study an auditor-assisted regime in which a trusted auditor enrolls claimed identities and prepares verification material before deployment, while audit-time verification uses only the claimed identity and released output, without runtime access to model internals, inference logs, routing decisions, or provider metadata. We propose SUMMARK, a summary-channel watermarking framework that uses user-visible reasoning summaries as a keyed audit surface. During setup, SUMMARK constructs identity-specific vocabulary carriers, trains lightweight summary adapters, and calibrates per-identity thresholds. At deployment time, a keyed statistical test assesses whether the released summary is consistent with the claimed identity and, when needed, attributes the most likely enrolled identity. Across model families, scales, and task domains, SUMMARK reliably detects cross-family and cross-scale substitutions at low false-positive rates while preserving task-facing answer quality. We further study FP16->INT8/INT4 precision-consistency diagnostics and robustness under bounded post-processing, rewriting stress tests, and text-only spoofing, revealing both strong performance and clear failure boundaries. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/trinitr0toluene/Summark.

title: Can It Actually Work? Synthesizing Functional CAD Mechanisms
authors: Wenqian Zhang, Yangyi Huang, Zigeng Xu, Weiyang Liu, Zhen Liu
abstract: While LLM agents can generate visually plausible CAD assemblies, these designs often fail to fulfill their intended physical functions. We study functional CAD design, a setting where agents interpret underspecified requests to construct and iteratively revise mechanisms that satisfy functional requirements in physical simulation. Verifying these requirements is nontrivial: different candidate mechanisms may realize the same function through entirely different components, controls, and operating sequences. To bridge this gap, we propose FunCAD-Harness, a framework that translates abstract requirements into candidate-specific physical tests and uses simulation feedback to guide design revisions. To systematically evaluate this capability, we introduce FunCADBench, a benchmark spanning 46 mechanism families with interdependent and multi-step operations. Experiments across frontier LLM agents show that FunCAD-Harness exposes subtle mechanical failures invisible to visual inspection, substantially improving functional success rates over standard simulation-augmented baselines. Ultimately, our work marks a step toward CAD agents capable of translating human intent into working mechanisms.

title: Boundary-Sensitive Quantum Order on Non-Amenable Lattices
authors: Xingzhi Wang, Zohar Nussinov, Gerardo Ortiz
abstract: We show that quantum systems on non-amenable lattices, whose boundaries constitute an extensive fraction of the system, host novel forms of bulk ordering with no Euclidean counterpart. Combining boundary-retaining iDMRG with an exact symmetry-fixing duality, we investigate $p<5$ state clock models on the coordination-3 infinite Cayley tree. We find that between the ordered and disordered phases lies an emergent intermediate phase with bulk order induced by an arbitrarily weak boundary field rather than by conventional spontaneous symmetry-breaking. This establishes boundary-sensitive order as a distinct quantum ordering mechanism defying Landau's spontaneous symmetry-breaking paradigm. The intermediate phase realizes a bulk-boundary correspondence in which the unpolarized boundary selects a specific ordered bulk state.

title: Isolated zeros of the Riemann zeta function and zeros of linear combinations of Dirichlet $L$-functions
authors: Youness Lamzouri
abstract: Let $0<γ_1\leq γ_2\leq \cdots$ be the ordinates of the non-trivial zeros of the Riemann zeta function in the upper half-plane, counted with multiplicity, and fix $c>0$. We say that a non-trivial zero $ρ_n=β_n+iγ_n$ is $c$-isolated if $\min(γ_{n+1}-γ_n, γ_n-γ_{n-1})>2πc/\log γ_n$. Note that any isolated zero is necessarily simple and on the critical line. We prove unconditionally that more than $50.87\%$ half of the non-trivial zeros are $1/6$-isolated. Previously, it was not known unconditionally that there are infinitely many isolated zeros. By allowing $c$ to be extremely small, we can push the above proportion to $13/20$. We also show that there are positive proportions of $k$ consecutive ``moderate'' gaps (gaps larger than a constant times the average local gap) between the ordinates of the zeta zeros, for $k=3, 4, 5$. As an application we combine our work on isolated zeros with an unconditional refinement of the Bombieri--Hejhal method to show unconditionally that at least $31\%$ of the zeros of a linear combination of two distinct primitive Dirichlet $L$-functions with the same conductor and parity lie on the critical line. The previous unconditional record for this proportion was $7.38\times 10^{-9}$, which was obtained by Dousselin who refined and made explicit a result of Selberg.

title: LatComm: Reusable Context Compression for Latent Communication between Large Language Models
authors: Huawei Lin, Jinting Liu, Tan Yu, Weijie Zhao
abstract: Systems that combine several large language models (LLMs) often use one context for many questions. When the context is passed between models as text, the receiving model processes all of its tokens again for every question. Avoiding this cost requires a context representation that is compact, reusable across questions, and readable by a different LLM. Existing compression and latent communication methods each provide only some of these properties. We introduce LatComm, a Latent Communication interface that provides all three by separating encoding from reading: the context is encoded once without the question, and the receiver selects what to read for each question. A frozen context encoder LLM compresses the context into a fixed-size packet and sends it to a different frozen receiver LLM, which reads the packet through cross-attention, with gates computed from its prompt. On 12 multiple-choice question-answering datasets, LatComm improves average accuracy over single-vector baselines by up to 10.2 points. On QuALITY, it reduces the receiver's input by 57x and answers the questions of an article 3x faster.

title: Elastic knots: compactness, contact, and variational structure
authors: Philipp Reiter, Heiko von der Mosel
abstract: We study bending-minimizing sequences of closed curves in a fixed knot class and the self-contact of their limits. A positive matrix-valued measure records a possible loss of curvature energy. Ambient variations, localized on arbitrary coincidence sets, force this measure to vanish and give strong convergence in $H^2$.
