abstract: The LUX-ZEPLIN (LZ) Collaboration recently reported a candidate event consistent with a high-energy nuclear recoil, motivating a possible interpretation by Lee, Takahashi, and Tsai involving the production of an invisible baryon-number-two scalar with a mass near $1.85$ GeV. Motivated by this hypothetical scenario, we investigate the $J^P=0^+$ $uuddss$ hexaquark system using QCD sum rules. We consider five local diquark-diquark-diquark interpolating currents with different scalar and axial-vector diquark combinations, together with a baryon-baryon current constructed from two $Λ$-type baryon currents. The operator product expansions are calculated up to dimension sixteen, and their numerical behaviors are examined under different OPE truncations. Among the currents considered, only the $SU(3)_{\rm flavor}$-singlet current $J_{SSS}$, consisting of three scalar color-$\bar{\mathbf{3}}_C$ diquarks, yields a low-mass solution at $D=12$, with $M_{SSS}=1.85^{+0.19}_{-0.20}$ GeV. Interestingly, scalar color-$\bar{\mathbf{3}}_C$ diquarks belong to the flavor $\bar{\mathbf{3}}_F$ representation, and their local color-singlet construction has a unique nonvanishing flavor structure, $[ud][ds][su]$, corresponding to $uuddss$. Analogous all-scalar-diquark currents vanish for other flavor configurations, such as $uuuddd$ and $uuudds$. Together with our QCD sum-rule results, this property highlights the special role of the all-scalar-diquark configuration, $[ud][ds][su]$, as a possible deeply bound structure. However, the higher-dimensional OPE contributions exhibit significant truncation dependence, and the low-mass solution remains conditional on the adopted OPE truncation rather than constituting a fully controlled mass prediction.

title: UtilityBench: Measuring Language Model Utility When Errors Have Different Costs
authors: Qifeng Lei, Zhiyong Yang, Zitai Wang, Shilong Bao, Linchao Zhang, Qianqian Xu, Qingming Huang
abstract: As language models are increasingly deployed in real-world scenarios with important outcomes, the impact of their mistakes often extends far beyond what correctness can capture. In domains like medicine, a single error can lead to serious consequences and put patient safety at risk. However, mainstream evaluation protocols still treat all errors as equal, overlooking the spectrum of real-world costs. To address this, we propose a utility-based evaluation paradigm that explicitly incorporates the varying consequences of errors. Guided by this principle, we develop UtilityBench, a large-scale benchmark of 15,000 instances with verifiable answers, quantifying error severity using Best-Worst Scaling to elicit meaningful, data-driven cost estimates. These quantified utilities shape when a model should answer or abstain, guiding it to make decisions that align with the true importance of each scenario. As another merit, we introduce UtilityAUC, a metric that measures the area under the utility curve determined by a model's response ordering, thereby enabling utility preference alignment beyond error frequency. Our theoretical analysis demonstrates that UtilityAUC can distinguish between models where standard accuracy and AURC fall short. Empirically, evaluating 20 state-of-the-art models, we find that greater accuracy or more advanced architectures do not reliably translate to higher UtilityAUC, highlighting a gap between problem-solving ability and responsible decision-making in language model evaluation.

title: CALM: Consistency-Aware Logit Masking in Decoding Space for Mitigating Overthinking of Large Reasoning Models
authors: Shengjing Liu, Feiyang Li, Yuxuan Yang, Yile Wang, Hui Huang
abstract: Large reasoning models (LRMs) have achieved strong performance on challenging mathematical and scientific tasks through long chain-of-thought reasoning, but they often suffer from overthinking with unnecessary reasoning steps. Existing truncation-based methods typically detect consecutive trial-answer agreement and force early exit, yet such local stopping signals do not necessarily indicate final-answer stability and can disrupt useful subsequent reflection or verification, potentially leading to performance degradation. We propose consistency-aware logit masking (CALM), a training-free decoding intervention for mitigating overthinking in LRMs. CALM first monitors trial answers at step boundaries and then applies logit masking to action transition point (ATP) tokens such as "Wait", "Alternatively", and "Hmm", suppressing redundant transitional reasoning while allowing the model to continue its thought process more naturally. Experiments across four advanced LRMs and five benchmarks show that CALM reduces token consumption by 18.6%-25.0% compared with full CoT reasoning while maintaining performance, and can even improve accuracy by 0.07%-1.48% by reducing redundant reasoning. LLM-as-a-Judge results also demonstrate that CALM provides more coherent and concise results.

title: The $(n-2)$-linear restriction estimate in $\mathbb R^n$
authors: Faruk Temur
abstract: We present a proof for the $(n-2)$-linear extension estimate for curved surfaces in $\mathbb{R}^n$, $n\ge5$, at the local product exponent $2(n-1)/(n-2)^2$, with an arbitrarily small power loss. The hypotheses are transversality of the normals and nondegeneracy of the compressed shape operators on their common two-dimensional orthogonal complement. The argument combines polynomial partitioning, a descent through algebraic varieties, localized multilinear restriction, and positive packet-energy estimates.

title: Exact extremizers for $\ell_p$-judicious bisections of triangle-free graphs
authors: Shufei Wu
abstract: Balogh, Clemen and Lidický asked how large the minimum $\ell_p$-norm of the internal-edge counts over balanced partitions of an $n$-vertex triangle-free graph can be. For each fixed $2<p<\infty$ and all sufficiently large even $n$, we determine this value exactly for bisections and characterize all extremal graphs. They are precisely the complete bipartite graphs $K_{a,n-a}$ for which $a\le n/2$ maximizes an explicit integer objective. All maximizing values of $a$ lie in an interval of length bounded in terms of $p$ alone. We also prove quantitative stability for the same range of $p$ and $n$: for sufficiently small $δ\ge 0$, every $n$-vertex triangle-free graph with bisection value at least the asymptotic optimum minus $δn^2$ is within $O_p(δn^2+n)$ edge edits of a complete bipartite graph with the optimal limiting class ratio.

title: Out-of-Distribution Detection in Continual Learning
authors: Nimeshika Udayangani, Flora D. Salim, Christopher Leckie, Sarah Erfani
abstract: Out-of-distribution detection in continual learning (OOD-CL) is highly challenging, as it requires (i) learning a sequence of tasks without catastrophic forgetting, and (ii) identifying unknown samples (OOD) without access to known (in-distribution (ID)) data from past tasks, where standard confidence-based OOD scores tend to degrade. Existing methods largely rely on a rehearsal buffer of past data or assume closed-world settings, limiting their scalability and reliability in real-world scenarios. In this paper, we propose a novel OOD detection framework for rehearsal-free continual learning, inspired by Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (KAN), which mitigate catastrophic forgetting via their inherent local neuroplasticity. To better leverage KAN in OOD-CL, we introduce a task-adaptive classifier architecture, TA-KAN, which mitigates recency bias and enhances ID--OOD separability through task-specific control of activation locality. Furthermore, we propose a geometry-guided OOD score that complements TA-KAN classifier confidence without relying on past ID data. Our method significantly improves OOD detection while maintaining strong ID classification performance, achieving state-of-the-art results in OOD-CL.

title: A high-Galactic-altitude scattering screen: scintillation from Globular Cluster pulsar M53A
authors: Qiuyi He, Xun Shi, Dejiang Yin, Di Li
abstract: While known interstellar scattering screens are largely confined to the Galactic disk, the scattering properties of the circumgalactic medium (CGM) in the deep Galactic halo have remained unexplored. Using observations from the Five-hundred-meter Aperture Spherical radio Telescope (FAST), we report the first detection of scintillation arcs in the secondary spectra of the high-latitude pulsar J1312+1810A (M53A). Under the 1D anisotropic and 2D isotropic thin-screen models considered here, the inferred scintillation screen distances are $12.8_{-3.5}^{+2.6}$ and $11.7_{-3.5}^{+2.8}$\,kpc, respectively. These model-dependent estimates correspond to Galactic heights of $12.6_{-3.5}^{+2.6}$ and $11.5_{-3.5}^{+2.7}$\,kpc, placing the candidate screen among the highest-altitude scattering structures inferred to date. The strong, time-variable scintillation asymmetry suggests substantial electron-density inhomogeneity within the screen. We speculate that this screen is associated with small-scale structures near the shock boundary of the northern eROSITA bubble. These results support the presence of discrete, inhomogeneous scattering structures deep within the Galactic halo, far beyond the regions where localized stellar feedback is typically concentrated, and highlight pulsar scintillation as a promising probe of small-scale ionized structures in the CGM.

title: Motor compound fault diagnosis using an attention-based cross-talk architecture
authors: Wonjun Yi, Wonho Jung, Junho Kim, Rismaya Kumar Mishra, Yong-Hwa Park
abstract: As physical AI increasingly relies on sensing to understand physical systems, reliable condition monitoring of industrial machinery has become more important. Motors are ubiquitous in industrial systems, and increasing system complexity raises the likelihood of simultaneous faults. Accordingly, compound fault diagnosis that identifies multiple fault components and their severities is increasingly required. Because different fault components jointly affect the same vibration signal, their severity classification can be formulated as related tasks, making multi-task learning (MTL) suitable for exploiting shared information. However, conventional shared-trunk architectures force tasks to share a common representation, potentially causing negative transfer because fault components are characterized by different time-frequency regions. To address this issue, this study proposes a Residual Neural Dimension Reductor with Time-Frequency Channel Attention (RNDR-TFCA), an attention-enhanced cross-talk architecture for multi-output compound fault diagnosis. RNDR-TFCA preserves task-specific feature extractors while selectively exchanging information across tasks. Time-frequency attention emphasizes informative intra-task regions, while channel attention enhances useful inter-task information after nonlinear feature fusion. Experiments on a rotor-bearing system with inner-race fault, outer-race fault, misalignment, and unbalance showed that RNDR-TFCA achieved a macro F1 score of 0.898, outperforming single-task, multi-class, shared-trunk, and cross-talk baselines. Ablation experiments confirmed the benefit of jointly applying both attention mechanisms. RNDR-TFCA required 713 K parameters and 170.42 MMACs, only slightly higher than RNDR. Channel-expanded baselines still underperformed RNDR-TFCA, indicating that the gain was not simply attributable to increased model capacity.

title: Global regularity and sharp decay rates for the one-dimensional hypo-viscous compressible Navier-Stokes equations in critical Besov spaces
authors: Chen Liang, Zhaonan Luo, Zhaoyang Yin
abstract: In this paper, we study the global regularity of the one-dimensional hypo-viscous compressible Navier--Stokes equations in the critical Besov spaces, where the initial data are close to the constant equilibrium state. We introduce an effective velocity, constructed as a combination of the density and the velocity, which is used to capture the high-frequency behavior of $a$. By performing elaborate high-frequency and low-frequency estimates together with a bootstrap argument, we obtain global existence for $\frac{1}{2}\leβ<1$. In particular, when $\frac{1}{2}\leβ<\frac{3}{4}$, we also prove the uniqueness of solutions. Furthermore, under an additional low-frequency assumption, we establish the optimal time decay rates.

title: Asynchronous On-Policy Self-Distillation
authors: Xidong Wu, Qi Qi, Yuqiong Ji, Shangqian Gao
abstract: Unlike on-policy distillation (OPD), which depends on a separate teacher model, on-policy self-distillation (OPSD) leverages a single language model acting simultaneously as the student and the teacher, with the teacher conditioned on privileged information. Despite this architectural simplicity, synchronous rollout generation dominates overall training time, creating a severe systems bottleneck when scaling OPSD. To address this, we introduce Asynchronous On-Policy Self-Distillation (AsyncOPSD), a framework that decouples rollout generation from learner updates to improve training throughput. Since the teacher and student share parameters, AsyncOPSD eliminates the multi-model coordination overhead inherent to OPD architectures in asynchronous training. As the student policy evolves, buffered trajectories generated by older policies become stale, potentially degrading performance. To mitigate this, we introduce a distillation objective based on staleness-aware policy control and token-level entropy weighting. Across three model sizes and mathematical reasoning benchmarks, AsyncOPSD improves the training throughput by $1.96$--$2.25\times$ over synchronous OPSD while increasing average benchmark accuracy.

title: Vision-Language-Delta-Action: Learning Compact Deltas as Actionable Transition Interfaces for Robotic Manipulation
authors: Lingsen Zhang, Wei Li, Jie He, Henghua Zhang, Kai Mo, Shiyong Li, Yanpeng Wang, Rui Shao
abstract: Robotic manipulation is not merely observation-to-action generation, but the realization of task-specified state changes in the physical world. Existing vision-language-action (VLA) methods directly learn observation-to-action mappings, imposing a substantial learning burden due to the gap between semantic understanding and action execution. Although world-action models (WAMs) improve control through future prediction, modeling complete future states wastes capacity on static appearance and action-irrelevant changes. We propose Vision-Language-Delta-Action (VLDA), a paradigm that reformulates full future prediction as compact actionable transition modeling. Its core is a compact Delta variable that captures latent world-state changes, serving as an interface between vision-language understanding and action generation. VLDA learns Delta through a unified objective composed of the Local Transition Filter (LT-Filter) and Global Transition Anchor (GT-Anchor). LT-Filter captures task-relevant manipulation-centric changes while suppressing static reconstruction biases. GT-Anchor provides coarse future-level regularization to preserve the overall direction of state changes. Delta-Driven Action Refinement (DDAR) further grounds Delta in the action manifold and injects it as a structured seed to guide action denoising. We implement VLDA within LoongForge, an open-source training framework for large-scale foundation and embodied models, using its modular and distributed infrastructure for unified two-stage optimization. Experiments show that VLDA improves long-horizon consistency, robustness, and generalization, validating actionable Delta as an alternative to direct action prediction and full future-state modeling.

title: Benefit-Targeted Routing and Bounded Revision for LLM-Based Evidence Screening in Manufacturing Supplier Discovery
authors: Yijiashun Qi, Hanzhe Guo, Yuxuan Li
abstract: An evidence-review system must allocate additional model judgments and control their use. We study these software decisions on 6,164 frozen manufacturing source-task pairs. Benefit-targeted routing learns recovered agreement minus newly introduced disagreement. On the original 300-case test, 60 consultations yield 202/231 agreements with two human references versus 189/218 for a logistic-risk router. An additional 300 cases were independently annotated twice using equal frozen evidence. Without retraining the historical policies, the corresponding counts are 164/190 versus 163/193; the differences do not resolve an advantage. Strict scalar-Ridge controls share preprocessing, regularization and fitting, and remain inconclusive. Quotation and requested-state replacement gates retain rejected cases and budget costs; their joint gate rejects one original and two additional consultations without changing primary outcomes. Evidence ablations, fusion and bounded updates supply further controls. A completed 200-pair identity audit yields 97.45 percent weighted merge precision after eight author adjudications. This audits a provisional map, while prospective company-disjoint performance remains untested.

title: Minimum-Cost Robust Evidence Certificates for Horn Reasoning under Correlated Source Failures
authors: Yukun Yang
abstract: A small justification for a rule-based conclusion may disappear when a source is withdrawn, and multiple derivations need not provide independent evidence. We study minimum-cost certificates that preserve a Horn conclusion under every withdrawal of at most k source domains. Evidence records remain distinct from asserted facts, supporting replicated attestations and overlapping failure dependencies. Transversals of minimal-support footprints characterize robustness and explain why disjoint-proof requirements can reject valid certificates. An exact procedure alternates weighted evidence selection with a source-failure oracle. A rule-closed counterinterpretation yields a globally valid selection cut without enumerating supports or failure scenarios. We prove correctness, finite termination, and cost optimality, establish coNP-completeness of unrestricted verification and NP-completeness of synthesis for every fixed budget, and identify a tractable reachability restriction. Experiments on controlled benchmarks, reachability graphs, and ontology-derived instances demonstrate that our counterinterpretation-guided synthesis achieves up to 92% optimum coverage within practical resource bounds, outperforming scenario expansion and general abduction while confirming the necessity of transversal-based reasoning over proof-packing heuristics.

title: The Exact Boundary of Linear Optimality in Witsenhausen's Counterexample
authors: Yikai Lu, Tongxin Li
abstract: Witsenhausen's counterexample has resisted a closed form solution for decades. However, it has remained unknown whether a mathematically tractable representation exists or not. In this paper, we solve this open problem, showing that the optimal policies are either linear or not tame and characterizing the exact regions where the two properties hold. Moreover, in the linear optimal region, we give an essentially unique closed form solution for the optimal policy, and show that no optimal first-stage policy is definable in any $o$-minimal expansion of the ordered real field in the nonlinear optimal region.

title: Rubrics Beyond Evaluation: Exploiting Rubric Structure in Reinforcement Learning
authors: Yuxun Huang, Yunyao Zhang, ZeLiang Chen, Yi-Ping Phoebe Chen, Junqing Yu, Zikai Song
abstract: Rubrics are widely used to evaluate open-ended question answering by breaking overall quality into explicit criteria. These explicit criteria make rubrics a rich source of learning guidance, yet their potential for guiding the training process has been largely overlooked. Existing methods use rubrics mainly as direct feedback signals, without explicitly modeling the capabilities behind their criteria. This leaves their capability structure largely unused in guiding the training process. We introduce Rubric-Structured Reinforcement Learning (RSRL), an RL framework that unlocks the full potential of rubrics by exploiting their structure throughout the training process, rather than treating them simply as direct reward signals. At its core, RSRL builds on three key designs: (1) Rubric-to-Capability Structuring first recovers the capability structure hidden in rubric criteria, (2) Self-Sufficient Capability Learning then uses this structure to bootstrap underdeveloped capabilities into effective learning, (3) Capability-Residual Credit Routing finally preserves capability-specific gains during optimization. Experiments show that RSRL consistently improves both overall performance and underdeveloped capabilities, boosting downstream scientific question-answering performance by up to 7.43 over the initial policy and 7.60 over non-rubric structured RL baselines, showing that reinforcement learning can substantially benefit from the capability structure encoded in rubrics.

title: Auditing Semantic and Relational Reliability in Open-Vocabulary Human-Object Interaction Evaluation
authors: S M Asif Hossain, Ruksat Khan Shayoni, Md Kishor Morol
abstract: Open-vocabulary human-object interaction detectors describe interactions in free text, and this creates a problem for evaluation. Category scoring rejects valid paraphrases, while semantic similarity scoring can reward predictions that name the wrong action or reverse the roles of the participants. We present a diagnostic protocol that holds every prediction fixed and scores it under five views, namely official category evaluation, an identity control, lexical normalization, graded semantic credit, and strict propositional equivalence. Comparing these views separates the effect of the matching engine from the effect of semantic credit. The protocol pairs controlled transformations that preserve or break meaning with a blinded audit of natural predictions, and we derive consistency checks that link mean credit, invalid acceptance, and transformation counts. Applied to six systems on HICO-DET, the views disagree on which system leads. GEN-VLKT leads under official evaluation, SL-HOI leads under SHOE, and GEN-VLKT leads again under strict equivalence. Semantic gains range from 1.6 to 20.3 mAP, and AgentHOI keeps less than half of its gain once equivalence is enforced. We recommend that semantic scores be reported together with relational validity and paired uncertainty, so that recovered credit is not read as better interaction understanding.

title: A Cue's Hidden Price: Auditing Seller Influence on AI Shoppers
authors: Felix Buecheler, Gerardo Berbeglia, Mingyu Guo
abstract: Large language models are increasingly asked to shop on a user's behalf, which lets seller-controlled content such as badges, endorsements, and framing steer what they recommend. That poses the question at the core of generative engine optimization (GEO): not whether seller content shifts an agent's choice, but how much. The usual gauge of that influence, how often a cue wins the choice, has a blind spot: once a cue is strong enough to be picked almost every time, the choice rate can no longer show how much stronger one cue is than another. We introduce price-equivalent (PE) auditing, which removes this ceiling by pricing the cue in money. In a counterbalanced, position-controlled forced choice, we raise the cued product's price until it is chosen only half the time, and report that premium as the cue's price-equivalent: a formally defined, policy-conditioned parity threshold that makes very different cues comparable. Priced this way, cues that look equally strong at equal price differ by a wide margin, so choice-rate audits substantially under-resolve seller influence. We run the audit over 113,472 trials, seven models across families, and two product categories. To our knowledge, we also run the first price-equivalent audit of a decision-native model, Jev, which outputs a choice probability directly instead of generating text; strikingly, its profile is unlike any text model we tested, resisting most cues yet remaining susceptible to the strongest social-proof claims. We release the stimuli, logs, and code as a benchmark that reports each model's cue-price profile rather than a single score, giving developers and auditors a common, reproducible way to measure how content moves AI shopping agents.

title: High-Efficiency Silicon-Lithium Niobate Grating Coupler enabled by Fully-Etched Subwavelength Structures
authors: Jing Wang, Yang Liu, Shitong Su, Weiwen Zou
abstract: A new approach of silicon-lithium niobate (Si-LN) grating couplers (GCs) with a fully-etched structure is proposed. The coupling strength is engineered through subwavelength structures, allowing improved directionality. The adjoint-based inverse design method is simultaneously adopted to achieve efficient coupling between photonic circuits and fibers. Considering the birefringence of LN, the proposed Si-LN GCs are optimized and fabricated for TE mode along the crystallographic Z and Y directions. The experimentally measured coupling efficiencies are -3.3 dB and -3.9 dB along the crystallographic Z and Y directions, respectively. The measured 3-dB bandwidths are broader than 54 nm and the back reflections can be suppressed down to -15 dB over 50 nm for both directions. The proposed Si-LN GCs are realized by only single-step Si etching, offering a practical solution for fast device prototyping in Si-LN photonic integrated circuits.

title: A New Proof of Wei's Theorem
authors: Zhiqaing Wei, Mengyan Xing, Xingya Zhao
abstract: In the paper \emph{Structure and realizability for rational maps}, Wei proved the following. Let \(k\) nontrivial partitions of an integer \(d\ge 3\) be given, satisfying the Riemann--Hurwitz formula for the case of maps between two spheres. If \(k>\ell+1\), where \[ \ell=\min_i|π_i| \] is the shortest partition length, then there exists a rational map whose branch datum is given by these partitions. In this paper we give a new proof of Wei's theorem on realizing a tuple of partitions as the ramification data of a rational function. The proof is inductive on the shortest partition length. Two auxiliary results are established: a two-cut partition theorem and a gluing theorem for marked spherical coverings. These reduce any counterexample with shortest length \(\ell\ge3\) to auxiliary data with either fewer factors or smaller shortest length, while preserving the total defect and the marked conditions. The base case \(\ell\le2\) is quoted from the literature.

title: Random Clocks on Computation Paths]{Random Clocks on Computation Paths: How Far Can They Reach, and When Does Stepping Back Help?
authors: Farzad Didehvar, Saman Farhat
abstract: We watch a computation only at moments chosen by a random clock that can leap ahead, pause, or step back, and we count looks rather than steps. How far can such a clock reliably see with polynomially many looks, and does stepping back help? Rare long leaps reach exponential and doubly exponential time, with infinitely many levels between polynomial and exponential time. A clock that tends to fall back sees only the start of the input, and below polynomial time we find infinitely many incomparable levels. Stepping back can help decisively. For clocks whose long leaps occur only at rare positions, no forward-only clock goes beyond polynomial time, while even single steps back raise the reach to exponential time. Stepping back cannot help, however, when the clock's leaps ignore its position.

title: MS-Bench: A Condition-Stratified Multi-Speaker ASR Benchmark
authors: Chunjiang He, Zheng Zi, Bingshen Mu, Yurun Li, Jingyi Wang, Zhonghua Fu, Lei Xie
abstract: Multi-speaker automatic speech recognition (MSASR) has advanced rapidly with end-to-end speech large language models. However, existing benchmarks cover limited ranges of specific multi-speaker conditions and scenarios, making it difficult to reveal system limitations under diverse conditions and scenarios. We introduce MS-Bench\footnote{\href{https://aslp-lab.github.io/MS-Bench/}{Demo page: https://aslp-lab.github.io/MS-Bench/}}, a condition-stratified benchmark for fine-grained MSASR evaluation. MS-Bench integrates both public and internal benchmarks and characterizes each recording along five dimensions: speaker number, overlap ratio, speaker similarity, speaker turn interval, and acoustic quality. We stratify these dimensions into condition ranges and construct MS-Bench with broad coverage of conditions, scenarios, languages, and recording devices. Evaluating representative commercial, open-source, and cascaded systems, we find that overlap affects both lexical recognition and speaker attribution, while other factors exhibit more task-specific effects on recognition, attribution, or temporal prediction. These results demonstrate that aggregate metrics alone obscure important MSASR failure modes and highlight the value of condition-stratified evaluation. MS-Bench aims to reveal condition-specific limitations of current MSASR systems and guide future improvements.

title: Optimizing Marketing Budgets for Social Influence: A Generalized Fractional Incentives Framework
authors: Abhishek K. Umrawal, Akhil Bhimaraju, Eliot W. Robson, Lav R. Varshney
abstract: Marketing managers routinely allocate limited budgets across individuals in social networks whose responsiveness and influence vary substantially. We study the problem of Budgeted Generalized Fractional Influence Maximization (BGFIM), which captures the allocation of continuous levels of marketing spend across users in the presence of heterogeneous response and network spillovers. In this framework, adoption probabilities are governed by user-specific response functions that capture both baseline propensity and marginal responsiveness, while incentive costs vary across users. We propose a scalable solution approach based on a discrete greedy procedure with provable approximation guarantees, enabling tractable optimization under realistic budget constraints. Our formulation generalizes prior influence maximization models by allowing heterogeneous response and cost structures, providing a more flexible representation of targeted marketing interventions. Using experiments on multiple large-scale networks, we show that continuous allocation strategies can outperform standard heuristics and improve influence outcomes under heterogeneous conditions, and we illustrate how the framework can support profit-oriented decision making by identifying budget levels that balance marginal returns and costs. Overall, our results highlight the value of fine-grained budget allocation in networked marketing environments and offer a scalable approach for data-driven marketing resource allocation.

title: When to Stop Asking: Factor Coverage Bias and LLM Determinability Judgments with Underspecified Information in Medicine
authors: Yusuke Watanabe, Yohei Kobashi, Taisei Tosaki, Takeshi Kojima, Yusuke Iwasawa, Yasushi Okuno, Yutaka Matsuo
abstract: Clinical decision-making often begins with underspecified information and requires not only gathering missing information but also knowing when to stop. This calls for judging determinability (whether the available information is sufficient for a decision) by considering whether missing information could change the conclusion, not simply the amount of available decision-relevant information. Reliance on this amount as a cue for determinability, which we term \textit{factor coverage bias}, could undermine the trustworthiness of large language models (LLMs) through premature conclusions or excessive information gathering, such as unnecessary invasive tests. Yet whether LLMs exhibit this bias remains insufficiently studied. To address this gap, we construct a controlled pairwise benchmark in which LLMs identify the determinable case within each determinable--undeterminable pair. We add a decision-relevant factor to either side while keeping each case's determinability unchanged, and similarly add irrelevant text to distinguish this bias from context-length effects. Adding a relevant factor made LLMs more likely to select the augmented case as determinable even when it remained undeterminable, an effect that persisted with increased reasoning effort, while adding irrelevant text made them less likely to select the augmented case, an effect that reasoning substantially reduced. These findings identify factor coverage bias as a failure mode distinct from context-length effects and a potential risk to LLM trustworthiness. Our work provides an evaluation framework for LLM trustworthiness under underspecification.

title: Global weak solutions for a two-species Riesz cross-attraction system with quadratic diffusion
authors: Zhenxing Liu, Shen Bian
abstract: We establish global existence for a two-species cross-attraction system on $\mathbb R^3$, with quadratic diffusion and the common interaction operator $(-Δ)^{-s}$, where $1/2<s<1$. Nonnegative initial data in $L^1\cap L^\infty$ with finite second moments require no smallness condition on the masses. A joint energy and second-moment estimate and a coupled $L^p$ iteration give uniform a priori estimates for the regularized solutions. Compactness then yields mass-conserving global weak solutions, bounded on every finite time interval and strongly continuous in $L^1\cap L^2$. The energy inequality holds at every pair of time endpoints. Uniqueness and bounds uniform for all positive times are not asserted.

title: The multiplicative Merino--Welsh inequality for chordal graphs
authors: Shaohan Xu, Fengming Dong, Kexiang Xu
abstract: For a connected graph $G$, let $τ(G)$, $α(G)$ and $α^*(G)$ denote its numbers of spanning trees, acyclic orientations and totally cyclic orientations, respectively. We prove that $α(G)α^*(G)\geqτ(G)^2$ for every connected bridgeless chordal graph.

title: Balanced Social Learning
authors: Andrew Koh, Ricky Li
abstract: When is social learning efficient if agents have heterogeneous preferences over a set of actions? When myopic agents generate information only about the action they choose, efficiency requires balance such that all high-value actions are discovered. We characterize the value of policies that control the flow of past information to future agents. Under full transparency of past information, the probability of efficient outcomes is approximately one if and only if the prior and preferences are balanced and the log-likelihood ratio distribution satisfies a set of intuitive moment conditions. Noisy bad news is a canonical example. By contrast, approximate efficiency is obtainable on the set of arbitrary adaptive information policies if and only if the prior alone is balanced. Moreover, it suffices to use adaptive evidence policies which permanently and fully disclose subsets of past information. When the prior is imbalanced and approximate efficiency is unattainable, we characterize the value of adaptive information and show that it is uniformly approximated by the value of adaptive evidence as the impact of each individual signal on beliefs vanishes.

title: Is it RL or Data? A Controlled Comparison of GRPO and Rejection-Sampling Fine-Tuning
authors: Lakshya Chaudhry
abstract: Bauer et al. (2026) showed that in low-data reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, training GRPO on mixed-difficulty prompts gives up to 5x the sample efficiency of easy-only prompts. They did not test whether this benefit is specific to GRPO, or whether another post-training method given the same data would obtain it too. We test this on their procedural counting task with Qwen3-4B-Base and LoRA, comparing GRPO to rejection-sampling fine-tuning (RFT) on the same prompts, verifier and token cap. Six primary arms cross the two methods with three prompt sets (Easy, Mixed, and a Curated subset of prompts the base model sometimes solves, which makes GRPO's implicit filter explicit). We use three seeds per arm. Hypotheses and falsifiers were registered before training. To rule out a poorly tuned baseline, RFT receives a 27-run hyperparameter sweep, while GRPO uses Bauer et al.'s recipe unchanged. GRPO outperforms RFT at every prompt set: by 10.9 points on held-out test problems with curated prompts, and, in post hoc comparisons with matched rollout budgets, by 8.4 and 9.2 points on the easy and mixed prompts. On test the advantage survives the least favorable treatment of truncated completions; out of distribution, truncation prevents a conclusion. Curating prompts does not help RFT (-2.7 points). Mixed-difficulty data helps RFT (+3.7 points), while for GRPO the evidence is inconclusive. A secondary iterated-RFT arm, which resamples from the current policy, recovers 3.2 of the 10.9-point gap (about 30%). These are controlled measurements on one synthetic task family and one base model with three seeds per arm.

title: OneChord: Distill What You Rank, Recommend in One Pass
authors: Zesheng Li, Chengchang Pan, Honggang Qi
abstract: Accurate product discovery on the Web requires recommendation models that rank catalog candidates within tight inference budgets. In semantic-ID recommendation, deployment can fuse code probabilities with item similarities, making the final ranking depend on their normalization and relative weights. This motivates a direct training principle: \emph{distill what you rank}. We present OneChord, which uses one learned, catalog-normalized fusion for next-item supervision, refinement distillation, and inference. A shared parallel decoder produces joint SID evidence and item-matching scores. During training, a frozen denoiser supplies legal partial SIDs; the student evaluates these states to construct refined fused targets. Matching direct and refined predictions on shared hard candidates transfers refinement into one-pass recommendation. We characterize the fusion weights induced by candidate conditioning and establish sufficient conditions for preserving the refined predictor's full-catalog Top-$K$ selection. Across six Amazon datasets, OneChord achieves the highest Recall@5 and NDCG@5 among the compared methods on every dataset, with average relative gains of 6.30\% and 7.12\% over the strongest baseline. It also achieves a 1.04--1.18$\times$ full-test generation speedup over the fastest baseline. OneChord makes the served ranking distribution the common object of recommendation learning and distillation.

title: Asymptotic low slopes of toric exponential sums
authors: Rufei Ren
abstract: Let $Δ$ be an integral Newton polytope containing the origin. We prove that the generic Newton slopes corresponding to Hodge slopes strictly smaller than one differ from their Hodge values by $O_Δ(p^{-1})$. No hypothesis is imposed on the semigroup generated by the lattice points of $Δ$. The proof combines an auxiliary prime and the Cartier operator to show that a coefficient of each required Dwork principal minor is nonzero. When the origin is interior to $Δ$, duality gives the same estimate for the corresponding high slopes and, in dimension two, for all slopes.

title: Can LLM User-Proxies Stand In for Humans in Reliance Measurement? Replicating Rel-A.I. with Simulated Users
authors: Shuai Wang, Rui Hu
abstract: Can language-model user proxies reproduce human reliance on an AI answer across contexts? Published simulated-user studies do not establish validity for this partial-answer decision, and Rel-A.I.'s released human record omits trial-level choices. We audit its 90 printed questions and 15 domain-by-marker reliance rates using sampled decisions and counterbalanced A/B probabilities from open models through 72B parameters. A matched crossover varies the printed agent specialty within each question, separating question content, label averages, and their interaction. Mistral Small's strong-marker math-minus-law label marginal is -0.4 percentage points, yet matching the agent label to the question domain raises reliance by 13.3 points on average across the five domains. The best A/B proxy has 22.5-point absolute-rate error and 8.3-point domain-effect error against the human table. A two-sample independent-binomial human replication has 3.5-point expected domain-effect error under the stated working model. The interaction is model dependent, and inference layout changes identical-prompt probabilities. This single-study audit does not establish proxy validity for human effect sizes or general directional screening.

title: From Trace to Fix: Residual Task State in Long-Horizon Agents
authors: Zile Huang, Ser-nam Lim
abstract: Recovering from failures in long-horizon, stateful language agents is challenging because the action introducing a defect, the symptom exposing it, and the persistent state requiring repair frequently diverge. Existing methods largely focus on retrospective failure attribution, leaving sequential diagnosis and state repair poorly integrated under constrained budgets. We introduce TRACE-FIX, a unified recovery framework centered on versioned residual task state. Trace transforms execution logs into a structured dependency-linked ledger, prioritizing unresolved task requirements rather than salient surface errors. Fix formulates recovery as budgeted planning over admissible actions, incorporating outcome forecasting and explicit repair-reserve constraints to prevent premature budget exhaustion. To rigorously decouple localization accuracy from downstream repair capability, we present LongH-Debug, evaluating root-cause attribution, verified-fault recovery, and end-to-end closed-loop execution independently. Our empirical analysis demonstrates that structured residual tracking substantially improves causal localization over raw-trace baselines, while budget-aware sequential planning converts verified fault signals into more reliable task recovery without destructive trial-and-error. Code is available at https://github.com/toffeecat/tracedp.

title: A Fourier expansion principle for coherent cohomology of powers of Tate curves
authors: Kenz Kallal
abstract: In the case of the totally degenerate split degenerations given by fibered powers of Tate curves over $\mathbf{Z}[[q^{1/w}]]$, this article proves a Fourier expansion principle that applies to higher coherent (equivariant) cohomology classes of rigidified line bundles on the $\mathbf{Z}((q^{1/w}))$-fiber. We do not require any ampleness hypotheses. This generalizes a previous Fourier expansion principle due to Faltings--Chai that applies only to sections of ample line bundles; that version was used as a key step in their proof of their classification of polarized degenerations and thus in the construction of toroidal compactifications of moduli spaces of polarized abelian varieties. This article can be considered as a theory of Fourier expansions for algebraic theta cocycles associated to possibly indefinite quadratic forms, and has application to arithmetic: in joint work with Venkatesh, we have used it to produce an algebraic theory of Kudla--Millson indefinite modular theta functions.

title: VHA: VQA-based Hallucination Assessment for Generative Image Super-Resolution
authors: Donghun Ryou, Inju Ha, Jaeyoo Park, Bohyung Han
abstract: Generative image super-resolution produces visually realistic high-resolution images, but may also introduce hallucinations by adding unsupported content or altering existing details. Because existing super-resolution metrics fail to measure whether generated details remain grounded in the reference image, we present a hallucination assessment technique based on bidirectional visual question answering (VQA), which we term VQA-based Hallucination Assessment (VHA). The proposed approach uses a vision-language model (VLM) to determine whether the semantic content and low-level visual evidence in a super-resolved image are supported by its ground-truth counterpart. To this end, it constructs question--answer pairs from each image and evaluates them on both images. Discrepancies between the resulting scores in both directions reveal missing or altered ground-truth information and unsupported additions. However, obtaining these scores requires computationally expensive VLM inference. We therefore develop VHA+, a learned, lightweight model that directly predicts VHA scores from ground-truth and super-resolved image pairs. We construct a hallucination benchmark, VHA-bench, through a human study and show that both VHA and VHA+ correlate highly with human judgments of hallucination. The code, benchmark, and model weights are available at https://github.com/dhryougit/Hallucination-Assessment

title: Jumps and Iterated Jumps of Perfect Subtrees of Positive Trees
authors: Wei Wang
abstract: An infinite (binary) tree is \emph{positive} iff its set of paths is non-null. As an elementary observation, positives trees always have positive perfect subtrees. Given a positive tree of certain complexity, here we present several theorems concerning the distribution of the Turing jumps or iterated Turing jumps of (positive) perfect subtrees of the given tree in the universe of Turing degrees.

title: Truncated Reasoning Under a Budget: Evaluating System-1 Models as Decision-makers
authors: Zhongyin Wang, Zhaoqian Xue, Junting Mu, Haozheng Liu, Ye Yuan, Haolun Wu, Lingyao Li
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often generate more reasoning tokens than needed. Limiting the reasoning budget reduces cost, but forcing an answer from an incomplete trace can hurt accuracy. System-1 decision models select among candidate options without producing a reasoning response. We evaluate Jev as a decision reader of truncated reasoning across seven LLM reasoners and five multiple-choice benchmarks (35 pairs). Jev achieves higher mean accuracy than forced answering at tested budgets from 500 to 16,000 tokens, including the estimated costs of reasoning and answering. At a 1,500-token budget, it improves accuracy by 4.1 pp overall and 8.6 pp on truncated questions, with significant gains in 17 pairs under Holm-corrected bootstrap tests. Offline replay estimates 34.5% of the full-run cost, with a 1.13 pp accuracy loss. A policy selected on training folds saves 71.3% of the estimated full-run cost on held-out folds, with a 0.58 pp accuracy loss. We also find that Jev shows strong question-only accuracy, exceeding 500-token forced answering on average (68.0% vs. 65.5%), although this advantage varies by benchmark. These findings suggest that System-1 decision models can complement LLM reasoning and reduce the need for costly reasoning completion.

title: ActTime: Action-Conditioned World Modeling for Time Series
authors: Xinxing Zhou, Xiaojie Yuan, Yanlong Wen, Ming Jin
abstract: Time-series models increasingly condition on known future inputs. In controlled systems, some of these inputs are actions that can be changed, compared, and optimized before execution. A model must therefore do more than predict the realized future: it must predict how outcomes change under different actions from the same observed history and support reliable comparison of candidate plans. We introduce ActTime, an action-conditioned world model for time series. Over the observed history, ActTime updates variable-specific latent states through an action-conditioned transition and corrects them using observations. It then rolls the same transition forward under candidate actions to generate future trajectories. Training uses only factual trajectories, without paired alternative-action outcomes or planning supervision. We construct a simulator-grounded evaluation suite across building energy, traffic, greenhouse climate, and inventory management, covering factual prediction, intervention-effect prediction, offline decision making, and closed-loop planning. ActTime ranks first in 12 of 16 domain-task settings. Across eight methods, the mean pairwise model-ranking reversal rate is 17.8% between factual prediction and intervention fidelity, and rises to 28.4% between intervention fidelity and decision ranking. These results show that factual accuracy, intervention fidelity, and decision quality are related but not interchangeable.

title: Hadamard Transforms for Dimension Reduction
authors: Mingxuan Sun, Zhiqiang Xu
abstract: Using the Hadamard matrix for dimension reduction can accelerate the computation due to the fast Hadamard transform. However, the previous target dimension bounds in terms of the Gaussian width depend on the ambient dimension. In this paper, we obtain the following ambient dimension free bound using three Hadamard-diagonal blocks. Let $H\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}$ be the normalized Walsh-Hadamard matrix, and let $D_1,D_2,D_3\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}$ be independent Rademacher diagonal matrices. We prove that for any symmetric set $T\subset \mathbb{S}^{d-1}$, \[ \mathbb P\left\{\sup_{\boldsymbol t\in T}\big|\frac dm\|P_ΩHD_3HD_2HD_1\boldsymbol t\|_2^2-1\big|\le\varepsilon\right\} \ge1-δ\] whenever \[ m\gtrsim\varepsilon^{-2}w(T)^2\log^2\frac eδ\,\log^4\!\left(e+\frac{w(T)}\varepsilon\log\frac eδ\right). \] Here $w(T)$ is the Gaussian width of $T$, and $Ω$ is a set of $m$ distinct coordinates chosen uniformly. This is the first ambient dimension free bound on the target dimension using Hadamard transforms, for an arbitrary symmetric set in terms of its Gaussian width. We also prove that it is impossible to obtain an ambient dimension free bound for an arbitrary set in terms of its Gaussian width using two Hadamard-diagonal blocks.

title: A Benders decomposition approach for hierarchical k-medoids
authors: Rick S. H. Willemsen
abstract: We study a hierarchical clustering problem formulated as a sum of k-medoids objectives. This problem is related to the multi-period p-median problem, but instead of having nested facilities, we consider a hierarchy of nested assignments. We present two Benders formulations from the p-median literature and show how the obtained nested p-median solutions can be converted into hierarchical k-medoids solutions. We validate our methods on various instances. First, we show on small-scale instances that a standard Benders decomposition approach achieves speedups of up to three orders of magnitude over an existing branch-and-price method, while producing hierarchical k-medoids solutions that are at most 5% away from optimality. Second, we present an aggregated Benders heuristic that can handle instances with more than 13,000 observations.

title: Topological Compression of Prediction Market Belief States for Event Forecasting
authors: Aadit Jerfy
abstract: Topological Data Analysis (TDA) and Persistent Homology (PH) have been utilized in numerous fields$-$from protein modeling to financial analysis$-$to understand the underlying structure of data. In this paper, we incorporate TDA and PH into forecasting models over a prediction market universe to determine whether the belief state of such markets forms an underlying structure whose shape can provide predictive insight. We conclude that single-parameter PH is able to improve predictive ability and calibrated accuracy of linear forecasting models, while two-parameter multipersistence produces similar benefits for nonlinear models.

title: Combinatorial Calabi flows on infinitely triangulated surfaces
authors: Yuerong Bian, Xu Xu
abstract: We study the combinatorial Calabi flow associated with vertex scalings on infinitely triangulated surfaces with piecewise Euclidean and piecewise hyperbolic metrics. Under the assumptions of uniformly bounded vertex degree and an $ε$-uniformly nondegenerate initial metric, we establish short-time existence of smooth solutions and prove uniqueness among solutions that are continuous in the $L^\infty$ norm.

title: Using Bayesian Sequential Logistic Regression to Model the Organ Transplant Selection Process
authors: Xukun Zhu, Tyler Schappe, Ursula Rogers, Roland Matsouaka, Jacqueline B. Henson, Norine W. Chan, Goni Katz-Greenberg, Lisa M. McElroy, Samuel I. Berchuck
abstract: Organ transplantation evaluation is a multi-stage process in which only patients who complete one stage remain eligible for the next, leading to patient attrition and reducing later-stage sample sizes. Covariate associations may differ across decision points, and identifying these stage-specific effects is necessary to target interventions and understand disparities. Conventional approaches that model each transition independently fail to distinguish stage-specific from shared associations and tend to produce imprecise estimates at later stages. We propose a Bayesian sequential logistic regression (BSLR) framework that represents progression as conditional Bernoulli distributions within a joint likelihood that preserves chronological ordering; we further show its equivalence to an adjusted continuation-ratio model. A hierarchical prior decomposes each covariate effect into an overall effect and a transition-specific deviation. This partial-pooling structure shares information across stages and stabilizes estimation where data are sparse, while a masking mechanism accommodates covariates structurally unavailable at particular stages without discarding records or imputing values. In simulations, BSLR achieved lower bias, posterior variance, and mean squared error than independent logistic regression. We demonstrated the utility of our model using a cohort of patients referred for kidney or liver transplant. Posterior estimates indicated that the associations of clinical indicators and social determinants of health with progression differed across care continuum phases. BSLR identified stage-specific heterogeneity in covariate associations, revealing factors whose effects reversed direction across evaluation stages and detecting associations at late-stage transitions that independent models failed to resolve due to insufficient precision.

title: The Eighth-Order Evolution Model for Closed Planar Curves
authors: Yanlong Zhang, Li Ma
abstract: We consider the $L^2(ds)$ gradient flow of $\frac12\int k_{ss}^2\,ds$ for smooth closed immersed planar curves. The stationary curves are precisely the multiply covered circles. We give an explicit sufficient condition under which the elastic energy is non-increasing and for each nonzero turning number, explicit small initial scale-invariant energy yields a global smooth solution with bounded positive length and exponential convergence to a fixed multiply covered circle, after reparametrisation. We note that that the qualitative rigidity and convergence results are already contained in the generalised ideal flow theory of McCoy and Wheeler. The present paper gives quantitative measure of small initial data, corrected evolution identities, and a complete argument in the case of the curvature energy $\frac12\int k_{ss}^2\,ds$.

title: Rational Points on Drinfeld Modular Curves of Prime Level
authors: Ryotaro Sakamoto
abstract: Let $q \ge 3$ be a prime power and let $\mathfrak{p} \subset \mathbf{F}_q[T]$ be a nonzero prime ideal of degree $d$. We prove that $Y_0(\mathfrak{p})(\mathbf{F}_q(T))=\emptyset$ if $d \ge 4$ is even or $d>q$, and that $Y_1(\mathfrak{p})(\mathbf{F}_q(T)) = \emptyset $ for every $d \ge 3$.

title: How Effectively Do Security Skills Guide Coding Agents in Vulnerability Detection in Linux Kernel?
authors: Haoran Xue, Nikta Akbarpour, Gias Uddin, Song Wang
abstract: Large language model (LLM) coding agents, such as Claude Code, are increasingly used for security auditing, with task-specific skills providing reusable vulnerability-analysis procedures. However, their effectiveness in detecting real vulnerabilities and the reasons for their failures remain unclear. We conduct the first large-scale empirical study of 37 security skills using Claude Code with four underlying LLMs on 100 real Linux kernel vulnerabilities across ten classes, totaling 14800 runs. We evaluate vulnerability detection at the function, statement, and vulnerability-class levels. Results show that 24.4 percent of runs locate the correct function, 18.3 percent identify both the function and responsible statement, and 15.7 percent correctly classify the vulnerability. Our failure analysis reveals limitations in evidence acquisition, state-relation reasoning, code interpretation, candidate verification, investigation coverage, and reporting. Based on these findings, we propose SKILL-SIF, a self-improving framework that iteratively evolves security skills by learning from missed vulnerabilities and failure patterns. We evolve five top-performing skills using the original benchmark and evaluate them on 100 previously unseen vulnerabilities. SKILL-SIF improves fully correct vulnerability detection by up to eight times (from 2 percent to 16 percent) on unseen vulnerabilities, while aggregate accuracy across four LLMs increases by 1.85 times (from 6.05 percent to 11.20 percent). These findings highlight the limitations of existing security skills and demonstrate the potential of failure-driven skill evolution to improve vulnerability detection in coding agents.

title: Sharp Holder regularity for autonomous Beltrami equations
authors: Jie Huang, Jian-Feng Zhu
abstract: Let $Ω\subset\mathbb C$ be a domain and let $\mathcal H:\mathbb C\to\mathbb C$ be Lipschitz with constant $0<k<1$. We prove that every weak $W^{1,2}_{\mathrm{loc}}$ solution of the autonomous Beltrami equation $f_{\bar z}=\mathcal H(f_z)$ belongs to $C^{1,γ}_{\mathrm{loc}}$, where $γ=3/(2K+1)$ and $K=(1+k)/(1-k)$. The exponent is optimal, resolving the conjecture of Astala, Clop, Faraco, Jääskeläinen and Koski.

title: Global hydrodynamic limit of the incompressible Navier-Stokes/Vlasov-Fokker-Planck system with large data
authors: Jian Li, Huanyao Wen
abstract: In this paper, we aim to investigate the global-in-time hydrodynamic limit of the incompressible Navier-Stokes/Vlasov-Fokker-Planck system for light particles. With a modified micro-macro decomposition yielding uniform a priori estimates with respect to the Deborah number $\varepsilon$, we prove that the solution of the original system tends to that of the target system, i.e., the incompressible Navier-Stokes/Kramers-Smoluchowski system, as Deborah number goes to zero, and that quantitative convergence rates are obtained in the $L_{x,v,t}^\infty$ norm. Compared with the existing results that the convergence is from ``weak solution" to ``strong solution", the convergence results in the present work are further developed globally in time from ``strong solution" to ``strong solution" with vacuum (i.e., the macroscopic particle density may vanish at far field or at any point) and large initial data for both the original system and the target system. In addition, the ill-prepared initial data for the microscopic component of the kinetic quantity are allowed.

title: Progress-Guided Preference Generation for Aligning Generative Control Policies
authors: Tung M. Luu, Tri Ton, Duc M. Nguyen, Xuan Thanh Nguyen, Nguyen Gia Binh, Quang Tan Nguyen, Vu Duong, Daniel Sonntag, Duy M. H. Nguyen, Vien Anh Ngo, Chang D. Yoo
abstract: Generative policies have achieved strong performance in imitation learning tasks, but their success is often constrained by the limited availability of expert demonstrations. Although preference-based fine-tuning can leverage suboptimal rollouts to improve performance, existing approaches heavily rely on expensive human annotations. In this work, we introduce Progress-Guided Preference Generation (PGPG), an unsupervised preference alignment framework that eliminates the need for human-in-the-loop supervision. Our method leverages ordered coverage alignment to measure sequential progress relative to a small set of expert demonstrations, enabling the automatic extraction of pseudo-preference labels from autonomously collected rollouts. Furthermore, we introduce key enhancements to improve the reliability of these progress-guided preferences, enabling effective fine-tuning of pretrained generative policies without requiring manually designed reward functions. Extensive experiments across a suite of challenging long-horizon manipulation tasks demonstrate that PGPG outperforms standard supervised fine-tuning baselines. Moreover, our conceptually simple framework is broadly applicable across multiple classes of generative policies, demonstrating strong versatility when integrated with both diffusion and flow-matching policies.

title: A Theoretical Perspective on Link Prediction Heuristics
authors: Jiajie Shi, David A. Meyer
abstract: In network analysis, nodes with different degrees are usually weighted differently in tasks such as link prediction. For example, two individuals connected to the same high-degree node (e.g., a celebrity) are often considered less likely to know each other than if they share a low-degree connection. In this paper, we theoretically justify the reasoning behind this heuristic using a graph generation model. In this model, nodes are embedded in a latent metric space, and edges are more likely to form between nearby nodes. We analytically derive degree-based weighting schemes for commonly used link prediction and similarity measures. In particular, we identify the optimal weighting scheme for the Common Neighbors index and extend our analysis to other popular heuristics, including the graph distance. Our theoretical findings align with previous empirical observations, and we further validate them through experiments on both synthetic and real-world networks.

title: Plate-YOLO: An End-to-End Object Detection Framework for Robust Astrometric Registration of Historical Plates
authors: Quanfeng Xu, Zhengjun Shang, Shiyin Shen, Yong Yu, Mingyang Ma, Zhenghong Tang, Meiting Yang, Jing Yang, Jianhai Zhao
abstract: Historical astronomical plates provide a long temporal baseline for time-domain astrophysics, but degradation and structural artifacts can hinder automated astrometric calibration. We present Plate-YOLO, a framework that combines source detection and stellar classification in one detector and supplies source catalogs to a separate astrometric solver. The detector adapts YOLOv5 with Space-to-Depth feature rearrangement, SimAM attention, a high-resolution P2 head, and a Normalized Wasserstein Distance loss for small bounding boxes. A Gaia-guided fine-tuning procedure uses initially solved plates to construct labels for a new archive. On 150 UBAI plates for which the conventional pipeline had failed, the Chinese-trained model solved 40 plates, and target-archive fine-tuning recovered a further 106, giving an overall recovery rate of 146/150 (97.3%). In the reported hardware configuration, source extraction took 6.61 s per plate for Plate-YOLO and 16.73 s for SExtractor. These results demonstrate the practical value of adapting source detection to degraded historical plates.

title: Non-Riemannian Holography: Long Strings and Soft Hair
authors: Shaun D. Hampton, Hyun-Cheol Kim, Jae-Hyuk Oh, Jeong-Hyuck Park
abstract: We propose an $\mathbf{O}(D,D)$-covariant holographic dictionary for two bulk completions of the Gomis--Ooguri boundary data: Riemannian $AdS_3$ supported by pure NS--NS flux and an everywhere non-Riemannian string Newton--Cartan geometry. An $\mathbf{O}(D,D)$-covariant Codazzi identity yields the boundary conservation law. Both branches share diagonal generalized-metric one-point functions, but only the non-Riemannian branch carries independent normalizable soft hair that couples to long strings without contributing to surface charges or the renormalized on-shell action. Supersymmetric non-Riemannian saddles admit arbitrary chiral Killing-spinor profiles, realizing "supersupersymmetry."

title: A LATE-Targeting Experimental Design for Multi-Arm RCTs
authors: Tetsuya Kaji
abstract: We study the design of multi-arm experiments that identify local average treatment effects under imperfect compliance. With three or more arms, conventional randomization fails to identify margin-specific effects even under strong extensions of monotone compliance. A choice-theoretic analysis unifies these extensions and motivates a two-stage design: subjects report a preferred arm and are randomized conditional on it. If treatment is confined to the assigned or reported arm, one-sided noncompliance is restored conditional on the report, identifying the effect between the two for their compliers. We discuss the design's applicability and feasibility in relation to the choice model.

title: PoSTCache: From Forecasting to Postdictive Smoothing for Revisable Diffusion Caching
authors: Liwei Lan, Hui Chen, Jungong Han, Guiguang Ding
abstract: Diffusion and flow matching models achieve impressive visual generation quality but remain computationally expensive due to iterative sampling. Caching-based acceleration provides a practical training-free solution by reusing or predicting intermediate features. However, existing methods largely enforce a forward-only information flow: approximations produced for skipped model evaluations are immediately committed to the sampling trajectory and cannot benefit from feedback generated by later full-computation steps. We propose \textbf{PoSTCache} (\emph{Postdictive Smoothing Trajectory Cache}), a training-free and plug-and-play framework that reformulates diffusion caching as revisable trajectory inference. PoSTCache first uses an existing caching strategy to construct forward proposals for skipped steps. At a later full-computation step, the discrepancy between the refreshed prediction and its forward proposal yields a correction signal, which PoSTCache propagates backward to refine and reintegrate the preceding predictions. Viewing full-computation steps as sources of corrective feedback also changes how they should be selected. We therefore introduce the Posterior Variance Reduction (PVR) strategy, which estimates cross-timestep dependencies from offline denoising trajectories and selects anchors according to their expected reduction in surrogate trajectory uncertainty rather than local approximation error alone. Experiments on representative image and video generation models show that PoSTCache consistently improves the quality--efficiency trade-off over representative caching methods.

title: FluidGen: Physics-Aware Fluid Video Generation via Motion-Guided Post-Training
authors: Yang Zheng, Zizhang Li, Boyang Deng, Jan Ackermann, Lei Shu, Yinghao Xu, Jiajun Wu, Gordon Wetzstein, Leonidas Guibas
abstract: Video generation models produce visually compelling motion but systematically fail on fluid phenomena, including smoke, fire, and explosion debris, where outputs lack coherent vortical structure and collapse to bland dynamics that violate the physics of real fluids. Classical solvers achieve high physical fidelity but require detailed 3D scenes and carefully tuned parameters, making them impractical for in-the-wild imagery and video generation. We address this gap by injecting a data-driven fluid prior into a pre-trained video model, trained on a mixture of high-fidelity Houdini simulation data with paired velocity-field ground truth and curated in-the-wild fluid video data for appearance diversity. The core of our approach is a dual stream architecture that predicts per-frame velocity fields alongside RGB, supervised by simulation ground truth. This auxiliary signal regularizes generation toward physically consistent motion and exposes an interpretable physical quantity that we further leverage as a reward for velocity-aware direct preference optimization. Our model produces substantially more realistic fluid dynamics sequences than strong video baselines and optimization-based methods. Project page: https://y-zheng18.github.io/FluidGen/

title: All-Dielectric Tight-Binding Photonics via a Band-Gap Vacuum
authors: Aodong Li, Jing Li, Tao Xiao, Biye Xie
abstract: Tight-binding photonics bridges condensed-matter physics and optics, providing a powerful framework for engineering band structures and topological phases with light. For photons, however, the vacuum is gapless, so resonators in air carry radiative tails that produce spurious long-range couplings. Here we embed resonators in a photonic band-gap vacuum (BgV), a photonic crystal whose band gap plays for photons the role vacuum plays for bound electrons. The BgV localizes each resonance exponentially, so designed short-range couplings define the lattice Hamiltonian. We thereby experimentally realize a faithful Benalcazar-Bernevig-Hughes Hamiltonian in an all-dielectric photonic crystal, resolving corner resonances and their orbitals in microwave measurements. Unlike the vacuum surrounding electrons, the BgV is itself designable, controlling relative couplings and closed-loop interference through its band dispersion and Bloch modes. Full-wave calculations and extracted models show that uniformly modifying the BgV, with all resonators fixed, switches the quantized polarization of a two-dimensional Su-Schrieffer-Heeger lattice and converts a zero-flux lattice into a $π$-flux one. We also numerically realize three-dimensional pyrochlore and hyperhoneycomb lattices with space groups $R\bar{3}m$ and $C2/c$, the latter a nodal-loop semimetal with topological drumhead surface states. These results establish the BgV as a designable vacuum for all-dielectric tight-binding photonics in two and three dimensions.

title: The classification of taut surface singularities via representations from logarithmic vector fields
authors: Heesang Park, Dongsoo Shin
abstract: We study logarithmic vector fields on exceptional cycles through finite-dimensional representations and recover Laufer's classification of taut normal complex surface singularities. For graphs with two nodes, restriction maps define representations of a fixed quiver, with dimensions bounded independently of the number of components and their self-intersections. We identify restriction cohomology with an extension group and use interval decomposition to reduce its vanishing to interpolation on a rational chain. These calculations determine the classification conditions, and vanishing on every analytic realization proves sufficiency, including the nonrational cases. The obstruction cycles also give a uniform criterion: a graph is taut if and only if $H^1(5E,S_X|_{5E})=0$ for every analytic realization, where $S_X$ is the ambient logarithmic tangent bundle. We prove that five is the smallest positive integer for which this criterion holds for all graphs.

title: A "feature ODE" describing the learning behavior of shallow MLPs on simple functions
authors: Joseph Turnbull, Berkan Ottlik, Jamie Simon
abstract: We study the gradient flow training dynamics of two-layer multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs) on anisotropic Gaussian data. Even in this simple setting, solving the dynamics in full is notoriously difficult, so we try something different. We propose a "feature ODE" that might be intuitively expected to describe the learning dynamics of a shallow MLP. We find that MLPs trained to learn simple target functions (low-order Hermite polynomials and staircase functions) actually roughly follow the loss trajectories from this feature ODE. This agreement is a surprise because of the size of the simplification and the fact that it does not come from a rigorous chain of approximations. We discuss this surprise and speculate on its reasons and uses.

title: Consistency Training Suppresses Cue Following Without Teaching Cue Selectivity
authors: Prakhar Gupta, Terry Jingchen Zhang, Zhijing Jin
abstract: Language models often change answers because of a cue, a hint such as "I believe the answer is B" that gives no valid evidence. Consistency training (CT) trains a model to answer the same with and without the cue. Four CT methods apply this idea to output tokens (BCT), residual activations (ACT), attention patterns (AttCT) and sampled-answer rates (RMCT). Prior work suggests some learn different solutions. We train all four on Gemma-2-2B-it and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct with the same data. We test predictions written in advance and inspect the models with a known circuit that carries cues to the answer. All four make the trained cue less effective, and their fixes share three properties. First, correct cues lose about as much influence as wrong ones. Second, the fix is usually large for cues before the answer options, as in training, and much smaller after them. Llama RMCT depends least on position. Third, the circuit heads still carry most remaining cue-induced errors. Making BCT targets depend on the cue's correctness mostly weakens the fix. CT thus weakens the trained cue without teaching models when a cue is right. Evaluations with only wrong cues at the trained position miss the first two properties.

title: The Forward/Inverse Duality of Controlled Emergence:A Computational Design Program from Explanation to Engineering
authors: Hao Li, Minghui Ren, Shaowen Lu
abstract: The macroscopic capabilities of intelligent systems arise from the local interactions of many simple units. When such systems are deployed in the real world, their behaviour must nevertheless be constrained, leaving designers caught between releasing adaptability and preventing loss of control, yet without formal tools to resolve the dilemma. This paper proposes a unified research program for controlled emergence that restates this tension as a pair of dual problems: the forward problem explains macroscopic behaviour from local rules, and the inverse problem solves for controllable rules and readout mechanisms from a desired target. We take an augmented quintuple as the formal object shared by both ends, and decompose ``engineering'' into three independently measurable coordinates: controllability, reproducibility, and degree of formalizability. On this basis we give three testable working hypotheses (critical scale; the cooperation and trade-off between constraint and adaptability; minimal constraint) and one feasibility criterion, which reduce inverse design from unconstrained optimization to interval checking. The program takes explicit failure boundaries as its premise, does not pursue complete control, and always preserves the system's room for self-organization. The reduced pilot experiment attached to this paper serves only to verify the executability of the research protocol and does not constitute a statistical test of the working hypotheses. This design language generalizes to multi-agent artificial intelligence, the industrial internet, and emergency response systems, all of which must confront emergence and controllability at once.

title: Zephyrus-R1: Agentic Reinforcement Learning for Weather Reporting
authors: Fengfei Yu, Marshall Fisher, Isadora White, Sumanth Varambally, Yasaman Jafari, Shivam Yadav, Samuel M. Bartlett, Shawn Roj, Benjamin J. Moore, Michael D. Warner, Luyu Han, Zhirui Xia, Duncan Watson-Parris, Taylor Berg-Kirkpatrick, Yian Ma, Rose Yu
abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has emerged as a key method for training AI models in scientific applications, but RL remains difficult when outputs cannot easily be verified against a known ground-truth answer. Natural-language weather forecast reports are one such domain: they translate atmospheric data into assessments of weather evolution, hazards, and uncertainty for both the general public and key decision-makers. Unlike numerical weather-analysis questions, they admit many valid outputs, which limits deterministic verification. To address this, we develop Zephyrus-R1, a practical framework for RL on scientific weather forecast reporting. We focus on three key components of the agentic RL pipeline: reward design, curriculum learning, and an analysis of human-expert alignment. To encourage both report legibility and factual accuracy, we design a reward function that combines a meteorological rubric with bidirectional claim entailment, both evaluated against National Weather Service reference reports. Our framework optimizes this reward in a simulated tool-calling environment, enabling vision-language agents to gather and analyze forecast evidence across regions and lead times before producing a report. We use annotations from three meteorologists to audit the claim labels produced by our LLM judges. Finally, a curriculum helps small models first develop tool use and scientific reasoning through RL on verifiable weather-analysis questions, then optimize the open-ended report reward. After training Qwen3.5-4B with Zephyrus-R1, we improve the mean across six judge-metric scores by 26% over the base model and achieve results competitive with frontier open-weight models. For Qwen3.8-27B, we improve the same mean by 13% over the base model, by 6.7% over Kimi-K3, and by 2.7% over GPT-5.6-Luna.

title: Which Immersions into Euclidean Space are Boundary Immersions?
authors: Austin Konkel
abstract: Here we study the problem of whether a given codimension one immersion $f$ of a closed and connected manifold into Euclidean space can be extended to an equidimensional immersion $F$ of some compact manifold $M$ whose restriction to the boundary parameterizes the image $S$ of $f$. Such an extension $F$ exists if and only if (i) simple conditions on orientations and wrapping numbers are satisfied and (ii) a distinguished finite subset of the first cohomology of $S$ with coefficients in a certain sheaf of finite groups contains the preferred point.

title: Tensorial pinching by deforming curvature cones in higher codimension mean curvature flow
authors: Tsz-Kiu Aaron Chow
abstract: We develop a pinching method for mean curvature flow in higher codimension. Motivated by pinching constructions for Ricci flow, the method uses a nonlinear deformation of the second fundamental form. We introduce two tensorial curvature conditions for closed immersions in Euclidean space which extend beyond the scope of classical scalar pinching results. In dimensions at least ten, we apply the method to prove convergence to a round point under the first condition and a canonical neighborhood theorem under the second.

title: Text Dominance in Paralinguistic Conflict: Tracing Suppression Through Audio LLM Circuits
authors: Ankur Banerjee, Vishnu Guntakala, Danity Pike, Advay Roongta, Kevin Yang, Ruizhe Li
abstract: Audio LLMs deployed in settings such as crisis hotlines and customer support are only useful beyond speech-to-text pipelines if they use acoustic cues rather than the transcript alone. We test whether they prioritise transcript content over paralinguistic cues (emotion, speaker identity, sarcasm) and trace the mechanism when they do. Across six audio LLMs under LISTEN-style conflict conditions, the mean text-dominance rate on mismatched text+audio items is 0.78 (0.86 excluding sarcasm). In the most text-dominant screened model, probing shows speaker identity remains linearly decodable at ceiling at the language model's input, so the failure is not perceptual. Back-patching, reported to repair lexical text dominance, has no measurable effect here; but it also fails on its own source task in our replication (n=300), so we treat its null as uninformative rather than as evidence of non-transfer. Attention knockout partially restores audio-grounded output by blocking the claim from propagating through intermediate tokens during open-ended generation, whereas blocking the answer position's direct connection to the conflicting claim has no effect. The claim's influence therefore travels through an intermediate relay rather than a single severable edge. The effect appears only in free-form generation and not in closed-set multiple choice, suggesting that benchmarks relying on that format may be systematically blind to interventions of this kind. Code and data are publicly available at https://github.com/AdvayRoongta/audio-llm-mech-interp.
