Existing defense methods struggle to balance the shareability of photos with effective protection, and often fail to sufficiently disrupt the implicit geo-evidence chains embedded in scene semantics. To this end, we propose GeoEdit, an adversarial de-evidencing framework for silent geoprivacy protection via image editing. Specifically, we apply minimal edits to high-risk evidence anchors in the image, thereby disrupting the underlying spatial reasoning chains while preserving overall scene semantics. We identify these anchors by combining structured knowledge with adversarially discovered geographic cues. To further navigate the large editing action space, we adopt a learnable policy to iteratively refine editing decisions, distilling successful trajectories into transferable natural-language insights for consistent and efficient editing. Evaluated on LifePhotoBench, GeoEdit achieves strong protection against 6 mainstream MLRMs, outperforming visual perturbation baselines by over 0.59 in image fidelity.

title: Wan-Alpha++: Animating a Single RGBA Asset into Controllable Transparent Video Effects
authors: Haotian Dong, Xin Wang, Wenjing Wang, Chen Li, Jing Lyu, Yan Tina Luximon, Ping Li, Wanchao Su, Ke Xu, Di Lin
abstract: RGBA video generation is essential for creating compositable visual assets in filmmaking, game development, and digital content production. However, generating high-quality RGB appearance alongside temporally coherent transparency remains a significant challenge. Existing text-to-RGBA video methods often entangle RGB and alpha distributions and offer limited control over the precise appearance of a target asset. In addition, incorporating image conditioning typically suffers from the emergence-disappearance effects, which fail existing first-frame or first-and-last-frame conditions due to their fully transparent boundary frames. To address these issues, we present Wan-Alpha++, a unified framework that brings controllable RGBA video generation to both text- and image-to-video diffusion backbones through a shared RGBA latent space, extending our conference version Wan-Alpha from the text-conditioned setting to image-conditioned generation with an interior reference frame. Our method first learns shiftable RGB-alpha distributions while preserving the pretrained RGB prior. Specifically, we introduce a transparency-aware bidirectional diffusion objective to produce distinguishable RGBA latent representations, and a transparency-guided mean sampler that shifts the noise distribution to improve transparency generation and enable spatial controllability. Building upon this RGBA generation prior, we introduce temporal phase reparameterization for image-conditioned effect generation. By cyclically transforming a zero-positive-zero alpha pattern into a positive-zero-positive pattern, it relocates visible content to both temporal boundaries, facilitating effective appearance conditioning with limited RGBA data.

title: Measurements of time-dependent b-hadron properties in LHCb
authors: Lucas Foreman
abstract: These proceedings present the latest measurements of time-dependent properties of $b$-hadrons using the LHCb Run 2 data set. Three results are presented. The first of these is a measurement of the CKM phase $φ_s$ with $B_s^0\to J/ψπ^+π^-$. This result improves the determination in this channel, obtaining a result of $φ_s = -77\pm34(\text{stat})\pm7(\text{syst})$ mrad. This result is included in the LHCb global average to obtain $φ_s = -41\pm17$ mrad. Additionally, a determination of the penguin contributions, $Δφ_s$, to measurements of $φ_s$ using $B^0\to J/ψρ^0(770)$ is presented. This measurement constitutes the first observation of CP-violation in $B_0 \to J/ψρ^0(770)$ decays. The CKM phase $2β$ is measured and is determined to be $2β^{\text{eff}}_{ccd} = 0.710\pm0.084\pm0.051$ rad. The most stringent constraint on penguin contributions is obtained and determined to be $Δφ_s = 5.0\pm4.6$ mrad. Finally, the first measurement of time-dependent CP-violation in a $b\to s l^+ l^-$ process using the decay $B_s^0 \to K_S μ^+ μ^- $ is presented. The time-dependent coefficients of this decay are determined to be $C=-0.13\pm0.32(\text{stat})\pm0.04(\text{syst})$ and $S=+0.82\pm0.29(\text{stat})\pm0.05(\text{syst})$.

title: Disc breaking and parametric instability in warped accretion discs driven by differential precession
authors: Loren E. Held, Gordon I. Ogilvie
abstract: We present the first local simulations of accretion disc breaking (or disc tearing) with differential precession. Precession can occur due to a non-spherical potential (e.g. tilted circumbinary discs), or relativistic effects (e.g. tilted discs around spinning black holes). This tends to induce a twist in the disc, potentially causing it to break into rings. We extend earlier work on free (unforced) warps in Held+2026 [arXiv:2511.18655v1] to include differential precession in the shearing box, and carry out quasi-2D, isothermal, high-resolution ($N = 32$ cells per scale-height $H$) numerical simulations in which an imposed precession drives a warp in a tilted disc in either the wavelike ($α< H/r$) or diffusive ($α> H/r$) regime. Our key finding is that, at sufficiently large tilts and precession amplitudes, the disc breaks into multiple (4-5) mutually tilted rings exhibiting a rich morphology: from wide ($\sim 10H$), flat rings to compact tori of width $\sim H$. Interactions between rings occur as a result of oblique shocks that form in the gaps between them, leading to instances of disc rejoining. Smaller tilts and precession amplitudes lead instead to parametric instability of inertial waves in the disc. We develop a linear viscous theory of bending waves under the influence of an imposed precession. Finally, we present a systematic study of the effects of grid-based dissipation on tilted discs, and find that numerical dissipation damps the tilt and induces precession. This effect decreases with resolution as $\propto (1/N)^β$, $2.3 \lesssim β\lesssim 3.9$.

title: Competitive roles of turbulence and magnetic field on the formation of unipolar outflows in isolated molecular cloud cores
authors: Daisuke Takaishi, Yusuke Tsukamoto, Miyu Kido, Shigehisa Takakuwa, Yoshiaki Misugi, Yuki Kudoh, Yasushi Suto
abstract: We investigate the impact of turbulence and magnetic field on the formation of unipolar outflows in the gravitational collapse of isolated low-mass cloud cores using three-dimensional non-ideal magnetohydrodynamics simulations. In the models explored in this study, we find that unipolar outflows are formed in cloud cores with the super-Alfvénic turbulence of $M_{\rm{A}}>1$, where $M_{\rm{A}}$ is the Alfvén Mach number of the initial cloud core. In contrast, bipolar outflows are formed in cloud cores with $M_{\rm{A}}\lesssim1$. Our results suggest that the relative strength of the turbulence to the magnetic field in the initial cloud core plays a key role in the formation of unipolar outflows. We also find that no outflow is formed in cloud cores with the strong magnetic field of the dimensionless mass-to-flux ratio $μ=2$. The outflow morphologies can be used as tracers to indirectly estimate the relative strengths of the turbulence and magnetic field of the parent cloud cores.

title: Quantum control as renormalization group flow
authors: Zuo Wang, Paul M. Schindler, Modesto Orozco-Ruiz, Nguyen H. Le, Florian Mintert, Marin Bukov
abstract: The Renormalization Group (RG) establishes relations between effective descriptions of physical systems at different scales; in Hamiltonian RG, these relations induce a flow in the space of Hamiltonians. In direct correspondence, we design an RG framework for quantum control by constructing a flow in the space of time-dependent Hamiltonians. A prescribed control subspace, selected to contain only experimentally accessible terms, forms the fixed-point manifold, while the flow preserves the target unitary and monotonically reduces the Hamiltonian weight outside this subspace. Exploiting the freedom in constructing the flow, we introduce flow-equation engineering to enhance the versatility of the framework for diverse control problems, including time-periodic and open-interval smooth protocols with prescribed endpoints. We provide two disparate applications to exhibit the utility of our approach: (i) Nonperturbative Floquet engineering beyond the regime of validity of high-frequency expansions, which we demonstrate by constructing an implementable time-periodic protocol for the Haldane model; (ii) Accessible fast-forward driving from unit-fidelity counterdiabatic evolution, which we showcase for large transverse-field Ising chains away from the adiabatic regime by compressing the long-range multibody adiabatic gauge potential into the original time-dependent Ising control schedules. Our control RG framework reveals a unifying perspective on Hamiltonian engineering and unitary quantum control, and can serve as an organizing principle behind seemingly disparate nonequilibrium quantum dynamics.

title: Bayesian Geometric Inversion for Wave Equation: Well-Posedness and Multiscale Multimodal Posterior Approximation
authors: Xiong-Bin Yan, Ming-Jia Pei, Guang-Hui Zheng, Ting Wei
abstract: Geometric full-waveform inversion aims to recover sharp subsurface interfaces from noisy waveform observations. We formulate this problem within a Bayesian level-set framework, where the unknown interface is represented as zero level set of a latent function endowed with a Gaussian prior. Although the level-set-to-medium-parameter map is discontinuous, we establish that the level-set-to-observation map is continuous almost surely with respect to the prior, thereby guaranteeing that the posterior measure is well-posed and locally Lipschitz continuous with respect to the data in the Hellinger metric. To enable tractable posterior computation under the severe nonlinearity of the inverse problem and the resulting multimodality, we develop a multiscale multimodal Laplace approximation. A frequency-continuation strategy incorporates waveform data progressively from low to high frequencies, identifying and propagating multiple candidate modes across successive scales. At the final frequency level, local Gaussian approximations are constructed around the retained modes and combined into a Gaussian mixture, whose weights are determined by least-squares fitting to the unnormalized posterior density. Numerical experiments demonstrate that the method accurately reconstructs anomalous interfaces while effectively capturing posterior multimodality and the local uncertainty associated with distinct plausible geometries.

title: Superstability of micrometer viscous jets surrounded by weakly-elastic viscous shells
authors: A. Rubio-González, D. Fernández-Martínez, M. Vakili, J. M. Montanero
abstract: Our experiments demonstrate the strong stabilizing effect of a viscoelastic shell on flow-focused viscous jets. The results suggest that stabilization occurs when the polymer viscosity, $η_p$, exceeds a critical threshold, provided the extensional relaxation time, $λ$, is large enough to allow the polymer molecules to undergo the coil-stretch transition. Under these conditions, substantial extensional viscoelastic stresses develop as the liquid accelerates. Since both $η_p$ and $λ$ increase with shell viscosity, the polymer concentration required to stabilize the viscous jet decreases accordingly. Remarkably, moderately to highly viscous jets can be stabilized with very small polymer concentrations, for which no beads-on-a-string (BOAS) instability is observed.

title: Zero products of Toeplitz operators with harmonic symbols on the Bergman space of the unit ball
authors: Jiawei Wang, Xianfeng Zhao
abstract: In this paper, using local boundary factorizations of harmonic functions and singular-value estimates for Toeplitz products, we study the zero-product problem for Toeplitz operators on the Bergman space of the unit ball in $\mathbb{C}^n$. We prove that a finite product of such operators is zero only if one of the symbols is identically zero, provided that all the symbols are harmonic on the open unit ball and continuous on the closed unit ball.

title: Short-Distance-Free Leptonic $g-2$
authors: Siyuan Li, Vladimir Pascalutsa, Maxim Pospelov
abstract: We note that the hadronic contributions to $a_e$ and $a_μ$ are strongly correlated, which potentially allows one to reduce the uncertainties associated with higher-energy contributions (and address the current discrepancy between lattice and data-driven evaluations) by improved measurements of $a_e$ and the fine-structure constant.

title: Smooth radial quantized Type II blow-up for the three-dimensional energy-critical nonlinear Schrödinger equation
authors: Taegyu Kim
abstract: We consider the focusing energy-critical nonlinear Schrödinger equation in three dimensions. In \cite{Schmid2026CVPDE}, Schmid constructed finite-time type II blow-up solutions with a continuum of blow-up rates, while the existence of smooth finite-time type II blow-up solutions remained open. We resolve this problem by constructing, for each integer $L\ge1$, smooth radial solutions concentrating a single ground state with the blow-up rate $λ(t)=(\ell+o(1))(T-t)^{2L}$ for some $\ell>0$. Our proof follows a forward construction based on modulation analysis with the energy method. The main obstacle is the lack of a repulsive structure that can be directly exploited to control the remainder. To overcome this obstacle, we adapt Kato's smoothing theory from asymptotic stability analysis to the forward construction. This yields a global spacetime Morawetz estimate for the linearized flow, providing the spacetime control needed to bound the higher-order energy in place of the monotonicity derived from repulsive structures in previous blow-up constructions.

title: Optimal Multi-Kernel Combination for Online Multi-Label Classification
authors: Tingting Zhai, Wei Liu, Renjian Yu
abstract: Multi-label classification is particularly challenging in streaming scenarios, where data arrives sequentially. Online kernel methods offer a promising solution. However, prevailing methods rely on a single preselected kernel, making them prone to suboptimal choices since the global data distribution is unknown in advance in online settings. Although the recent method, Online Kernel Selection for Online Multi-label Classification (OKS-OMC), enables data-driven kernel selection, it fails to fully harness the complementary information from multiple kernels and encounters the curse of kernelization. To address these limitations, this paper introduces a novel online multi-kernel combination method for large-scale multi-label classification. First, an efficient and robust online single-kernel multi-label method is designed. Second, learning an optimal convex combination of multiple multi-label kernel classifiers is formalized as a structural risk minimization problem. An improved alternating optimization procedure is developed, in which the combination coefficients are updated by directly minimizing the objective function, while each kernel classifier is updated by minimizing a surrogate upper bound. This procedure decouples the learning of kernel classifiers from combination coefficients, allowing independent classifier updates via our single-kernel method and accelerating convergence to high-quality solutions. Our multi-kernel method is proven to asymptotically converge to the optimal fixed convex combination of the best fixed single-kernel models chosen in hindsight. Ablation studies confirm that our method's components outperform their counterparts in OKS-OMC. Comprehensive evaluations across 11 datasets and seven metrics demonstrate our method's overall superiority over existing online multi-label methods.

title: Multi-path Security in Quantum Networks with Trusted Nodes
authors: Muhammad Kumail Haider, Aeysha Khalique
abstract: Quantum communication networks promise information-theoretic security but this security collapses if intermediate relay nodes are compromised, a risk that grows sharply when compromised nodes cannot be identified. We address this twofold: first, we show that multi-path routing provides quantifiable protection against unidentified compromised nodes. Second, we provide a comprehensive statistical and graph-theoretic analysis of network and node security under compromise, covering full and partial node compromise, optimal placement of additional edges via an iterative method, and comparative hacking-probability analysis across network topologies. Together, these results identify the topology and multi-path routing strategy that most improves security for a given network. We apply this framework to quantum key distribution across multiple network topologies, demonstrating a scalable route to secure, reliable quantum communication under realistic, unidentified adversarial threats, without relying on quantum memory.

title: Variance-Aware Non-Stationary Bandits:All-Budget Regret Bounds and Adaptation Costs
authors: Xiaojin Zhang
abstract: Low reward variance reduces estimation cost, but does not eliminate monitoring of arms that may improve while unobserved. We refine the variance--variation tradeoff and characterize how both costs depend on supplied variance and variation budgets in bounded, non-stationary multi-armed bandits. Let $A$ be the number of arms, $T$ the horizon, $B$ a bound on consecutive mean variation excluding the initial vector, and $Q$ a bound on the sum of the largest per-round reward variances. For every admissible pair $Q,B$, the minimax expected dynamic regret is, within a single logarithmic factor, \[ \min\{T,\;A+\sqrt{AQ}+(AQBT)^{1/3} +\sqrt{AT}\min\{B,\sqrt B\}\}. \] The deterministic boundary $Q=0$ is characterized without logarithms. For small positive budgets, a safe calibration phase identifies a common interval containing all future means of surviving arms. Clipping observations to a wider interval reduces the cost of restarting a prior hybrid static-regret algorithm; an original-mean analytical reference controls its residuals without charging the variation of clipped means. Balancing clipping bias and monitoring closes the small-budget noisy regime. Fixed oblivious constructions give the matching lower bound. We also quantify adaptation costs: on a disclosed deterministic one-improvement family, a stationary-regret budget has a matching worst-case change-regret frontier, including a finite improvement pulse. This implies an $Ω((T/A)^{1/4})$ loss when one policy competes with all supplied-budget deterministic oracle rates. The budget-free low-noise scheduling problem remains separate.

title: Dunnett's and Tukey's procedures under mixed model covariance structures: dimensional reduction of multivariate-t integrals
authors: Dmytro Ivanchenko, Rostyslav Yamnenko
abstract: Dunnett's test compares several treatments with one control, and Tukey's test compares every pair for independent samples with a common variance. We investigate which designs and covariances for a linear mixed model remain on the ordinary Dunnett and Tukey integrals, and in which direction the constants move when the correlation changes. It is shown that for Dunnett's procedure AR(1), the Toeplitz band, alternating ante-dependence, and the random slope have roots below the ordinary analysis-of-variance value, while heterogeneous compound symmetry and heteroscedastic groups have roots above that value. For Tukey's procedure every computed non-spherical covariance lowers the root. The second goal is the dimensional reduction of these multivariate-t integrals: a normal probability mixed over one chi-square scale. Conditioning on the latent variables shared by the contrasts replaces that probability by a product of univariate normals, and the integral has the dimension of the conditioning vector plus one. Balanced compound symmetry leaves a double integral. The studentized range reduces to the Pearson-Hartley integral. The reduction stops for asymmetric overlap of four or more treatments, for four or more autoregressive or unstructured follow-up times, for pair-dependent variances or correlated disjoint pairs, and for a separate variance estimate in each group.

title: Full-horizon magnetic control of the Vlasov--Poisson system for plasma confinement
authors: Giacomo Albi, Giacomo Dimarco, Federica Ferrarese, Lorenzo Pareschi
abstract: We study the full-horizon control of a two-dimensional Vlasov--Poisson system through an externally imposed magnetic field. The control is represented by time-dependent coefficients associated with smooth, spatially localized basis functions, and is designed to steer selected position and velocity moments of the distribution function while limiting particle dispersion and the control effort. Starting from the kinetic constrained optimization problem, we derive the continuous first-order optimality conditions, including a backward Vlasov equation, an elliptic adjoint equation, and the variational inequality associated with bounded controls. We then project this system onto a particle--grid representation and identify the resulting particle adjoints and control gradient. The full-horizon field is then computed on a reduced particle ensemble, initialized by an instantaneous control, and subsequently applied to a larger set of particles. Numerical experiments indicate that the instantaneous control field already provides an effective baseline, while the full-horizon correction can further reduce the relative thermal energy near the boundaries and improve confinement over the prescribed time interval.

title: An $8+9$ gluing computation for the Ramsey number $R(F_3,F_4)$
authors: Hanxin Jiang, Zehui Shao
abstract: Let $F_t$ be the graph consisting of $t$ triangles with a common vertex and otherwise disjoint vertices. We prove that $R(F_3,F_4)=17$ using an $8+9$ gluing computation. Neighbourhood matching arguments give degree and clique restrictions that reduce the search on seventeen vertices to $88,294,674$ ordered seed pairs. The verified main computation excludes $88,294,634$ pairs. A cross-edge counting argument excludes thirty-four of the forty exceptional pairs, and independently checked finite-domain certificates exclude the remaining six. Together with the construction whose red graph is the complete bipartite graph $K_{8,8}$, these results establish $R(F_3,F_4)=17$.

title: Learning from a Bandit Learner
authors: Michela Petriconi, Nicolas Menet, Claire Vernade
abstract: Classical inverse bandit methods typically aim to recover true reward parameters. In contrast, we infer a demonstrator's subjective beliefs, specifically its internal estimates of suboptimality gaps. We consider no-regret demonstrators that follow randomized policies, such as Thompson sampling, and characterize a family of algorithms for which per-step inversion is possible. This enables gap estimates to be recovered directly from the arm-selection distribution. Our analysis identifies an inherent stability-coverage trade-off: inversion becomes ill-conditioned as the demonstrator concentrates its probability mass on a single arm, while the number of informative rounds depends on the rate at which its policy converges. We establish conditions under which inversion is reliable and provide theoretical guarantees on the resulting estimation error. Experiments on simulated data support the analysis and illustrate how these conditions affect gap recovery in practice.

title: Provable Adversarial Detection: Prime Quantization meets Gromov--Wasserstein
authors: Manohar Kaul, Sadbhavana Babar, Aditya Ramesh, Aditya Saibewar, Fumiyoshi Kasahara, Maki Inui, Hiroaki Kurihara
abstract: Adversarial vulnerability persists across modern vision architectures from CNNs to vision language models (VLMs), yet existing detection methods rely on heuristics without theoretical guarantees. We address the fundamental question of when adversarial perturbations can be provably detected from a geometric perspective. Our key insight is that adversarial perturbations cannot simultaneously preserve geometric structure across spaces with fundamentally different properties. Accordingly, we construct two such complementary metric spaces. First, we use a standard CNN embedding space $Z$, where adversarial samples exhibit significant displacement patterns. Second, we build a novel prime-quantized space $P$, that absorbs small perturbations through number-theoretic discretization, resulting in minimal displacement, while preserving discriminability. We then leverage the geometric discrepancies across spaces $Z$ and $P$ to detect adversarial samples. To the best of our knowledge, we establish the first rigorous separation theory for adversarial detection, proving that adversarial samples create unavoidable geometric inconsistencies across both spaces. Our framework provides theoretical guarantees including pixel-level absorption bounds, neighborhood diameter concentration, Gromov-Wasserstein (GW) separation theorems, and practical risk control. Extensive experiments validate our theoretical predictions and achieve consistently strong detection performance across a wide range of attack types and model families.

title: Distributing Quantum Circuits Using Pre-Distributed Entanglement Pairs over Quantum Networks
authors: Yukun Yang, Ranjani G. Sundaram, Himanshu Gupta
abstract: Distributing quantum circuits across a network of quantum devices is a recent approach to improve the scalability of quantum computation. Entangled pairs of qubits distributed across network nodes are used as a communication resource for executing inter-node (remote) gates. However, establishing these entanglement pairs incurs significant latency, and doing so during the circuit's execution may lead to the decoherence of logical qubits. Instead, it may be beneficial to distribute certain entanglement pairs before the circuit is executed. Thus, we consider the problem of distributing a quantum circuit across a quantum network containing some pre-distributed entanglement pairs and seek to minimize the execution time of the circuit. We address this problem in three steps. First, given the quantum network and (optionally) a probability distribution over training circuits, we determine a set of pre-distributed entanglement pairs under a specified budget. Second, we compute a qubit-to-memory allocation that minimizes the expected execution time given these pre-distributed resources. Finally, we identify any additional entanglement pairs required during execution, generate them concurrently, and execute the circuit gates. We evaluate our methods on a broad range of benchmark circuits.

title: From Code to Playable Systems: CEGame-Bench for Long-Horizon Game Creation Agents
authors: Zixuan Dong, Yanghai Wang, Hanyan Bian, Jiaxi Tao, Junze Li, Jiadong Wang, Xinyu Che, Lin Liu, Baoyun Peng, Xiaodong Wang, Jiaheng Liu
abstract: A game ships when a player can launch it, finish it, and return to a saved world, none of which a successful build guarantees, yet game-creation agents are mostly tested on one engine or on one-prompt browser games. We present CEGame-Bench, the first long-horizon benchmark for complete-game creation across five production engines: Defold, Godot, Roblox Studio, Unity, and Unreal Engine. Agents build each game from an empty project and a design document in runs averaging up to 295 steps and 65M tokens; the document doubles as a contract, and a hidden evaluator accepts a game only by real-input play. Under four scaffolds, agents earn most integration points but usually under half the gameplay points, and their games reach the ending in only 16% of runs, while references built by engineers with coding agents score near the maximum, which places this artifact-to-play gap in the agents. No two engines rank configurations alike (Kendall's tau 0.14-0.62), and the same game usually scores higher on Unity and Unreal Engine, which check more before play. We release Game Completion Boost, an agent skill for requirement-driven playtesting and repair that raises the execution-based score of three models by 14.1-24.3 points.

title: PnP-Transformer: A Neural Pose Solver for 6D Object Pose Estimation
authors: Emirkan Burak Yilmaz, Yakup Genc
abstract: We present PnP-Transformer, a neural pose solver designed as an iterative-free, differentiable alternative to classical PnP-RANSAC algorithms. PnP-Transformer regresses the 6D object pose by processing predicted semi-dense 2D-3D correspondence fields alongside confidence scores, while mapping geometric inputs into a continuous latent space. To evaluate its practical utility, we integrate PnP-Transformer into a zero-shot 6D pose estimation pipeline, where the correspondence module and pose solver are trained separately. PnP-Transformer achieves a 41.2% mean AR score with low latency (0.46 s/obj) on seven core BOP benchmark datasets, surpassing all prior baselines (such as RayPose with 39.1% AR) but one (Co-op with 58.4% AR). When the pose solver is replaced with EPnP-RANSAC (similar to Co-op) while keeping the correspondence module unchanged, the RANSAC alternative outperforms PnP-Transformer on six of the seven datasets by reaching 52.2% mean AR at a cost of an additional 60 ms per object, revealing an accuracy-latency trade-off. Code and pretrained models are available: https://github.com/ebylmz/pnp-transformer

title: LeakBench: Auditing Reward Hacking through Prediction-Time Leakage in Clinical Modeling Agents
authors: Xiaoyuan Bao, Jingsi Jiang, Jiao Shan, Yulong Cao, Haoyu Wang, Zida Liu, Jun Gao
abstract: Autonomous clinical-modeling agents can optimize predictive performance while violating conditions that make a model usable. We introduce LeakBench, an executable, guideline-derived audit suite that tests agent decisions for prediction-time leakage, calibration, site-level evaluation, support awareness, and decision-curve net benefit. LeakBench combines a synthetic task with known failure structure and two real-data settings: MIMIC-IV (430k admissions) and governed multi-hospital inpatient record front-page (MHFP) data. Our primary analysis uses reward hacking descriptively, without attributing intent: an agent selects prediction-time-invalid inputs because they improve its validation reward. A deterministic optimizer and every evaluated unconstrained local-model configuration select a fatal leaking feature. In fully logged September 2026 A/B runs, DeepSeek Flash and GPT-6-astra each leak in 10/10 unconstrained runs and 0/10 runs with an explicit admission-time constraint. This contrast is version-sensitive: a blinded Claude/Fable-5.1 chat run does not leak in either condition, while explicit-constraint violations appear only in a historical August 2026 slice lacking raw trajectories. Replacing AUROC with AUPRC does not remove leakage selection. Renaming or disguising the leaking inputs changes neither selection nor provenance-based detection; a name-based filter fails. A deterministic provenance verifier-in-loop removes the leak, making the LLM repair loop defense-in-depth. Specific verifier feedback clears fatal leakage in a hosted agent, and a three-seed ablation finds principle-only feedback clears decision-level defects, though these mitigation results are limited. LeakBench treats trustworthy clinical prediction as a property of an agent's modeling process, not merely its score; it is an audit testbed with known-failure controls, not yet an expert-validated benchmark.

title: Context-Aware Topological Distillation Graph Network for Asymmetric EEG-Eye Movement Emotion Recognition
authors: Peijun Shi, Xiujin Zhu, Zhenguo Lao, Chee-Onn Chow, Wei Ru Wong, Zhen Liu, Xiaobing Jiang
abstract: EEG-eye movement emotion recognition can support mental-health monitoring and adaptive interfaces, but most fusion models treat the two signals as parallel features, classify each window alone and degrade when eye data are lost. We propose the Context-Aware Topological Distillation Graph Network (CTD-GNet), in which EEG features form the nodes of an electrode graph, and eye movements and preceding windows modulate its edges, nodes and readout, the edges through electrode-specific prompts. Bidirectional distillation of the graph, node relations and predictions couples this multimodal teacher with a single-window EEG student, improving the teacher and aligning the two graphs 35-fold. In leave-one-subject-out tests on SEED and SEED-IV against 17 baselines, CTD-GNet has the highest mean accuracy, 84.91% and 76.17%, significantly above 9 and 6 of 13 eye-based baselines after Holm correction, the smallest cross-subject spread among multimodal models and the highest worst-subject accuracy. It is the most accurate model at every rate of missing eye data on SEED-IV, keeps 66.1% on SEED without eye data, more than any EEG-only model, and stays 9.3 and 11.9 points above all single-window fusion models under eye-movement noise of one standard deviation. On film clips unseen in training, it leads on SEED with 77.1%.

title: DCR-TSF: Dual-Level Compositional Reasoning with Triadic Spherical Fusion for Training-Free Zero-Shot Composed Image Retrieval
authors: Gwang-Ho Na, Ho-Joong Kim, Seong-Whan Lee
abstract: Zero-shot composed image retrieval (ZS-CIR) aims to retrieve a target image that reflects an intended textual modification while maintaining semantic consistency with a reference image. Existing training-free ZS-CIR methods typically rely on fine-grained generated target descriptions, which often overemphasize reference-specific visual details and lead to appearance-biased retrieval. Moreover, since these descriptions are generated through multimodal large language models (MLLMs), the direct influence of the original image-text query can be weakened in the final retrieval representation. In this paper, we propose DCR-TSF, a training-free ZS-CIR framework that combines Dual-level Compositional Reasoning (DCR) and Triadic Spherical Fusion (TSF). DCR generates fine- and coarse-grained descriptions from the reference image and modification text, capturing complementary target-side semantics across different granularities. To preserve the original image-text query information, TSF constructs a composed-query anchor by spherically interpolating the reference image feature and modification text feature, and fuses it with the fine- and coarse-grained representations using a weighted Karcher mean on the unit hypersphere. The resulting final query representation balances detailed visual evidence, high-level semantic abstraction, and direct preservation of the original composed query. Extensive experiments on CIRCO, CIRR, and Fashion-IQ demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance among training-free methods.

title: Risk Decomposition for Hallucination-Aware Video Sampling
authors: Chenyan Zheng, Fan Wu, Ruibo Li, Jiaxing Li, Minghao Yang, Bang Zhang, Guosheng Lin
abstract: Despite achieving high visual fidelity, video models still suffer from physical hallucinations, limiting their reliability as world simulators. Existing methods leverage model-internal or external signals to improve physical plausibility, but their roles and limitations require a unified explanation. We propose a two-dimensional physical-hallucination risk framework that defines low-density sampling risk and high-density drifting risk. The first risk captures generations assigned low likelihood by the video model, for example, a ball suddenly teleporting despite the model favoring continuous motion, while the second risk captures physical inconsistencies in high-likelihood generations, for example, a ball bouncing progressively higher without additional energy. Our analysis explains how model-internal signals steer sampling toward higher-density regions of the learned distribution to address low-density sampling risk. However, higher model likelihood does not guarantee physical plausibility, motivating external guidance to address high-density drifting risk. Based on this framework, we develop Hallucination-Aware Sampler (HA-Sampler), which applies external physical guidance within latent refinement to generate physically plausible videos, and HA-Scorer, which derives a likelihood-based signal from the generator itself for evaluating generated videos using continuous normalizing flow (CNF), with coarse ODE integration and finite-difference divergence estimates. Experiments on Physics-IQ and VideoPhy benchmarks support our theoretical analysis and demonstrate that our methods outperform the compared sampling and scoring SOTA baselines.

title: On Carmichael Numbers Constructed from Consecutive Jacobsthal Numbers
authors: Hayat Bensella
abstract: We prove that no Carmichael number has the form \[ N=(2^mJ_n+1)(2^mJ_{n+1}+1)(2^mJ_{n+2}+1), \] where \[ J_n=\frac{2^n-(-1)^n}{3} \] is the Jacobsthal sequence, \(m,n\ge1\), and all three factors are prime. Assuming that such an \(N\) is Carmichael, Korselt's criterion yields divisibility conditions relating consecutive Jacobsthal numbers to powers of two. Combining these conditions with the Binet formula and a finite case analysis for \(n\le4\), we obtain a contradiction. Consequently, this family contains no Carmichael numbers.

title: Learning the Dose Manifold: A Latent Diffusion Framework for Volumetric Dose Prediction in Automated Radiotherapy Treatment Planning
authors: J. Boyer-Chammard, R. Vauclin, M. C. Biston, P. Maury, M. Gau, S. Stathakis, V. Grégoire, N. Paragios, E. Deutsch, N. Komodakis
abstract: Automated treatment planning (ATP) aims to reduce the unwarranted inter-planner variability of manual planning, while improving treatment quality and efficiency. Most ATP pipelines rely on the prediction of the achievable three-dimensional dose distribution for a given anatomy and the subsequent optimization of machine parameters to reproduce it. Diffusion-based methods are largely slice-wise due to the high dimensionality of radiotherapy data, and assume a one-to-one mapping between anatomy and optimal dose despite the multi-objective nature of treatment planning. They are evaluated on their ability to match reference doses and rarely on their integration in ATP frameworks. We present LaDose, a latent diffusion framework for fully volumetric dose prediction. An autoencoder learned on dose distributions, trained so that perturbed latents decode to plausible doses, compresses dose maps 128-fold and enables 3D diffusion on a single GPU. Prescription values are represented as exact scalar vectors that bypass the image encoder, avoiding resampling and latent compression. Multiscale classifier-free guidance allows for the modulation of clinical trade-offs at inference, without retraining or additional labeled data. On 900 clinically delivered head-and-neck volumetric modulated arc therapy plans from five centers, LaDose reached a median absolute error of 1.18 Gy (1.4--1.8\% of the prescription) and was the only one of six frameworks free of systematic bias with respect to the reference distribution. Guidance scales acted predictably on target coverage and organ-at-risk sparing. Integrated with direct aperture optimization, the pipeline generated plans in 15.2 minutes; in a blinded review, senior clinicians rated 14 of 15 plans acceptable without editing.

title: Single-graph rational exponents in mixed multicolour Ramsey theory
authors: Yuang Yang
abstract: For every rational number $γ>1$, we construct a fixed bipartite graph $H_γ$ such that $r_k(H_γ;K_N)=Θ_{γ,k}((N/\log N)^γ)$ for every fixed $k\ge 3$. Here $r_k(H;K_N)=r(H,\ldots,H,K_N)$, with $k$ copies of $H$. The lower bound uses a symmetric random algebraic graph which avoids a fixed rooted power and has sufficiently strong local density for the Alon-Rodl method. The main algebraic step establishes a nonzero obstruction within the full symmetric coefficient space; the upper bound uses the rooted graphs from the proof of the rational exponents conjecture. We also obtain induced even-cycle asymptotics in the same construction.

title: A 36.34-day Sub-Neptune Candidate Transiting the Nearby K Dwarf TIC 402710280
authors: Rishit Vora
abstract: We report a transiting sub-Neptune candidate with a period of 36.34 days around TIC 402710280 (TYC 9041-03677-1), a K dwarf of TESS magnitude 9.24 at 66.8 pc that the Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite (TESS) has observed only in full-frame images. Four transits, recorded between 2021 and 2026 in Sectors 39, 93, 100 and 102 and reduced by three independent pipelines, share a depth of $2092 \pm 47$ ppm and a duration of $5.27 \pm 0.05$ h. Two of them fall on consecutive cycles, and every shorter period predicts transits in covered data that are absent at $\geq 18.6σ$; the period is $P = 36.33986 \pm 0.00051$ d. A transit model gives $R_p/R_\star = 0.0421^{+0.0007}_{-0.0005}$ and a stellar density consistent with the host's. The candidate has a radius of $3.75 \pm 0.22 R_\oplus$ and an equilibrium temperature of $498 \pm 21$ K. Difference-image centroids place the signal $1.5'' \pm 1.3''$ from the target. The only catalogued star close enough to contribute, a background star $3.5''$ away, would have to host an eclipsing binary whose eclipse shape is disfavoured for any main-sequence pair ($Δχ^2 \geq 142$). No secondary eclipse is detected, and TRICERATOPS gives a false-positive probability of $0.003 \pm 0.004$. No high-resolution imaging exists, so companions within about $1''$ are constrained only by Gaia astrometry. The mid-times scatter about a linear ephemeris by 21.8 min (rms). Quick-Look Pipeline light curves reproduce the 29-min excess in the interval between the two 2026 transits, so it does not arise in our photometry; we report the scatter without choosing between an instrumental and a dynamical origin. The light curve also contains a $407 \pm 26$ ppm signal with a period of 3.78 days whose source, the target or the background star, the present data cannot identify. We predict transit times, including one in TESS Sector 114 on 2027 February 19.

title: New Maximum Hermitian $d$-Codes and New Invariants from Skew Polynomial Rings
authors: Paolo Santonastaso, Yue Zhou
abstract: Maximum rank-distance codes were introduced independently by Delsarte (1978) and Gabidulin (1985) for unrestricted matrix spaces, and their study was subsequently extended to the classical form spaces of alternating, symmetric, and Hermitian matrices. For Hermitian $d$-codes, Schmidt (2018) established the upper bound and constructed optimal additive codes for all admissible parameters except when $n$ and $d$ are both even and $4\le d\le n-2$. We settle this final open existence case, more generally, construct additive maximum Hermitian rank-metric codes for every admissible length and minimum distance. Rather than working directly in the space of Hermitian matrices, we construct our objects within central simple algebras with unitary involution arising from quotients of skew polynomial rings. We also introduce scalar-field and Lyapunov operators in these algebras, leading to new invariants for the equivalence of additive Hermitian codes. Explicitly determining these invariants yields strong necessary conditions for Hermitian equivalence and demonstrates that our construction contains a large number of pairwise inequivalent codes.

title: Compactness and weak compactness of linearized Holomorphic-Lipschitz maps
authors: Frédéric Bayart, Mathis Lemay, Colin Petitjean
abstract: Any holomorphic Lipschitz map $f$, defined on the open unit ball $B_X$ of a complex Banach space $X$ and taking values in a complex Banach space $Y$, can be uniquely and canonically associated with a bounded linear operator $\widehat f : \mathcal G_0(B_X) \longrightarrow \mathcal G_0(Y)$ between the corresponding holomorphic Lipschitz-free spaces. The aim of this paper is to establish necessary and sufficient conditions for the compactness and weak compactness of such operators. In particular, we obtain a general characterisation of the compactness of $\widehat f$ in terms of metric properties of its symbol $f$. We then focus on the case where the target space is a subspace of $\ell_p$, $1\leq p<\infty$. When the target space is $\ell_1$, we show that compactness and weak compactness of $\widehat f$ are both equivalent to $\widehat f$ not fixing a copy of $\ell_1$. Finally, when the target space is $\ell_p$ with $1<p<\infty$, we obtain a metric characterisation of the weak compactness of $\widehat f$. As a consequence, we show that compactness and weak compactness need not coincide, even when the target space is $\ell_p$.

title: After the Federation: Benchmarking Knowledge Portability to Heterogeneous Newcomers
authors: Xinyuan Zhao
abstract: Once historical clients become unavailable, a federation must serve newcomers through the artifact it leaves behind. How much of its knowledge remains useful in an architecture chosen afterward? We introduce FEDNBO, a seven-dataset benchmark that separates knowledge supply, policy identification, and private-model compilation under disjoint data roles. Controlled studies expose inflated oracle gains, architecture-dependent transfer reversals, and a gap between teacher accuracy and private-model utility. Ordinary public-response distillation provides a competitive reference without public task labels or newcomer samples: gains over strengthened local training are 23.52 and 16.62 percentage points on 300 CelebA identities and 300 FedEMNIST writers, respectively. In a complete-pipeline FedEMNIST comparison, this reference reaches 97.13% accuracy with 12.4 seconds of compilation per architecture, versus 97.03% and 67.5 seconds for a HeteroFedTTA reconstruction at the same epoch budget. Equal-count public-input interventions extend support sensitivity to trainable visual backbones. Together, these results establish an auditable benchmark and a strong reference for evaluating the utility, cost and reliability of post-federation knowledge transfer.

title: Multimodal Decoupling for Diversified Recommendation through Semantic and Structural Shaping
authors: Changran He, Jiaming Wei, Jianghong Ma, Tianjun Wei, Haijun Zhang, Xiaofeng Zhang
abstract: Recommender systems often suffer from over-concentrated results when optimized for accuracy, limiting recommendation diversity. While diversity has become an important objective, existing methods still face fundamental limitations from both semantic and structural perspectives. On the one hand, multimodal recommender systems provide rich semantic signals, yet are often treated as auxiliary to ID embeddings, leading to ineffective semantic utilization for diversity. On the other hand, the accuracy--diversity trade-off persists during training, where accuracy gains often come at the cost of diversity. We show that this phenomenon is fundamentally governed by both the structural properties of learned representations and the dynamics of optimization. To address these challenges, we propose MOSS, a unified framework for multimodal decoupling through semantic and structural shaping. Specifically, we first introduce an MLLM-based Decoupled Feature Extraction module to disentangle multimodal content into informative representations. To enhance semantic utilization, we design a Category-aware Embedding Selection module that extracts compact, category-aware semantic features. To address structural limitations, we propose two complementary modules: Alternating Dual-Graph Propagation, which alleviates representation collapse by integrating collaborative and multimodal propagation, and Entropy-based Diversity Regularization, which mitigates optimization bias by promoting balanced category exposure. Extensive experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate that MOSS consistently achieves a superior accuracy--diversity trade-off over strong baselines.

title: Scenario Generalization and Sector Transfer in Real Surface Irrigation Surrogate Modelling with Tabular Models
authors: Alessandro Cagiano, M. Aybars Seyhan, Fabiola Gangi, Matteo Zignani, Daniele Masseroni
abstract: Surface irrigation planning requires screening many operating conditions and spatial configurations, while high-fidelity shallow-water-equation (SWE) simulations are expensive. We study tabular surrogate models for predicting maximum water height from drone-derived field morphology, terrain, hydrological, spatial, and scenario descriptors, where each row represents a spatial cell under one irrigation scenario. To assess deployment feasibility, we evaluate gradient-boosted trees, neural tabular models, AutoML, and tabular foundation models (TFMs) under two regimes: same-sector generalization, where a model predicts unseen scenarios after observing a limited set of configurations in the same sector, and sector-out transfer, where knowledge learned from source sectors is transferred to an unseen sector. The main findings are twofold: a) under the evaluated fixed 8/32 same-sector split, surrogates achieve strong performance, especially with raw spatial coordinates; b) sector-out transfer is substantially harder because the target sector has different coordinates and geometry. Sector-frame normalization of spatial coordinates improves transfer across similarly structured sectors, but does not solve cross-shape generalization. Overall, tabular surrogates appear useful for same-sector scenario screening under this fixed split, while robust transfer to unseen sectors remains open.

title: Map-Distribution Mixture-of-Experts for Multi-Agent Pathfinding
authors: Fumimaro Suzuki, Keisuke Okumura
abstract: Designing capable neural policies for multi-agent pathfinding (MAPF), which map local observations to action distributions, represents an important challenge in multi-agent learning, with practical relevance to scalable collective automation problems such as warehouse logistics. In contrast to prior studies focusing primarily on individual policy design, this study explores a meta-level Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) approach to learning-based MAPF. Specifically, given a collection of compact yet high-performing experts specialised for different map distributions, our architecture learns a router that selectively fuses their outputs according to each agent's local situation. We instantiate and validate this MoE approach with a commonly used graph neural network-based policy as well as a newly developed recursive action-token refinement model. Combined with supervised and reinforcement learning fine-tuning of the experts, our experiments show that MoE generally improves upon the pretrained policy and outperforms existing leading methods. At the same time, our findings reveal that appropriately trained, parameter-matched monolithic models still outperform MoE, highlighting a nuanced role for map-distribution MoE for MAPF.

title: On Higher-Form Fracton Hydrodynamics with Momentum Conservation
authors: Ben Bobell, Rahul Nandkishore, Andrew Lucas
abstract: Momentum conservation is common in fluids, yet it may be incompatible with the hydrodynamics of theories with exotic conservation laws (such as fracton hydrodynamics) unless symmetries are spontaneously broken. Using the Martin-Siggia-Rose (MSR) effective field theory formalism, we develop a representation-theoretic framework for the hydrodynamics of translationally invariant systems with exotic conservation laws without spontaneous symmetry breaking. Under mild assumptions on the form of hydrodynamics, we show that such theories must satisfy two representation theoretic consistency conditions and a generalized Gauss's law constraint. Higher-form symmetries satisfy these conditions and we derive their ideal hydrodynamics; in three dimensions, the one-form case produces ideal non-relativistic magnetohydrodynamics. Finally, we prove that no other theories are compatible with momentum conservation in SO(3) nor SO($d$), for sufficiently large odd $d$.

title: VideoMaMa++: Temporally Consistent Video Matting via Preserve-and-Refine Token
authors: Sangbeom Lim, Seoung Wug Oh, Heeji Yoon, Seungryong Kim, Joon-Young Lee
abstract: Diffusion-based video matting has recently emerged as a leading approach, leveraging video diffusion priors from internet-scale pretraining to achieve strong zero-shot generalization from limited synthetic data. However, the heavy compute of these diffusion backbones limits inference to a short chunk of just 6 to 24 frames, so even ordinary videos span multiple chunks. Because each chunk is matted independently from coarse mask guidance, existing methods fail to maintain consistency across chunk boundaries, producing flickering edges and discontinuous transparency. We address this with a mask-guided diffusion-matting framework built on two ideas. The RGB and mask conditioning are represented as separate token streams that interact through full spatio-temporal self-attention, letting the model adaptively combine fine RGB texture with coarse mask layout rather than committing to a fixed channel-wise fusion. On top of this, we propose a novel pair of learnable embeddings, the preserve token and the refine token, that act as a per-frame conditioning interface and enable a sliding-window inference scheme in which already-generated mattes are propagated across chunk boundaries for local temporal consistency, complemented by a globally shared reference anchor at every chunk to prevent error accumulation in long sequences without any additional training. Across standard video matting benchmarks and in-the-wild long footage, our framework outperforms prior diffusion-based methods in both fine-detail accuracy and temporal consistency, and uniquely maintains consistency across chunk boundaries on long videos.

title: Manga2Animate: An Agentic Framework for Faithful Manga Animation with Script and Storyboard Planning
authors: Sheng-Wei Zhang, Hsi-An Chen, Yan-Ting Liou, Chih-Hsuan Chen, Shih-Chen Tseng, Yu-Lun Liu
abstract: Adapting existing manga into coherent animation that stays faithful to the source is a valuable yet challenging task. Existing methods either access the manga mainly through text, losing its characters and art style, or feed manga pages directly into video generation models, which misinterpret the manga's structure and produce incorrect storylines. In this paper, we propose Manga2Animate, a multi-agent framework that grounds every stage of generation in the source manga. We decompose the task into two intermediate representations, an animation script and a visual storyboard. Each representation is produced by a creator agent and reviewed against the source panels by a paired reviewer agent. We tailor representation-specific selection and dual-level feedback to progressively refine both before synthesizing the final animation. Extensive experiments and a user study demonstrate that Manga2Animate produces animations more faithful to the source manga and more consistent across shots than state-of-the-art approaches. Project page: https://annchenn.github.io/Manga2Animate/

title: Train An Imaginative Agent
authors: Jiaxin Ge, Junyi Zhang, Tianning Chai, Hanjun Yoo, Chenyang Wang, Xiuyu Li, Weijia Shi, XuDong Wang, Sewon Min, Luke Zettlemoyer, Trevor Darrell, Haiwen Feng
abstract: A seemingly reasonable push in Sokoban can make the puzzle unsolvable. To avoid such mistakes, an agent has to anticipate the consequences of its actions before execution, especially when feedback from the real environment is sparse or actions are irreversible. We introduce Agentic Imagination (Agima), a training framework that trains an agent to imagine before acting, i.e. to be imaginative. Agima trains a single omni model to propose actions, generate images of their outcomes, and then reason over these imagined futures to decide what to execute in the real environment. Rather than committing to a single plan, the agent can simulate a sequence of actions, explore alternatives, and compare possible futures. We first use supervised fine-tuning (SFT) to unify policy and world modeling within a single omni model. This enables the agent to predict future outcomes and perform basic forms of imagination, such as forward thinking and counterfactual branching. We then use agentic reinforcement learning (RL) to teach the agent to reason with its imagined futures and use them effectively for planning. Across four environments spanning Maze2D, Sokoban, Pacman, and PushT, Agima generalizes to harder settings unseen during training. Trained with SFT alone on two-box Sokoban, Agima solves 40% of four-box puzzles while seeing the real board only once every five moves, compared with an action-only planner that only solves 2%. After RL, new behaviors emerge in how Agima uses its imagination: it learns a new unified format that was unseen during the SFT stage, learns to conduct forward thinking only when necessary, and branches more frequently at critical decision points. An agent that can picture where its actions lead can learn when and where to look ahead, that is, to plan. Project page: https://agima.net/.

title: SpecKCast: Spectral Kalman Forecasting for Diffusion Acceleration
authors: Javad Rajabi, Hakki Can Karaimer, David B. Lindell, Babak Taati, Michael S. Brown
abstract: Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) achieve high-fidelity image and video generation, but they suffer from substantial inference costs due to repeated transformer evaluations across many denoising steps. Feature caching reduces this cost by reusing features across denoising steps. Recent forecasting methods extend this idea by extrapolating features to skipped steps instead of reusing them. However, existing forecasting methods extrapolate the features they predict uniformly, even though the spatial-frequency components of these features change most at different stages of denoising. They also overlook that denoising progresses nonuniformly, so equal step intervals can correspond to very different amounts of change. These mismatches amplify forecast errors as more steps are skipped, limiting the achievable acceleration. We propose SpecKCast, a training-free method that forecasts the model output in the frequency domain. SpecKCast applies a 2D discrete cosine transform (DCT) to the output and tracks each coefficient with a lightweight Kalman filter along a band-specific time coordinate derived from the noise schedule. The filter tracks each coefficient's value and rate of change, and the transformer is evaluated only when the filter's forecast uncertainty exceeds a threshold. Experiments on FLUX.1-dev, Qwen-Image, Wan2.1-14B, and HunyuanVideo show that SpecKCast achieves a better trade-off between acceleration and fidelity than existing caching and forecasting methods, reaching up to 6x speedup with less than 0.05 GiB of additional memory.

title: ASTOR: Benchmarking and Improving Autoformulation for Soft-Constraint Optimization with a Formal Grammar
authors: Amer Goel, Yeganeh Alimohammadi, Andrew Daw
abstract: Real-world decision problems combine two qualitatively different kinds of constraints: requirements that must be satisfied, called hard constraints, and preferences that can be violated, called soft constraints. Because these problems are often posed to decision-makers in natural language, large language models offer a natural tool for assisting with their solution. This has given rise to autoformulation, which focuses on using LLMs to translate natural-language descriptions of decision problems into executable mathematical optimization models. However, this research often neglects soft constraints like those proposed by consumers, managers, and planners, despite the fact that many practical problems require modeling them explicitly. We introduce ASTOR, an inference-time framework that maps a natural-language decision problem to a grammar-guided abstract syntax tree (AST) before deterministically compiling the resulting representation into executable optimization code. We also introduce SoftOR, a unified benchmark of natural language problems which focuses on soft constraint formulations. On SoftOR, ASTOR achieves the best aggregate accuracy among comparable single-request and multi-agent LLM methods while remaining competitive on standard autoformulation benchmarks that include only hard constraints. Code and data are available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/astor-softor-iclr-E34C/README.md.

title: State World Models: Execute the Rules, Generate the Pixels
authors: Chan Yan Ki, Yanran Zhang, Wenzhao Zheng, Xiaofeng Wang, Zheng Zhu, Lei Chen, Jie Zhou, Jiwen Lu
abstract: Existing world models can generate action-conditioned video from a single image. Many focus on camera movement, allowing users to explore the generated scene. However, navigation alone does not ensure that an action follows persistent rules when its outcome depends on state that is invisible in the current frame. We present Stateful Harness, a framework that separates world evolution from video rendering to support stateful and rule-governed interaction. It maintains an evolving world state under specified rules, renders each resulting event with a frozen video model, and uses the generated clip to update the world state for the next turn. At each turn, the harness resolves the action selected by the user and compiles the resulting event into an instruction, while a preview clip from an editable 3D scene provides spatial and camera guidance. To evaluate rule compliance, we build WorldState-Bench, a benchmark of 50 counterfactual twin pairs that share an initial frame and action but differ in hidden state and required outcome. Under rule-only prompting, the best of the 11 evaluated video backends produces the required endings for both cases in 32% of pairs. For MiniMax-H3, specifying the required endings raises this rate from 32% to 64%, while the full harness reaches 92% with the same frozen model. These results support separating rule execution from video rendering for world interactions with hidden state.

title: Bio-inspired Thrust-Assisted Trotting on a legged-Aerial Robot via Real-Time QP-MPC
authors: Shreyansh Pitroda, Eric Sihite, Alireza Ramezani, Morteza Gharib
abstract: This paper presents the hardware implementation of a quadratic program-based controller on Harpy: thruster-assisted bipedal robot to perform thruster-assisted trotting. This is inspired by wing-assisted locomotion observed in birds such as the chukar partridge, which employ thrust vectoring to manipulate the ground reaction force. The proposed controller formulates the thruster-assisted spring-loaded inverted pendulum dynamics as a condensed QP-based model predictive control problem, enabling simultaneous regulation of ground contact force and active thrust vectoring at 500 Hz. A decoupled control architecture is used, where the robot's sagittal dynamics are controlled using QP-MPC while the frontal dynamics is regulated using a cascade orientation stabilization controller. Two experiments were conducted with different forward reference velocities of 0 m/s and 0.1 m/s. While the instantaneous velocity oscillates, the mean velocities can track their respective reference. Additionally, joint tracking error remains within 1 deg while tracking the desired leg length given by the leg trajectory controller and desired swing trajectory given by Raibert's heuristic. The QP-MPC problem is consistently solved with 0.18ms, which is well within the 2ms computation budget while satisfying the GRF friction cone constraint.

title: High-dimensional covariate-assisted ranking
authors: Yujia Liu, Yuanyuan Lin, Ruijian Han, Yiming Xu
abstract: Ranking data in modern applications often involves covariate vectors whose dimension grows with the number of objects. Identifying relevant covariates and integrating them with item-specific utilities can yield better predictive performance. In this work, we study a Plackett--Luce model that incorporates both item-specific utilities and high-dimensional covariate effects. Under a sparsity assumption on the covariate coefficients, we establish a necessary and sufficient condition for identifiability in terms of the Kruskal rank of the restricted covariate design. We then propose an $\ell_1$-regularized maximum likelihood estimator for the covariate coefficients. Under suitable design and connectivity conditions, we establish the existence and uniqueness of the estimator with probability tending to one, as well as its uniform consistency. With an additional minimum-signal condition, we further establish exact support recovery. Our analysis combines a hypergraph-based chaining technique with a profile-likelihood perturbation analysis, yielding estimation rates that explicitly capture the effects of the comparison hypergraph's connectivity and the underlying sparsity level. Numerical experiments using synthetic data and a horse racing dataset corroborate our theoretical findings.

title: Two hidden layer suffice: the caterpillar net
authors: Jakob Paul Zimmermann
abstract: Every continuous piecewise linear (CPWL) function is a finite signed sum of maxima of affine functions, making maximum representation a central problem in the study of the expressiveness of ReLU networks. A now-disproved conjecture predicted logarithmic depth for maxima. Inspired by the proof by Brunck et al. (2026) that two hidden layers suffice for general CPWL functions, we give the Caterpillar Net, a nonrecursive construction for the maximum of $N$ inputs with two hidden layers of widths $O(N^2)$ and $2^{O(N\log N)}$. The construction has a direct geometric interpretation.

title: Cooperative Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for Market Making on Prediction-Market Order Books
authors: Skander Lejmi
abstract: A market maker provides liquidity by quoting prices to buy and sell an asset, earning the spread while managing inventory risk. We study market makers trained with multi-agent reinforcement learning on prediction markets, specifically Polymarket, whose thin order books pose distinct challenges. Three challenges underpin this research: adverse selection may cause a policy trained on real data to stop quoting; the consequences of a quote can arrive many steps after the action; and prediction-market L2 data does not identify individual orders needed for simulation. We address these challenges by reconstructing order-level LOBSTER-format data from Polymarket and training agents in JaxMARL-HFT on 417 real markets. We enrich the baseline market maker's observation space with the book and recent flow, redesign its actions and inventory controls, and propose a cooperative multi-agent decomposition into a quoter and a risk manager trained using recurrent Independent Proximal Policy Optimisation (IPPO) with RNN policies. We investigate reward shaping, particularly reward blending and post-fill markout, to mitigate credit-assignment difficulties between the agents. Our redesigned single-agent market maker quotes more frequently and incurs smaller held-out losses than the retrained JaxMARL-HFT baseline, although the contributions of jointly changed observations, actions and risk constraints are not separately identified. Decomposition alone performs poorly; careful reward design substantially improves the desk relative to the unshaped split and yields our best result. Models are evaluated on realised end-of-episode portfolio value on held-out markets. None establishes positive average portfolio value in periodic held-out evaluation, and each configuration was trained with one seed. The environment, data and protocol lay a foundation for makers that quote many linked markets at once.

title: Monsoon: Scalable Spontaneous Speech Collection for Low-Resource ASR in 50 Languages
authors: Shobhit Banga, Manas Dhir, Aaditya Pareek, Amritansh Walecha, Bhaskar Singh, Hanuman Sidh, Manmeet Kaur, Sagar Jain, Supriya Paul, Vanshika Chhabra, Utkarsh Singh
abstract: For most languages, automatic speech recognition (ASR) is limited less by model architecture than by a lack of accurately transcribed spontaneous speech. We present Monsoon, a framework for collecting such data at scale. It elicits unscripted conversations between paired contributors, screens recordings with automated classifiers, corrects transcripts over five levels of human review, and selects segments for lexical and acoustic coverage. It has collected speech in 50 languages; we analyse seven 3,500-hour corpora. At equal volume, its quality stages reduce semantic word error rate (WER) by 10-39% relative to a conventional protocol. Compared with an architecture-matched baseline trained on public corpora, Whisper fine-tuned on Monsoon performs comparably on the baseline's own test sets and reduces semantic WER by 20-44 points on conversational benchmarks. The gains transfer to a second architecture and grow with data volume. We release the framework, its quality-control models, and the fine-tuned models.

title: Weights of KZ motives and quantum groups
authors: Prakash Belkale, Najmuddin Fakhruddin
abstract: The Knizhnik--Zamolodchikov (KZ) connection is defined on the constant bundle determined by $n$ finite-dimensional irreducible representations of a simple Lie algebra $\mathfrak{g}$ and a nonzero complex parameter $κ$, over the configuration space of $n$ distinct points on the affine line. Work of Schechtman--Varchenko and Looijenga shows that, when $κ$ is rational, the resulting local systems admit natural motivic realizations, called KZ motives. The Kazhdan--Lusztig equivalence identifies the local systems underlying these motivic variations with certain representations of the pure braid group arising from the corresponding Lusztig quantum group at a root of unity. We formulate conjectures relating the weight filtrations of KZ motives to structures in quantum-group representation theory, particularly tilting modules and the Jantzen and Andersen filtrations, and provide evidence for these conjectures. Our methods use a new deformation of the representation ring that records the first moments of the weight filtration, together with Schmid's theorem on limiting mixed Hodge structures and results on the Hodge filtration obtained in earlier joint work with S. Mukhopadhyay.

title: Small subgraphs of large minimum degree
authors: Zach Hunter, Barnabás Janzer, Oliver Janzer, Benny Sudakov
abstract: In 1991, Erdős, Faudree, Rousseau and Schelp asked to estimate the smallest $u=u(n,d,s)$ such that every $n$-vertex graph with average degree at least $d$ has a subgraph on at most $u$ vertices with minimum degree at least $s$. We resolve this problem up to polylogarithmic factors for all even values of $s$. More precisely, we prove that every $n$-vertex graph with minimum degree $d\geq s$ has a subgraph on $O_s\left(\max\left\{\frac{n}{d^{s/(s-2)}}(\log n)^{180},\log n\right\}\right)$ vertices with minimum degree at least $s$, whenever $s\ge 4$ is even. This improves a result of Janzer, Sudakov and Tomon, who obtained a similar conclusion for subgraphs of average degree at least $s$. We also prove that for every positive integer $s$ and every $\varepsilon>0$, there exists a finite family $\mathcal{H}$ of graphs with minimum degree $s$ such that $\operatorname{ex}(n,\mathcal{H})=O(n^{2-2/s+\varepsilon})$. This is tight and is the first result of similar kind that applies to odd values of $s$ greater than 3.

title: Finite convexification by Minkowski summation
authors: Mark Meyer
abstract: Let $A\subset\mathbb{R}^n$ be a nonempty compact set and let $K\subset\mathbb{R}^n$ be a nonempty compact convex set. We study the problem of when there exists $λ>0$ such that the Minkowski sum $A+λK$ is convex. First, we show that this finite convexification is equivalent to a uniform covering condition on the exposed sets of $A$ and $K$. We then show that another characterization is possible in terms of the covering radii of the iterated exposed sets after translating each exposed face of $K$ so that its relative centroid is $0$. In the case of convex polytopes, we show that it suffices to check the exposed sets in the first level of the iteration. We also study several special cases, such as strictly convex convexifiers, lower-dimensional convexifiers, strongly isomorphic polytopes, and the planar case.

title: Polar Switch: Fast Muon Orthogonalization with Polynomial Circuits
authors: Zhehang Du, Weijie Su
abstract: Muon, a 2024-born optimizer for language models, differs from the 2015-born spectral gradient descent mainly in its fast, GPU-friendly Newton--Schulz polynomial for orthogonalizing the gradient matrix. Accordingly, a line of research proposes faster polynomial iterations for gradient orthogonalization, such as Polar Express and Gram Newton--Schulz, both built on quintic polynomials. In this paper, we introduce Polar Switch, a new approach to polynomial gradient orthogonalization. Using simple polynomial circuits, Polar Switch reaches a given high polynomial degree at a lower FLOP cost than quintic iterations. We define a circuit as a short sequence of symmetric matrix products on a few square buffers, and circuits with $k$ products form a restricted family of odd polynomials of degree up to $2^{k+1}+1$. We choose the sequence of products in each circuit, their coefficients, and how the circuits are composed by numerically minimizing a worst-case bound on the polar approximation error. This minimization is subject to a FLOP budget that accounts for symmetric matrix multiplication kernels and a rounding constraint for numerical stability in half precision. Our two recommended Polar Switch methods have 15.5--18.7\% lower runtime than Polar Express on square matrices and 8.6--16.2\% lower runtime than Gram Newton--Schulz on rectangular matrices with aspect ratios 3.25, 3.5, and 8, with comparable approximation accuracy. In pretraining Modded-NanoGPT \#91, Qwen3-0.6B, and Gemma 3-1B, Polar Switch reaches final validation losses similar to those of established orthogonalization methods. Across the more than 14 million matrices that each of the two recommended methods orthogonalized in these runs, the estimated output spectral norms never exceed the designed bounds by more than 3\%, demonstrating their numerical stability.

title: System Identification for Nonlinear Stochastic State-Space Models Using Ensemble Kalman Inversion with Application to Lithium-Ion Batteries
authors: Farzaneh Barat, Rachel Carter, Sara Wilson, Huijeong Kim, Xinfan Lin, Huazhen Fang
abstract: Nonlinear state-space system identification has attracted decades of interest, yet remains challenging because of the interplay among unknown parameters, nonlinear dynamics, and latent state variables. Its difficulty increases dramatically when the state and parameter dimensions increase. To address this challenge, we develop an ensemble Kalman inversion (EnKI)-based approach. This approach leverages EnKI to perform maximum a posteriori parameter estimation through successive local Gaussian approximations, enabling an iterative and incremental search for unknown parameters. The search combines Monte Carlo sampling with Kalman-type updates to evolve an ensemble of parameter samples, thereby offering empirical stability and the ability to handle strongly nonlinear models. The EnKI search is coupled with state estimation conditioned on the latest parameter estimates. This enables parameter identification along with latent state recovery. To improve scalability for large datasets, we further develop a cascaded EnKI (CasEnKI) method, which assimilates subdatasets sequentially to accelerate computation. We validate the proposed methods using a lithium-ion battery model with ten state variables and 18 unknown parameters. Simulation results show that the EnKI approach offers high identification accuracy and empirical stability in parameter search. Further, experimental results illustrate the computational efficiency and scalability of the CasEnKI method for large battery datasets.

title: The Structure of the Ghost and Swapping Algebras
authors: Caleb Ashley, Ming Hong Tee
abstract: The swapping algebras and the ghost algebras were introduced in the papers of Labourie and Bridgeman--Labourie to encode the Poisson structure on spaces of length functions and generalized cross-ratio functions associated to $Θ$-Anosov representations. They used these algebras to show that correlation functions are stable under the Poisson bracket associated to Atiyah-Bott-Goldman's symplectic form and that length functions are convex along the Hamiltonian flow of other length functions. In this paper, we study the algebraic relationship between these two algebras. In particular, we show that the kernel of a natural surjection from the ghost algebra onto the extended swapping algebra is generated by five families of relations. Consequently, we obtain an isomorphism from an explicit quotient of the ghost algebra onto the extended swapping algebra.

title: Deep Pontryagin Learning for Continuous-Time Stochastic Control with Jumps
authors: Jean-Loup Dupret, Patrick Cheridito
abstract: We develop a deep Pontryagin learning framework for high-dimensional continuous-time stochastic control problems that naturally accommodates jump-diffusions. In contrast to direct policy optimization, which repeatedly differentiates the objective through the entire time-discretized dynamics, our method separates adjoint learning from policy improvement by explicitly incorporating state-sensitivity information from the Pontryagin stochastic maximum principle. For a fixed Markov control, we first compute pathwise adjoint labels by backpropagating the reward through time along simulated state trajectories, and project these labels onto the Markov state through a supervised regression step. The control is then updated by enforcing the pointwise Hamiltonian stationarity condition. We prove that the resulting projected adjoint process satisfies a discrete-time Pontryagin principle and converges, as the time step tends to zero, to the solution of the corresponding continuous-time adjoint backward stochastic differential equation. Numerical experiments illustrate the accuracy, stability, and scalability of the approach.

title: Global Dynamics and Periodic-Annulus Bifurcations in a Reversible Quintic Liénard System
authors: Chen Cao, Nasrin Sadri, Yilei Tang, Zhaoxia Wang
abstract: We study the global dynamics and bifurcations of the reversible quintic Liénard system $\dot{x}=y$, $\dot{y}=a_0x+a_1x^3+a_2x^5+y(b_0x+b_1x^3)$, with $a_2\ne0$. In the original five-parameter space we treat both signs of $a_2$ and determine all global phase-portrait types on the Poincaré disc with one, three, or five finite equilibria. The analysis covers generic and generalized pitchfork, saddle-node, Bogdanov--Takens, and Hopf bifurcations; nilpotent and Hamiltonian degeneracies; bifurcations at infinity; and homoclinic, heteroclinic, limit-cycle-breaking, and periodic-annulus-breaking transitions. For a parameterized class of generalized polynomial Liénard systems whose unique finite equilibrium is the nilpotent origin with exactly one elliptic and one hyperbolic sector we establish a unique critical value of the higher-order damping parameter in the intermediate-degree range, nonexistence of a large-scale periodic annulus in the critical-degree case, and its persistence when the restoring degree dominates. Here large-scale means that the annulus closure meets the boundary of the Poincaré disc. In the degree range relevant to the quintic system the critical value gives a large-scale periodic-annulus--homoclinic-orbit-family bifurcation marked by a unique separatrix connection to infinity.
